But it demonstrated the seriousness with which credentialed scientists could engage with it, and produced a documentary record of what the encounter between shamanic ayahuasca tradition and Western molecular biology actually looked like when it happened.

pieces.title: Intelligence in Nature: The Sequel
pieces.pullQuote: Narby's 2005 follow-up extended the Cosmic Serpent hypothesis into plant intelligence, fungal networks, and bacterial communication. By 2025, the science of plant sentience had moved from fringe to mainstream research program.
pieces.body:
Intelligence in Nature (2005) was Jeremy Narby's follow-up to The Cosmic Serpent, less autobiographical, more scientific, and focused on a specific question that the DNA hypothesis had generated: if plants communicate information through chemical and electrical signals, what is the nature of that communication, and can it be called intelligent?

Narby interviewed biologists working on plant signaling, mycelial networks, and bacterial quorum sensing. He was attempting to document what professional scientists were finding at the research frontier of plant and microbial intelligence, to show that the question The Cosmic Serpent had raised (whether plants can 'communicate' with humans through ayahuasca) was related to questions that mainstream science was actively pursuing through conventional methods.

In 2005, this was still fairly marginal territory. By 2025, it had become a significant research field. Suzanne Simard's work on mycorrhizal networks, published in Nature in 1997 and popularized in Finding the Mother Tree (2021), showed that trees communicate, share resources, and respond to each other's distress through underground fungal networks in ways that parallel nervous system function. Monica Gagliano's research on plant learning and memory published in mainstream peer-reviewed journals showed plant species modifying their behavior in response to experience.

The field that Narby surveyed in 2005 as an emerging and contested area of research had by 2025 produced textbooks, university programs, and a heated philosophical debate about what 'intelligence' and 'communication' mean when applied to organisms without neurons.

The Cosmic Serpent's central question, whether the plants have something to communicate and whether humans can receive it, has not been definitively answered. But the subsidiary question, whether plants have information to communicate at all, has been answered affirmatively by mainstream science.

pieces.title: The Activist Work: Nouvelle Planète
pieces.pullQuote: For thirty-five years, Narby worked as Amazonian projects director for the Swiss NGO Nouvelle Planète, backing indigenous land rights, education, health, and botanical preservation projects in Peru and Brazil.
pieces.body:
Jeremy Narby is sometimes discussed primarily as the author of The Cosmic Serpent, the DNA hypothesis, the ayahuasca visions, the anthropologist who went native in the theoretical sense. The practical work that grounded the book and occupied most of his professional life is less well known.

From 1989 to 2024, thirty-five years, Narby served as Amazonian projects director for Nouvelle Planète, a Swiss NGO. The work was not theoretical. It involved land rights negotiations for indigenous communities whose territories were threatened by oil, timber, and agricultural development. It involved primary education projects. It involved village health programs. It involved fish farms, tree nurseries, and botanical documentation.

This practical work is the foundation that makes The Cosmic Serpent's arguments credible rather than merely interesting. Narby was not a theorist visiting the Amazon, he was a working development professional with sustained relationships in specific communities, who happened to encounter something in those communities that his training had not prepared him for.

The combination, rigorous field presence, institutional accountability, and a willingness to report what he actually observed rather than what his framework could accommodate, distinguishes his work from the more credulous ayahuasca literature that has proliferated since 1998.

His departure from Nouvelle Planète in 2024, after thirty-five years, marked the end of what is probably the most sustained engagement between a Western anthropologist and specific Amazonian communities in the context of plant medicine knowledge. The network he built and the documentation he created represent a resource that the communities themselves, as much as Western researchers, will determine how to use.

pieces.title: Biopiracy: When Science Takes Without Asking
pieces.pullQuote: In 1986, a US patent was granted for the ayahuasca vine, a plant sacred to Amazonian peoples who had cultivated knowledge of it for millennia. It was eventually cancelled. The patent race since then has only accelerated.
pieces.body:
One of The Cosmic Serpent's sharpest political arguments concerns the ethics of how Western science engages with indigenous botanical knowledge. Narby frames it as a rule embedded in shamanic tradition: the sacred is not for sale. The accumulation of personal power from spiritual knowledge is, in indigenous frameworks, the definition of black magic.

Western pharmaceutical and biotechnology industries operate by different rules. The drug discovery pipeline depends on identifying active compounds, isolating them, synthesizing modifications, and patenting the resulting intellectual property. Indigenous knowledge has served as a map for this process: which plants to study, which combinations to investigate, which compounds to isolate. The knowledge guides the research; the patent captures the value.

In 1986, US Patent 5,751,559 was granted to Loren Miller for a variety of the ayahuasca vine (Banisteriopsis caapi) he claimed to have discovered. The grant outraged indigenous organizations across the Amazon, who submitted a legal challenge arguing that the vine had been known and cultivated by their communities for millennia and could not constitute a novel invention. After a decade of legal proceedings, the patent was cancelled in 2003 on the grounds that prior art existed, the plant's use was documented in scientific literature before Miller's application.

The ayahuasca patent case is the clearest example of what critics call biopiracy: the appropriation of indigenous knowledge and genetic resources for commercial benefit without consent, benefit-sharing, or acknowledgment. The Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit-Sharing, which entered into force in 2014, created a legal framework for addressing this. As of 2024, 138 countries have ratified it. Enforcement remains weak.

The psychedelic patent race accelerated after 2020, with pharmaceutical companies filing patents on therapeutic protocols, dosing regimens, and molecular derivatives of classical psychedelics. The defensive patent movement, initiated by researchers at Johns Hopkins and others, attempts to prevent any single entity from monopolizing psychedelic therapy.

pieces.title: What the Critics Got Right
pieces.pullQuote: The Cosmic Serpent's critics were not wrong that Narby confuses his enthusiasm for evidence. The book's value survives this criticism, but the criticism should be held alongside the value.
sources: Publishers Weekly review, The Cosmic Serpent (1998)
Goodreads review by geneticist, The Cosmic Serpent
pieces.body:
The Cosmic Serpent attracted serious critical attention from scientists who engaged with its argument rather than dismissing it. The most pointed came from biophysicist Jacques Dubochet, who would receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2017, and from the reviewer at Publishers Weekly.

Dubochet's criticism was methodological: Narby had proposed a hypothesis, that shamans access molecular-level information through ayahuasca visions, but had not designed any test for it. The hypothesis is falsifiable in principle, but Narby had not attempted to falsify it.

Publishers Weekly's criticism was epistemological: Narby 'confuses his own enthusiasm for evidence' and takes 'similarities of form', any helical pattern, any double structure, any serpentine shape, as 'proof of identity or causal connection.' A Goodreads reviewer who identified as a geneticist made a similar point: the hypothesis is scientifically framed but poorly executed as science. The visual similarity between the DNA double helix and shamanic serpent imagery is suggestive but not probative.

These criticisms are fair. Narby does make analogical leaps that the evidence doesn't fully support. He does take resemblance as more significant than resemblance alone can bear. His defense, that 'the presuppositions of science are too narrow to permit the test', is the kind of argument that, if unchecked, can immunize any hypothesis from falsification.

The appropriate response to these criticisms is not to dismiss the book but to read it with them in mind. The combinatorial problem, how did indigenous peoples discover the ayahuasca combination?, is real and unresolved by any alternative explanation. The pragmatic reliability of indigenous pharmacological knowledge is documented and impressive. The question Narby poses is genuine. The answer he proposes is speculative. Both things are true, and both matter.

pieces.title: What Dennis McKenna Believes
pieces.pullQuote: Dennis McKenna became one of the most rigorous neuropharmacologists working on tryptamines. His assessment of what happened at La Chorrera, calibrated, affectionate, skeptical, is the other side of True Hallucinations.
sources: D. McKenna, The Brotherhood of the Screaming Abyss (2012)
D. McKenna, various interviews 2010-2025 [Source not found; under review]
pieces.body:
Dennis McKenna's memoir, The Brotherhood of the Screaming Abyss (2012), provides the other account of La Chorrera, written by the person who, by all evidence, went furthest into the altered state and came back most intact.

Dennis recalls the episode with clarity that his brother's True Hallucinations does not always provide. His assessment is careful: something happened at La Chorrera that was extraordinary. The nature of what happened, whether it was a genuine encounter with plant intelligence, a pharmacologically induced psychosis, or something between, he does not definitively resolve. What he has said in interviews is that he does not believe the specific claims Terence made (the Timewave, the alien mushroom intelligence) but that he cannot fully dismiss the experiential reality of what they both went through.

Dennis completed a doctorate in neuropharmacology at the University of British Columbia and spent decades doing rigorous scientific research on tryptamines, ayahuasca pharmacology, and the interaction between psychedelic compounds and human neurobiology. His scientific work is careful and precise. It coexists with his account of La Chorrera in ways he navigates openly: he doesn't let the experience override his scientific judgment, and he doesn't let his scientific training negate the experience.

He has spoken about Terence's brain tumor, the glioblastoma that killed Terence in 2000, with a speculation that he acknowledges is unverifiable: that the decades of high-dose psychedelic use may have had a relationship to the tumor. He does not state this as fact. He states it as something he wonders about, as a neuropharmacologist who loves his brother.

The relationship between the two brothers is the human center of True Hallucinations, more interesting, finally, than the theories. Dennis's ongoing presence as a scientist, commentator, and advocate for rigorous psychedelic research is the most concrete evidence that La Chorrera produced something real, whatever that something was.

pieces.title: The Mathematics of Novelty
pieces.pullQuote: The Timewave was a mathematical model of time's qualitative structure. McKenna derived it from the I Ching. The mathematics was criticized by professional mathematicians. The underlying philosophical claim, that time is textured, remains interesting.
sources: Various mathematical critiques of the Timewave, 1990s [Source not found; under review]
pieces.body:
The Timewave Zero theory began as an attempt to make a specific phenomenological observation mathematically rigorous: that some periods of time feel more 'novel', more full of unexpected connections, more generative of new forms, than others.

McKenna's starting point was the I Ching, the Chinese system of sixty-four hexagrams used for divination since antiquity. He observed that the sequence of hexagrams, when treated as a numerical series, had a structure that could be interpreted as a wave function. He mapped this wave function onto historical time, aligning it so that its predicted 'singularity', the point of maximum novelty, coincided with December 21, 2012.

Professional mathematicians who examined the theory raised multiple objections. The derivation from the I Ching was arbitrary, McKenna had chosen a particular mapping of hexagrams to numbers that produced the desired wave, but other mappings were equally justifiable and produced different results. The theory was not derived from empirical data about historical events but was fitted to historical data post hoc, which violates basic principles of predictive modeling.

McKenna acknowledged some of these criticisms and adjusted his mapping of the I Ching values at least once in response. He never fully resolved the mathematical objections, and the 2012 endpoint was falsified without drama when nothing of particular significance occurred.

What remains from the Timewave is the philosophical claim McKenna derived from the I Ching insight: that time has qualitative structure, that novelty is not uniformly distributed, that history has what he called 'attractor basins', periods toward which events seem to converge. This claim, stripped of the specific mathematical apparatus and the 2012 prediction, is a genuine philosophical proposition. Whether it is true is a question that the available evidence neither confirms nor refutes. It is the kind of question that the Timewave was supposed to answer and instead preserved as a question.

pieces.title: After McKenna: The Entity Research
pieces.pullQuote: In a 2020 Johns Hopkins survey (Davis et al., J. Psychopharmacol. 34(9):1008-1020) of 2,561 people who had already had a DMT entity encounter, many respondents described features similar to McKenna's; the survey cannot show how common such encounters are. A 2023 Imperial College EEG-fMRI study (Timmermann et al., PNAS 120(13)) mapped DMT's global brain effects but did not isolate entity contact. Similar reports keep appearing; the neuroscience has not explained them.
sources: Sexton et al., J. Psychopharmacol. 33(9) (2019) [Source not found; under review]
pieces.body:
When Terence McKenna first described encountering 'merry elfin, self-transforming, machine creatures' during his DMT experiments in Berkeley in the early 1970s, he had no way of knowing whether the experience was idiosyncratic. He was, as far as he knew, one of very few Westerners who had smoked synthesized DMT.

The subsequent decades revealed that the entity report was not idiosyncratic at all.

Rick Strassman's clinical DMT study at the University of New Mexico (1990-1995), the first human DMT research in decades, found that a majority of his sixty volunteer subjects reported entity contact. Many described the entities in terms strikingly similar to McKenna's: small, playful, insectoid or elfin, engaged in the production of objects or language.

In a 2020 Johns Hopkins survey (Davis et al., J. Psychopharmacol. 34(9):1008-1020) of 2,561 people who had already had a DMT entity encounter, respondents described the encounter in detail. It documents the phenomenology in detail but sets no prevalence rate, because every respondent was recruited for having had an encounter; the 97% figure often attached to it appears in no published paper. The most common entity types were humanoid beings, gods or supernatural figures, and what respondents described as aliens or interdimensional beings. The emotional tone of the encounters was predominantly positive; most respondents described entities as benevolent and the encounter as meaningful.

A 2023 Imperial College London fMRI study (Timmermann et al., PNAS 120(13)) mapped DMT's global brain effects, large increases in global functional connectivity, network disintegration and desegregation, and compression of the principal cortical gradient. It did not isolate entity contact as a distinct neural signature, and no published imaging study yet has: the phenomenology is well documented, the neural specificity is not.

McKenna's phenomenological report has survived into the era of neuroscience intact as description. What it describes, whether external entities, projections of the unconscious, or something else, the neuroscience has not resolved. What it has confirmed is that the consistency of the report across fifty years and thousands of independent subjects is not random. Something consistent is being encountered. McKenna described it first and most vividly. What it is remains open.

pieces.title: Oo-koo-he: The Drug They Were Looking For
pieces.pullQuote: The McKennas went to La Chorrera specifically to find oo-koo-he, a Witoto plant preparation that produced effects described as similar to orally active DMT. They never found it. They found psilocybin mushrooms instead.
sources: Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979)
pieces.body:
True Hallucinations does not begin with the mushrooms. It begins with oo-koo-he.

Oo-koo-he was the Witoto name for a plant preparation described in the ethnobotanical literature as producing effects similar to ayahuasca, oral DMT activity through some combination of beta-carboline inhibitors and tryptamine-containing admixture plants. Schultes had documented its use in the Colombian Amazon. The McKenna brothers went to La Chorrera specifically to find it, study it, and attempt to synthesize an orally active DMT compound that could extend the brief experience of smoked DMT into something more sustained.

The expedition was scholarly in intention if adventurous in execution. Dennis was studying botanical pharmacology. Terence had read extensively in the ethnobotanical literature. They brought field guides, laboratory equipment, and a level of prior knowledge about Amazonian plant pharmacology that distinguished them from simple psychedelic tourists.

They never found oo-koo-he. The Witoto population in the La Chorrera area had been devastated by the rubber boom, reduced from forty thousand to five thousand in the preceding sixty years, and the ceremonial practices that Schultes had documented were no longer intact in the community they reached.

What they found instead, growing abundantly in the cattle pastures of the mission station in the fog and rain, were Psilocybe cubensis mushrooms, the same species they had encountered in California, growing wild in equatorial abundance. The expedition that had traveled thousands of miles to find one psychoactive plant found a completely different one.

The way science actually works, sometimes, is that you go looking for one thing and come back with something else. True Hallucinations is the account of what happened when the McKennas accepted the substitution.

pieces.title: The Man Who Wore a Suit in the Amazon
pieces.pullQuote: Schultes wore a suit and tie in the field. Not from vanity, from respect. He treated the people and their knowledge with the same formality he would have brought to any scientific collaboration.
pieces.body:
The image of Richard Evans Schultes in a suit and tie, deep in the Colombian Amazon in the 1940s, is the central image of Wade Davis's portrait of his mentor in One River. It was not affectation. It was methodology.

Schultes spent twelve years in the Amazon at a time when the dominant attitude of Western scientists toward indigenous knowledge was either condescension or romanticism, either the native practices were superstition to be corrected, or they were evidence of a lost paradise to be mourned. Schultes brought a third attitude: rigorous empiricism. He wanted to know what the plants did and how the people used them, and he approached both questions with the same objectivity he brought to his laboratory work.

The suit was part of this. He treated the communities he worked with as professional collaborators, as sources of systematic knowledge accumulated over generations, rather than as subjects of study or objects of rescue. The formality communicated respect. The respect communicated seriousness. Seriousness was what allowed the knowledge transfer that produced his herbarium.

His students, Davis most memorably, but also Mark Plotkin, Tim Plowman, and dozens of others, describe Schultes as a demanding teacher who showed his students the Amazon the way it had to be understood: on foot, by canoe, in rain, in seasons, with the people who knew it from birth. He didn't lecture about plants in classrooms, he took his students to where the plants grew and introduced them to the people who used them.

The Harvard faculty colleague quoted in the Peabody Museum lecture video, 'whatever you do, stay away from Schultes; he's a dinosaur who spent a decade in the Amazon alone', missed the point entirely. The decade alone in the Amazon was not an eccentricity. It was the research.

pieces.title: From Arrow Poison to Operating Room
pieces.pullQuote: Schultes went to the Amazon to study arrow poisons. What he learned, the chemistry of curare and its derivatives, became essential to modern surgery. It was not what he went looking for.
sources: Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979)
pieces.body:
Richard Evans Schultes's original 1941 Amazon grant was to study curare, the arrow poison used by Amazonian indigenous groups. The substance had fascinated Western pharmacologists since the sixteenth century, when European explorers reported indigenous hunters using darts dipped in a dark paste that paralyzed prey. The mechanism was unknown and the compound had obvious potential medical applications.

Schultes's contribution to curare research was botanical and taxonomic: he identified the plant species that produced it (primarily Chondrodendron tomentosum), documented regional variation in preparation methods, and collected specimens that allowed systematic chemical analysis. The alkaloid tubocurarine, isolated from the specimens he collected, became the prototype for modern neuromuscular blocking agents used in surgery.

Anesthesiologists use curare derivatives in virtually every general anesthetic today. The muscle relaxation that allows surgeons to operate without the patient's reflexes interfering, and that allows intubation for mechanical ventilation, derives from a class of compounds whose botanical identification was largely the work of Schultes and his collaborators.

This is the model that Plants of the Gods argues for applying to other Amazonian plant knowledge: not the selective appropriation of individual compounds for pharmaceutical development, but the systematic documentation of the full pharmacopoeia, what plants are used, for what conditions, in what preparations, by which communities.

Curare became a surgical tool because Schultes could identify the plants and researchers could isolate the chemistry. Schultes's argument was that this should happen with the full range of psychoactive plants before the knowledge and the plants themselves disappeared, that the Amazon represented a pharmacological database that had already produced one surgical revolution and might produce others.

The aspirin pill was destroying that database faster than any political force could. And the time Schultes had was running out.

pieces.title: Chiribiquete: The Paintings in the Rock
pieces.pullQuote: Among Schultes's discoveries was the tepui plateau Chiribiquete, now the world's largest rainforest national park, containing the largest known repository of pre-Columbian rock paintings. He found it in the 1940s. It was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2018.
pieces.body:
In the early 1940s, while traveling through the Colombian Amazon on his rubber-tapping assignment, Richard Evans Schultes encountered a massive sandstone plateau that rose from the jungle floor like a fortress. The Chiribiquete tepui, a table mountain in the style of the Guyana Highlands, was unknown to Western science and was home to extraordinary biodiversity and extraordinary archaeology: thousands of years of rock paintings in ochre and red, covering exposed cliff faces with images of animals, humans, rituals, and what appeared to be shamanic vision content.

Schultes documented what he found and moved on. He had rubber to track and plants to catalog. The Chiribiquete plateau was one discovery among many.

The plateau's significance took decades to fully emerge. Colombian archaeologist Gaspar Morcote-Ríos has spent years studying the rock paintings, which extend across hundreds of sites and represent one of the most extensive archives of pre-Columbian visual culture in South America. Some of the oldest paintings may date to 20,000 years before present, among the oldest rock art in the Americas.

In 2018, UNESCO designated Chiribiquete a World Heritage Site. The park is now the world's largest rainforest national park, covering more than four million hectares. It protects three groups of uncontacted indigenous peoples and extraordinary levels of biodiversity, including plant species that Schultes documented and that have never been fully analyzed pharmacologically.

The Harvard Magazine obituary of Schultes in 2022 used Chiribiquete as the emblem of his legacy: a place he found in the 1940s that became, seventy years later, a globally recognized conservation priority. His presence in the Amazon was not destructive tourism, it was discovery that eventually enabled protection.

pieces.title: Schultes and the Native American Church
pieces.pullQuote: Schultes testified on behalf of the Native American Church's right to use peyote in religious practice. He described it as a sacrament, not a drug. His testimony helped establish the scientific and ethnographic record that eventually supported legal protection.
sources: Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979)
pieces.body:
The Native American Church's peyote sacrament is one of the oldest and most continuously practiced religious uses of a psychoactive plant in North America. The Huichol and other indigenous groups in Mexico have used peyote ceremonially for at least five centuries; the pan-tribal peyote ceremony that became the Native American Church in the early twentieth century extended this tradition across dozens of nations.

Schultes was one of the most important scientific voices defending this practice against legal challenge. In testimony, in published writing, and in the direct authority of his field research, he consistently described peyote use within the Native American Church as a sacramental practice, not drug use in the sense that warranted criminal sanction, but religious practice warranting First Amendment protection.

His argument was both ethnographic (the practice was ancient, embedded in ceremonial tradition, and pharmacologically managed through cultural knowledge) and pharmacological (peyote's safety profile in the sacramental context, low doses, controlled setting, experienced guidance, was fundamentally different from the abuse scenarios that motivated federal drug law).

The American Indian Religious Freedom Act of 1978 formally protected indigenous religious practices, but court decisions in subsequent decades threatened peyote use. The Employment Division v. Smith decision (1990) held that the AIRF Act did not protect peyote use from prosecution under neutral drug laws. The American Indian Religious Freedom Act Amendments of 1994 specifically exempted Native American Church peyote use from the Controlled Substances Act.

Schultes's testimony and published work contributed to the evidentiary record that supported these legal protections. The distinction he made consistently, between sacramental use embedded in cultural tradition and recreational or experimental use, was the distinction that legal frameworks eventually codified.

pieces.title: Two Kinds of Knowledge: Schultes and Hofmann
pieces.pullQuote: The collaboration between Schultes and Hofmann was the collaboration between field knowledge and laboratory analysis, between knowing which plants indigenous peoples used and knowing what the plants contained. Neither alone was sufficient.
sources: Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979)
pieces.body:
Richard Evans Schultes and Albert Hofmann were the ideal collaborators for Plants of the Gods because they represented complementary forms of knowledge that were, individually, incomplete.

Schultes's knowledge was ecological, ethnographic, and taxonomic. He knew which plants indigenous communities used, in which preparations, for what purposes, within what ceremonial contexts. He had watched curanderos prepare ayahuasca, attended peyote ceremonies, and collected specimens of the sacred mushrooms that Wasson's publications had brought to Western attention. What he lacked was the chemistry: he was a botanist, not a pharmacologist.

Hofmann's knowledge was chemical. He had synthesized LSD from ergot alkaloids, isolated psilocybin and psilocin from Schultes's mushroom specimens, and analyzed the chemistry of morning glory seeds. He understood how these compounds interacted with human physiology. What he lacked was the field context: the knowledge of how the plants were used, who used them, in what forms and quantities and ceremonial frameworks.

Plants of the Gods combined these two forms of knowledge in a way that neither could have produced independently. The botanical and ethnographic descriptions are Schultes's. The chemical structures and pharmacological notes are Hofmann's. The book argues, by its structure, that both are necessary for understanding what these plants are and why they matter.

This argument has institutional implications. The current psychedelic renaissance tends to separate the clinical and the cultural: researchers at Johns Hopkins study psilocybin in controlled trials; anthropologists study ayahuasca in indigenous contexts; they rarely read each other. Plants of the Gods was written by two people who talked to each other across the laboratory/field divide and produced something neither could have produced alone. The model is still the right one.

pieces.title: From Reducing Valve to REBUS: Huxley's Neuroscience, Seventy Years On
pieces.pullQuote: Huxley proposed a mechanism in 1954. Carhart-Harris and Friston named it in 2019. The interval between them was sixty-five years of neuroscience arriving at the same place.
sources: Carhart-Harris & Friston, REBUS and the Anarchic Brain, Pharmacological Reviews (2019)
Carhart-Harris et al., Default Mode Network Modulation by Psychedelics (2022) [Source not found; under review]
pieces.body:
In May 1953, Aldous Huxley took mescaline under Humphry Osmond's supervision and spent eight hours observing the world with an attention he had not previously been able to bring to it. The flowers on his table were not simply flowers, they were flowers as flowers actually were, without the filtering by biological utility and social convention that ordinarily reduced them to objects with names and functions.

To explain this, Huxley reached for Henri Bergson's 1896 proposal that the brain's primary function is not to produce consciousness but to restrict it. The brain, Bergson argued, is a reducing valve, it filters out most of what could be perceived, allowing through only what is relevant to survival and action. Huxley borrowed C.D. Broad's elaboration of this hypothesis and gave it the name it has carried since: the reducing valve.

Mescaline, in his account, impaired the valve. More of Mind at Large, the field of consciousness that the valve ordinarily suppressed, was allowed through. The result was not hallucination but perception: not the addition of something foreign but the removal of a filter that had been eliminating most of what was there.

For sixty-five years, this remained philosophy and phenomenology, coherent, intuitively compelling, and without rigorous neuroscientific support. The tools to test it didn't exist.

In 2019, Robin Carhart-Harris and Karl Friston published a paper in Pharmacological Reviews proposing the REBUS model, Relaxed Beliefs Under Psychedelics. Their framework, derived from the predictive coding theory of brain function, proposes that the brain operates as a hierarchical inference machine: it generates predictions about what it expects to perceive (top-down priors) and compares them against incoming sensory signals (bottom-up prediction errors). When predictions are accurate, sensory signals are suppressed, they don't need to reach higher processing because they match what the brain already predicted.

Psychedelic compounds, in the REBUS model, reduce the 'precision weighting' of these top-down priors. The predictions become less certain, less heavily weighted, which means they suppress incoming sensory information less aggressively. More bottom-up signal reaches awareness. The brain's filtering function is relaxed.

This is Bergson's reducing valve, formalized in the vocabulary of computational neuroscience, derived from fMRI studies of psilocybin and LSD, and expressed as a falsifiable hypothesis rather than a philosophical intuition.

The convergence between Huxley's 1954 proposal and the 2019 neuroscience is not coincidental, Huxley was describing a real phenomenological event, and his philosophical framework was an attempt to capture something that was genuinely happening in the brain. But the specificity of the confirmation is remarkable. Carhart-Harris and Friston are not simply saying that Huxley was approximately right. They are saying that the mechanism he described, impairment of the brain's filtering function, resulting in richer but less organized perceptual experience, is precisely what the neuroimaging evidence shows.

The default mode network (DMN) is the system most associated with self-referential processing, mind-wandering, and what neuroscientists call 'top-down' modulation of sensory experience. It is, in functional terms, the neural correlate of Huxley's reducing valve, the system that normally constrains perception within the boundaries of what is already known and expected. Under psychedelics, the DMN shows systematic suppression in fMRI studies. Its internal connectivity decreases. Its ability to modulate other networks is compromised.

The result, as Huxley described and as the clinical literature consistently confirms, is not chaos, it is a different kind of order. Subjects do not report random sensory noise; they report heightened salience of specific features of experience, a quality of direct presence with ordinary objects, and an inability to maintain the usual narrative framing that filters experience through its relevance to the self.

The self, in Huxley's phenomenological terms and in the REBUS framework's technical terms, is a product of the filtering process, the prediction-generating system's attempt to maintain a stable model of what things are in relation to the organism. When the filter relaxes, the self relaxes with it. Ego dissolution is not a bizarre drug effect. It is what happens to the self-model when the system that maintains it is temporarily suspended.

For clinicians, this has direct implications. Depression, in the predictive coding framework, has been proposed to involve over-rigid top-down priors, the system is too certain about negative predictions, and bottom-up signals that contradict them are discounted. Psilocybin-assisted therapy, by temporarily relaxing these priors, may create a window in which the predictions can be revised, in which the certainty that the world is hostile, that the self is defective, that recovery is impossible, can be loosened sufficiently to allow new experience to register.

This is what the clinical evidence suggests, and it is what Huxley's philosophical framework, worked out in an afternoon with mescaline and Bergson, predicted. The neuroscience has arrived at a more detailed account of the same territory he mapped with a metaphor. The metaphor was accurate.

pieces.title: The Mystical Experience as Medicine: What the Trials Are Measuring
pieces.pullQuote: The MEQ30 measures six features: unity, noetic quality, sacredness, deeply felt positive mood, transcendence of time and space, and ineffability. These are Huxley's criteria, operationalized seventy years later.
sources: Griffiths et al., Psilocybin can occasion mystical-type experiences, Psychopharmacology (2006)
Yaden et al., The Varieties of Self-Transcendent Experience, Review of General Psychology (2017)
Barrett & Griffiths, Classic Hallucinogens and Mystical Experiences, Curr Top Behav Neurosci (2018)
pieces.body:
Aldous Huxley called the mescaline experience a 'gratuitous grace', not necessary to salvation but potentially helpful, to be accepted thankfully if made available. He located it within the category of mystical experience as defined by the philosophical and theological literature: a direct encounter with what he called 'the divine Ground,' characterized by unity, noetic quality (a sense of having received genuine knowledge), and a quality of sacredness that he distinguished from ordinary religious feeling.

In 2006, Roland Griffiths and colleagues at Johns Hopkins published the first rigorous modern trial of psilocybin's ability to occasion mystical experience. They used the Mystical Experience Questionnaire (MEQ30), derived from the philosopher Walter Stace's phenomenological analysis of mystical states. The MEQ30 measures six features: unity, noetic quality, sacredness, deeply felt positive mood, transcendence of time and space, and ineffability.

These are Huxley's criteria, operationalized. Not quite in his language, Stace and Griffiths use the vocabulary of phenomenology and psychology rather than Vedantic philosophy, but the underlying structure is identical. The MEQ30 is measuring what Huxley described as the 'gratuitous grace': the direct encounter with what the reducing valve ordinarily prevents.

The Griffiths 2006 trial found that psilocybin could reliably occasion complete mystical experiences (MEQ30 score above 60 percent of maximum) in a significant proportion of participants in appropriate conditions. At fourteen-month follow-up, the majority of those who had complete mystical experiences rated them among the most meaningful of their lives. The finding has been replicated multiple times since.

What has been more significant for clinical practice is the subsequent finding that mystical experience quality predicts therapeutic outcomes better than drug dose alone. In studies of psilocybin for depression, end-of-life anxiety, and alcohol use disorder, MEQ30 scores correlate with treatment response at follow-up. Participants who have complete mystical experiences are more likely to show sustained therapeutic benefit than those who have sub-threshold experiences, even when the dose is the same.

This finding has profound implications. It suggests that the therapeutic mechanism of psychedelic-assisted therapy is not simply pharmacological, not just the drug acting on receptors to produce symptomatic relief. It suggests that the quality of the experience, whether it reaches the threshold of genuine transformation, is what drives the outcome. The medicine is not the molecule but what the molecule occasions.

Huxley articulated this distinction in 1954: the drug is a vehicle, not a destination. What it delivers is not itself the healing; what it delivers is a quality of experience that the person must then bring into their life. The letters to Osmond contain his worry that people who focused on the drug rather than the experience it opened would miss the point entirely.

The two industry Phase 3 trials of synthetic psilocybin, reporting in June 2025 and February 2026 respectively, showed statistically significant reductions in MADRS (Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale) scores in treatment-resistant depression patients who received a single high dose of synthetic psilocybin alongside psychotherapeutic support. Twenty-five percent of participants achieved clinically meaningful reduction at six weeks, with durability through twenty-six weeks. The NDA submission is targeted for Q4 2026.

These are modest numbers by the standards of antidepressant trials, but the comparison is inexact. Standard antidepressants require daily dosing indefinitely; synthetic psilocybin is one or two doses. Standard antidepressants produce response rates that cluster around 40-50 percent in treatment-naive patients and fall sharply in treatment-resistant patients; synthetic psilocybin is being tested in patients who have already failed at least two antidepressants.

What the trials are measuring, beneath the MADRS scores and the Phase 3 endpoints, is what Huxley proposed in 1954: that direct perceptual encounter with something beyond the ordinary reducing valve's output can produce lasting change in how a person relates to their experience. The clinical infrastructure for testing this claim did not exist in 1954. It now does, and what it is finding is that the claim was substantially correct.

The EPISODE trial, published in JAMA Psychiatry in May 2026, found that high-dose psilocybin produced treatment response (defined as ≥50% reduction in Hamilton Depression Rating Scale) in significantly more participants than active placebo at six weeks, in a German multicenter Phase 2b trial. The effect sizes are clinically meaningful and the safety profile is well-characterized. Huxley's 'gratuitous grace' is being measured in clinical endpoints. The measurement doesn't reduce what it measures.

pieces.title: The Discoverer's Dilemma: Hofmann, LSD, and the Problem of Intention
pieces.pullQuote: Hofmann spent sixty years watching his discovery be used in ways he had not intended. He remained remarkably clear about what those ways were and what would have been right instead.
sources: Wacker et al., Crystal Structure of an LSD-Bound Human Serotonin Receptor, Cell (2017)
Grof, LSD: Doorway to the Numinous (2009)
Carhart-Harris et al., Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2022) [Source not found; under review]
pieces.body:
Albert Hofmann died on April 29, 2008, at the age of 102, having lived long enough to see the clinical research program he had hoped for begin again, but not long enough to see it produce a regulatory approval. He had been waiting for sixty-five years.

The patience required for this waiting, and the clarity of mind with which he sustained it, are what make My Problem Child more than a memoir. It is a sustained meditation on the relationship between a discovery and the world that receives it, on what it means when what you create goes somewhere you did not intend, is used in ways you did not design, and becomes, for a generation, the symbol of something you neither endorsed nor recognized.

Hofmann's account of LSD's history has a specific shape: a decade of legitimate clinical research (1947-1957), a period of controlled dissemination through psychiatric and philosophical communities (1957-1963), and then a collapse, Leary's public advocacy, the counterculture appropriation, the manufacturer's withdrawal in 1965, the Schedule I designation in 1968. From the discovery's perspective, this is a history of progressive misuse followed by catastrophic over-correction.

But Hofmann's account of this history is not primarily a lament. It is an analysis. He identified, with precision, what the right use would have been: careful preparation of the person, careful attention to setting, experienced guidance, integration of what happened afterward, and a framework that situated the experience within a larger context of human development, religious, philosophical, or therapeutic, but not recreational. These conditions, in his view, were sufficient to make LSD safe and beneficial. Their absence was what made it dangerous.

The crystal structure of LSD published in Cell in 2017 confirmed what Hofmann had observed empirically: the drug binds to the 5-HT2A serotonin receptor with unusual duration because a protein 'lid' in the receptor traps it inside. The twelve-hour experience he had not anticipated on Bicycle Day now had a molecular explanation. The extraordinary potency that meant the drug was active at doses too small to see also had a structural explanation: the molecular fit between LSD and its receptor is nearly perfect.

Hofmann was 100 when this crystal structure was solved; he had died two years before it was published. He knew the mechanism only in pharmacological outline. But the specificity of the confirmation, that the chemistry he had studied for decades was as precise and elegant as he had intuited, would have gratified him.

His legacy as a pharmacologist is secure. The discovery of LSD, the isolation of psilocybin and psilocin, the analysis of morning glory alkaloids, these are substantial achievements in natural product chemistry that would have built a distinguished career even without LSD's cultural significance. But what he cared about, in the final decades of his life, was not the pharmacology. It was whether the discovery would eventually be used correctly.

As of 2026, the evidence suggests: partially. The industry trials have demonstrated, in Phase 3, that a single high dose of synthetic psilocybin (structurally analogous to LSD in its receptor activity) alongside psychotherapeutic support produces significant and durable antidepressant effects. The conditions of the trial, preparation, guided session, integration, approximate what Hofmann prescribed. The therapeutic framework Stanislav Grof built from 4,000 LSD sessions at the Maryland Psychiatric Research Center, and which is now being applied to psilocybin therapy, is Hofmann's model implemented at clinical scale.

What has not happened is the religious and philosophical use Hofmann considered most important. No Western institution has created the context he envisioned, what he called 'the integration of LSD into a cultural framework that would allow it to serve genuine human development.' The therapeutic framework exists. The philosophical framework does not yet.

Hofmann's word for this, the purpose for which LSD was, in his view, best suited, was 'sacred drug.' He used the phrase deliberately and never retracted it. Not a psychiatric tool, not a recreational substance, not an intelligence weapon, but a sacred drug: something that opened access to an experience that human beings have recognized, across traditions and millennia, as the most important class of experience available.

He was 102 when he died. He took LSD on his hundredth birthday. He said it restored the quality of perception he had known as a child. He waited sixty-five years for the rest of the world to figure out what it was.

pieces.title: April 19, 1943: What Hofmann Didn't Know He Was Starting
pieces.pullQuote: On the day Hofmann rode his bicycle home from work, Germany was fighting on the eastern front, the Holocaust was at its peak, and the Allies had not yet landed in Europe. The world LSD was born into was not the world it would transform.
pieces.body:
Albert Hofmann synthesized LSD for the second time and accidentally absorbed a small amount through his fingertips on April 16, 1943. He rode his bicycle home from the drug company laboratory in Basel on April 19, 1943, now celebrated annually as Bicycle Day.

April 19, 1943 was also the day the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising began, the largest single act of armed Jewish resistance to the Nazi genocide. The coincidence is not meaningless. The world in which LSD was discovered was a world in which the most extreme expressions of human cruelty were operating at industrial scale, a world in which the Enlightenment's confidence in reason's ability to produce better institutions and better people had been catastrophically tested.

Hofmann knew nothing of this context on his bicycle ride. He was experiencing the most dramatic perceptual event of his life and trying to stay on his bicycle while doing so. He reached home. His neighbor brought him milk. She looked like a witch. By morning the world was luminous and ordinary.

What he had discovered would spend the next thirty years being used by people who were partly responding to the world the war had left: a world in which the confidence in Western civilization's adequacy had been shattered, in which the administrative machinery of the rational state had been used for mass murder, in which existentialism and pessimism about the human condition had displaced the Progressive Era's optimism. The countercultural use of LSD in the 1960s was not only about pleasure or rebellion, it was about the search for a different basis for human life than the one that had produced the concentration camps.

Huxley, who first took mescaline in 1953, was a man who had watched the twentieth century's catastrophes from a position of intelligence and literary achievement and found them evidence that Western civilization's confident project was failing. The Doors of Perception was written by someone who had read Huxley's dystopia in Brave New World and then found, in a living room in Los Angeles, what he thought might be a correction.

Hofmann, in My Problem Child, places his discovery in this broader context more gently than Huxley did. He argues that the mystical experience LSD occasions is one of the few things that reliably produces the quality of consciousness that ecological and ethical crisis requires: a sense of connection to the natural world, a reduction in the ego's monopoly on significance, a direct encounter with the sacred that religion was increasingly failing to deliver to secular minds.

The 2017 crystal structure of LSD bound to its receptor, solved at the University of North Carolina, shows a molecule that fits its receptor with nearly perfect complementarity, held in place by a protein lid that explains its twelve-hour duration. The chemistry is elegant in ways that feel intentional, though intention is not something molecules have. Hofmann would have found this structural confirmation satisfying: it shows that what he synthesized was not a crude blunt instrument but a pharmacologically precise key that fits a specific receptor architecture shaped by evolution.

The receptor it fits, the 5-HT2A serotonin receptor, is found in the prefrontal cortex, the anterior cingulate cortex, and the regions of the brain most associated with self-referential processing. Activating it with a molecule of LSD's precision disrupts the default mode network's ability to maintain its ordinary filtering function. The result is what Hofmann described on the morning after Bicycle Day: a world that seemed newly created, luminous, more itself than it ordinarily was.

He had discovered this on April 19, 1943, in the middle of the worst war in human history, in a pharmaceutical laboratory in Switzerland, while trying to make a drug for postpartum hemorrhage. The discovery was not intended. The discovery was not planned. The discovery was, as he always said, something that came to him, a presentiment, a hunch, a return to a compound he had filed away five years before because the animal tests showed nothing.

The world it entered was a world in desperate need of something it could not name. The problem child spent the next eighty years being what the world needed and what the world, repeatedly, refused to use correctly.

pieces.title: The Stoned Ape: Between Hypothesis and Myth
pieces.pullQuote: The stoned ape hypothesis is neither proven nor falsified. It is something rarer: a genuinely interesting question that the available evidence neither confirms nor eliminates.
sources: Shao et al., Psilocybin induces rapid and persistent growth of dendritic spines in frontal cortex in vivo, Neuron (2021)
D. McKenna, The Brotherhood of the Screaming Abyss (2012)
pieces.body:
The stoned ape hypothesis, in its strongest form, proposes that Homo sapiens' distinctive cognitive capacities, language, abstract thinking, religious consciousness, tool innovation, were catalyzed by the regular consumption of psilocybin-containing mushrooms during a critical phase of human evolution in East Africa, approximately 200,000 years ago.

Terence McKenna's version, articulated in Food of the Gods, is specific: as African grasslands expanded and the forests contracted following climatic changes, ancestral hominids followed large herbivores across open savannahs. Psilocybe cubensis, which grows in the dung of cattle and similar herbivores, would have been abundant in this environment. McKenna proposed three mechanisms by which psilocybin consumption at low, medium, and high doses could have conferred evolutionary advantages: enhanced visual acuity (useful for hunting), increased sexual arousal and group bonding, and at high doses, the dissolution of ego boundaries and expansion of social and symbolic consciousness.

The hypothesis has been criticized on multiple grounds. No archaeological evidence of psilocybin use by early hominids has been found, the time scale is too remote and the evidence too fragile. The proposed mechanism is speculative: it assumes that the selective advantages of psilocybin-enhanced cognition were sufficient to produce significant evolutionary change, and that early hominids were encountering mushrooms at the right frequency and in the right quantities to produce that change. Both assumptions are untestable with current methods.

Most importantly for the specific McKenna claim: Psilocybe cubensis is not native to East Africa and probably was not present during the critical period of human cognitive evolution. The mushroom's range has expanded with cattle domestication; its presence in East Africa as early hominid habitat is not documented.

What the hypothesis gets right, or at least what it points at correctly, is the broader question: what role did psychoactive plants play in human evolution and cognitive development? This is a real question, and the evidence that human cultures have consistently used psychoactive plants, that no known culture lacks plant medicine practices, is itself significant. The relationship between humans and these plants is ancient and universal enough to suggest it is not accidental.

A 2021 Neuron paper by Shao et al. at Yale provides the most relevant recent data: psilocybin induces rapid and persistent growth of dendritic spines in the prefrontal cortex of mice, suggesting that it promotes synaptic plasticity, the mechanism underlying learning and memory formation. The growth was detectable within 24 hours of a single dose and persisted for at least a month. This is a neuroplasticity mechanism that could, in principle, provide cognitive advantages, though the leap from mice to hominids to evolutionary selection is large.

Dennis McKenna, who has done rigorous neuropharmacological research on tryptamines for decades, has said that the general hypothesis, that psychoactive plants were part of the hominid ecological niche and may have had effects on cognition, is plausible. The specific mechanism Terence proposed is not something the evidence currently supports. Dennis is comfortable with this distinction. He has described the experience at La Chorrera as real, the mushroom monologue as real in some sense he cannot fully specify, and the stoned ape hypothesis as an interesting story that may contain truth without being literally true.

This is perhaps the most honest relationship available to the hypothesis: not proof, not dismissal, but residence in a category that McKenna himself inhabited, the genuinely interesting question that the available evidence neither confirms nor eliminates, that calls for more research without promising what that research will find.

What Food of the Gods contributes to this question, regardless of the hypothesis's truth value, is the framework: the idea that the human relationship with psychoactive plants is not a deviation from some drug-free baseline but a consistent and possibly constitutive feature of human culture. Every known traditional society has plant medicine practices. The current pharmacological environment, which excludes most traditional psychoactive plants from legal use, is the historical anomaly, not the norm.

Whether psilocybin shaped the hominid brain or merely reflects what that brain already was, the relationship between the two is real. McKenna's contribution was to take that relationship seriously as a subject of inquiry when taking it seriously was not academically respectable. Whether the specific hypothesis survives is less important than whether the question does.

pieces.title: The Dominator Screen: McKenna's Media Critique in the Algorithm Age
pieces.pullQuote: McKenna wrote his television critique in 1992. He did not live to see TikTok. Every sentence has gotten more accurate.
sources: Various psychedelic ecology literature [Source not found; under review]
pieces.body:
In Food of the Gods, Terence McKenna devoted a chapter to television as a drug, arguing not metaphorically but pharmacologically that passive screen consumption alters brain states in ways that serve the dominator culture's interests. His specific claims: that television is by nature a tool of coercion because it controls content, enforces content uniformity, and makes content repeatable; that it produces passivity rather than agency; and that it replaces direct experience with mediated representation.

He wrote this in 1992. The internet was a research network. The World Wide Web had just been opened to the public. Smartphones did not exist. TikTok did not exist. The algorithmic feed did not exist.

By 2024, what McKenna described as television's dominator properties had been implemented at incomparably greater precision and scale. Variable-ratio reinforcement schedules, the mechanism that makes slot machines compulsive, were engineered into social media feeds. Sean Parker, founding president of Facebook, acknowledged in a 2017 interview that the platform had been deliberately designed to exploit psychological vulnerabilities for engagement. Jonathan Haidt's 2024 book The Anxious Generation documented the epidemiological consequences: dramatic increases in depression, anxiety, and self-harm among adolescents correlating with the adoption of smartphone-mediated social media from 2012 onward.

McKenna's critique of television was correct and insufficient. He diagnosed the mechanism, control of content, uniformity, passivity, but the 2024 version of the problem is worse on every dimension. The algorithmic feed does not merely offer passive content; it actively optimizes content selection for maximum emotional engagement, which in practice means maximum emotional provocation. The uniformity is statistical rather than explicit, not a single channel but an individually tailored stream that nonetheless converges people toward content that increases cortisol and outrage. The passivity is not the passivity of watching; it is the pseudo-activity of scrolling, liking, and sharing, actions that feel like agency but are responses to an optimization system.

McKenna's proposed corrective was also correct but insufficient: 'Stop consuming images and start producing them.' The argument for active creation over passive consumption, for direct experience over mediated representation, for psychedelic attention over screen-induced dissociation, was right. But in 1992, the tools for passive consumption were limited to television schedules and video rental. The tools available in 2024 are incomparably more effective at producing exactly what he warned against.

What connects the television critique to the larger argument of Food of the Gods is the claim that the dominator culture systematically prefers intoxicants that produce compliance over intoxicants that produce questioning. Alcohol sedates; television sedates; social media, in its effect on attention and critical thinking, sedates. Psilocybin disrupts sedation. The drug war, in McKenna's framework, is a war against a specific kind of consciousness: the kind that notices what's wrong with the system.

The current psychedelic renaissance exists partly in tension with this critique. The therapeutic framing of psychedelic research, psilocybin as antidepressant, MDMA as PTSD treatment, is entirely compatible with the existing healthcare system and represents no threat to the attention economy. A drug that makes you a better compliant consumer of the social order is not the drug McKenna was describing.

Huxley drew the same distinction: soma versus moksha. The dominator drug produces happiness without liberation. The liberation drug produces questioning without comfort. What McKenna diagnosed as the television problem, the systematic substitution of sedating spectacle for consciousness-expanding experience, has not been addressed by the psychedelic renaissance. It has gotten worse while the renaissance proceeded.

pieces.title: One Hundred Years of Failure: The Drug War in Full
pieces.pullQuote: A hundred years. Forty billion dollars annually. The highest incarceration rate in the world. Drug overdose deaths at record highs. The policy has been both very expensive and counterproductive by its own stated measure.
sources: ACLU, A Tale of Two Countries (2020)
Ehrlichman, John, quoted in Dan Baum, Harper's Magazine (2016)
pieces.body:
The Harrison Narcotics Tax Act became law on December 17, 1914. One hundred and twelve years later, the United States is spending approximately forty billion dollars annually on drug enforcement and incarceration, has the highest rate of drug overdose deaths in its history, and maintains the world's largest incarcerated population, with drug offenses accounting for a substantial portion of those sentences.

By the policy's own stated measure, reducing drug use, reducing addiction, reducing the social harm of psychoactive substances, it has not worked. Drug use rates in the United States are not lower than they were in 1914. Addiction rates in the United States are not lower than they were in 1914. The specific harms that prohibition generates, adulterated drug supply, violence over market control, criminal records that perpetuate the social conditions that drive addiction, did not exist before the policy created them.

Chasing the Scream was published as the centenary of the Harrison Act approached, and Hari structured it as a reckoning with what a century of this policy had produced. The evidence he assembled, following the war from Anslinger's appointment in 1930 to Portugal's decriminalization in 2001, from Billie Holiday's persecution to the Vancouver safe injection rooms, is not primarily an argument about drugs. It is an argument about what happens when a society organizes its response to suffering around punishment rather than treatment.

The racial targeting that John Ehrlichman confirmed in 2016 was not a flaw in the drug war's design, it was, in Nixon's administration's explicit framing, part of the design. The drugs were the pretext; the communities were the target. This is the darkest part of Hari's argument, and the one most solidly supported by primary documentation: the Harrison Act, the Marihuana Tax Act, the Controlled Substances Act, and the mandatory minimums of the 1980s and 1990s were all applied with systematic racial disparity that cannot be explained by differential use rates because use rates across racial groups are broadly similar.

The ACLU documented in 2020 that Black Americans are 3.73 times more likely than white Americans to be arrested for marijuana possession despite similar use rates. The disparity is not a statistical artifact. It is a policy outcome.

What has changed since Hari wrote in 2015 is significant but incomplete. Recreational cannabis is now legal in 24 US states. The DOJ proposed rescheduling cannabis from Schedule I to Schedule III in May 2024. The Biden administration issued mass pardons for federal cannabis convictions in October 2022. Oregon decriminalized personal possession of all drugs in 2020, then partially reversed course in 2024 as implementation challenges mounted. The harm reduction infrastructure has grown: the first sanctioned safe injection site in the US (OnPoint NYC) opened in November 2021 and had reversed over 1,200 overdoses by 2025 without a single on-site death.

And yet: overdose deaths reached a record 107,500 in 2023, primarily from fentanyl and synthetic opioids that entered the supply chain as a consequence of prohibition-driven quality uncertainty. The drug supply is more dangerous, not less, after a century of enforcement.

The Portugal model that Hari cited as the strongest evidence for decriminalization has shown mixed results over twenty years, strong on HIV transmission, weaker on overdose rates when the social investment in treatment and services has been insufficient. The lesson is not that decriminalization fails but that decriminalization alone is insufficient. What works, when it works, is decriminalization combined with substantial investment in the social conditions that drive addiction: housing, employment, community, treatment capacity.

Hari summarized the alternative in the book's final pages: what if the money currently spent on enforcement and incarceration were redirected to the conditions that determine whether people reach for drugs in the first place? This remains the unimplemented proposal. A century of data supports it. The political will to implement it has not yet materialized at federal scale.

pieces.title: The Psychedelic Foundation of Western Philosophy
pieces.pullQuote: If Wasson, Hofmann, and Ruck are correct, Western philosophy did not emerge from pure reason. It emerged from a psychedelic sacrament that Plato, Aristotle, Sophocles, and Cicero all received.
sources: Wasson, Hofmann & Ruck, The Road to Eleusis (1978)
Mylonas, Eleusis and the Eleusinian Mysteries (1961)
pieces.body:
Western philosophy begins, in the standard account, with the pre-Socratic speculation of the sixth and fifth centuries BCE: Thales proposing that everything is water, Heraclitus insisting on universal flux, Pythagoras discovering the mathematical structure of music. Plato synthesizes these into the theory of Forms, the claim that the material world is a shadow of a higher reality that reason can apprehend. Aristotle systematizes Plato's intuitions into the categories of logic and natural science. These are the foundations.

The Road to Eleusis, published in 1978 by three scholars who had spent lifetimes studying mycology, chemistry, and classical philology respectively, proposes a supplement to this account: that the direct encounter with 'higher reality' that Platonic philosophy describes did not arise purely from rational speculation. It arose from a specific experience, the experience of the kykeon, the ritual drink at the center of the Eleusinian Mysteries, which Wasson, Hofmann, and Ruck argue was psychoactive through ergot alkaloids contaminating the barley.

The initiates of the Eleusinian Mysteries included, by historical record, virtually the entire intellectual and cultural leadership of classical Greece and Rome. Plato participated. So did Aristotle, Sophocles, Pindar, Aeschylus, and Cicero. The Mysteries lasted from approximately the seventh century BCE to 395 CE, nearly a thousand years. They were, as Cicero wrote, 'the best thing Athens ever gave the world.'

If the kykeon was psychedelic, if it produced, in the Telesterion's darkness, a direct encounter with something beyond ordinary consciousness, then Platonic philosophy has a phenomenological source that the standard account omits. The theory of Forms, the claim that this visible world is a shadow of a more real, more permanent, more meaningful world apprehensible through a higher faculty than ordinary sense perception, is precisely what you would construct if you had experienced, in the Telesterion, something that made ordinary reality feel like a shadow.

The experience initiates described: fear and trembling in the limbs, nausea, vertigo, and then a vision, a direct encounter with the divine that transformed their understanding of death and what lay beyond it. This phenomenological pattern is not consistent with theatrical presentation. It is consistent with the ingestion of a psychoactive substance in appropriate conditions.

Critical classicists, most notably Walter Burkert, the preeminent scholar of Greek religion, have argued that the Mysteries worked through theater, suggestion, and the powerful context of the ritual without pharmacology. Burkert died in 2015 and did not see the finding from Mas Castellar de Pontós published in 2019-2020: ergot alkaloids in a ritual vessel associated with the Demeter cult in ancient Catalonia. The 2026 Scientific Reports paper by Antonopoulos and colleagues demonstrated experimentally that lye, available as wood ash in antiquity, converts toxic ergopeptides into water-soluble psychoactive forms at doses achievable through ancient preparation.

The hypothesis has moved from speculative to experimentally feasible and archaeologically evidenced. The direct confirmation, ergot residue at Eleusis itself, has not yet been found, though excavation and analysis are ongoing.

If the hypothesis is correct, the implications for intellectual history are significant. Western philosophy's most foundational distinction, between the apparent world and the real world, between the cave's shadows and the sunlit reality outside, is not a purely rational construction. It is a philosophical articulation of an experienced reality: the reality that initiates encountered in the Telesterion and that Plato, having encountered it himself, spent his life trying to describe in the vocabulary of reason.

This does not undermine the philosophy. The theory of Forms is either true or false regardless of whether it arose from a psychedelic experience or a purely rational argument. But it changes the intellectual history: the beginning of Western philosophy may not be reason alone but reason encountering a specific quality of experience and trying to account for it.

Brian Muraresku's The Immortality Key (2020) extended the argument into early Christianity, proposing that the psychedelic sacrament of the Mysteries survived its formal prohibition in 392 CE through underground transmission into Christian Eucharistic practice. The evidence for this extension is more suggestive than for the Eleusinian hypothesis itself, but the trajectory is clear: if the foundation of Western philosophy is psychedelic, the question of whether the foundation of Western religion is psychedelic becomes unavoidable.

pieces.title: What the Clinical Record Actually Showed: LSD Therapy 1947-1968
pieces.pullQuote: Over a thousand published papers. Forty thousand patients. Roughly fifty percent of treated alcoholics achieving lasting sobriety. The program was not stopped because it failed.
sources: Krebs & Johansen, Lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) for alcoholism: meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, J Psychopharmacol (2012)
Hoffer & Osmond, J. Mental Sci. (1961) [Source not found; under review]
Medical History of Psychedelic Drugs, Cambridge HPS dissertation (2007) [Source not found; under review]
Chwelos, Blewett, Smith & Hoffer, Quarterly Journal of Studies on Alcohol (1959)
pieces.body:
When the Schedule I designation for LSD took effect with the 1970 Controlled Substances Act, it ended a clinical research program that had been running for twenty-three years and had produced results that no subsequent psychiatric intervention has matched in several key areas.

The program began in 1947 when the manufacturer first distributed LSD to psychiatric researchers under a trade name. The accompanying package insert described two potential research applications: as a model of psychosis (for training clinicians in the phenomenology of schizophrenia), and as a treatment for various neurotic conditions by facilitating the surfacing and processing of psychological material.

By 1965, when the manufacturer withdrew its LSD product in response to the counterculture controversy, the clinical literature encompassed over one thousand published papers and reports from dozens of research centers. The patient population was heterogeneous: alcoholics, end-of-life anxiety patients, treatment-resistant depressives, and patients with neurotic disorders of various kinds.

The most robust results came from the alcoholism trials. Hoffer, Osmond and colleagues in Saskatchewan treated many alcoholic patients with LSD-assisted therapy in the 1950s and reported that roughly half improved or stopped drinking (for example Chwelos and colleagues, Quarterly Journal of Studies on Alcohol, 1959). These were uncontrolled reports, and later controlled trials found smaller effects. Their methodology was not by modern standards rigorous, the trials were not randomized and controlled by current criteria, but the consistency of the result across variations in method was sufficient for serious clinical attention.

A 2012 meta-analysis by Krebs and Johansen (Journal of Psychopharmacology) pooled six randomized controlled trials of LSD for alcoholism (536 participants) and found a significant beneficial effect on alcohol misuse, clearest at the earlier follow-ups. The meta-analysis was limited by the quality of the original trials, but its conclusion, that the effect was real and clinically meaningful, was consistent with the broader clinical record.

The end-of-life anxiety results were comparable. Early trials by Walter Pahnke, Sidney Cohen, and others found that LSD-assisted therapy significantly reduced death anxiety in terminal cancer patients and was associated with reported acceptance of death rather than dread. The mechanism, in Pahnke's account, was the mystical experience: patients who had complete mystical experiences during sessions showed the greatest reduction in anxiety.

This finding, that mystical experience quality predicts therapeutic outcome, has been confirmed in the current psilocybin research (Barrett & Griffiths, 2018; Yaden & Griffiths, 2021) and is one of the most consistent findings across the fifty-year interruption. What was established in the LSD trials of the 1950s and 1960s, lost in the prohibition, and reestablished in the psilocybin trials of the 2010s and 2020s, is: the mechanism of psychedelic-assisted therapy is the quality of the consciousness it occasions, not only the pharmacology.

What was stopped in 1968-1970 was not a research program that had reached its natural conclusion. It was a research program in full development, accumulating positive results, refining its methodology, and approaching the stage at which it might have produced regulatory submissions for specific indications.

The industry Phase 3 trials of synthetic psilocybin, reporting in 2025 and 2026, are the research program that the 1970 Controlled Substances Act would have produced forty years earlier if it had not been halted. The clinical evidence for psychedelic-assisted therapy for depression and end-of-life anxiety is now, as of 2026, at Phase 3 quality. This evidence would have existed by approximately 1985 if the program had continued uninterrupted.

Hofmann knew what was being lost in 1968. He had watched the clinical program from inside the company, contributed to it through his pharmacological analysis, and understood its potential. My Problem Child is partly a document of grief: grief for a research program that was working, for patients who needed it, for a medical opportunity that political decisions eliminated.

pieces.title: The Connection Model: Evidence, Limits, and What It Gets Right
pieces.pullQuote: The connection model is not a refutation of pharmacology. It is a correction of the pharmacological-only model. Both things are true: addiction has chemical dimensions and social dimensions, and the policy implication is that you have to address both.
sources: Robins et al., Vietnam Veterans Three Years After Vietnam, Am J Addict (2010 reprint); Robins, Addiction (1993)
Alexander et al., Pharmacology Biochemistry and Behavior (1981)
Bozarth, Murray & Wise, Pharmacology Biochemistry and Behavior (1989)
Robins, Helzer & Davis, Archives of General Psychiatry (1975)
pieces.body:
The central claim of Chasing the Scream, 'the opposite of addiction is connection', is a formulation that clarifies and overstates simultaneously. It clarifies because it redirects attention from the drug to the person and the person's environment. It overstates because pharmacological dependence is real, withdrawal is a physiological process, and social connection, however necessary, is not sufficient to reverse all forms of addiction.

Bruce Alexander and colleagues at Simon Fraser University ran the Rat Park studies in the late 1970s and published them between 1978 and 1981 (Alexander, Coambs and Hadaway, Psychopharmacology, 1978; Hadaway and colleagues, Psychopharmacology, 1979; Alexander and colleagues, Pharmacology Biochemistry and Behavior, 1981). Rats kept alone in standard cages drank more morphine solution than rats living together in a large open colony. Later attempts gave mixed results. Bozarth, Murray and Wise (1989) found that rats housed alone and rats housed in groups both learned to give themselves heroin and reached similar levels after a few weeks. Petrie (1996) could not repeat the housing difference: the isolated rats in his studies drank less than Alexander's had, and he suggested the supplier's rat strain had changed. The original result has not been reliably replicated, although the broader idea that surroundings can change drug taking still has support from other animal and human research.

The Vietnam natural experiment provides the strongest human data. Lee Robins's studies of Vietnam veterans (Archives of General Psychiatry, 1975; Addiction, 1993) found that most men who had been addicted to heroin in Vietnam did not become addicted again after returning home: about 5 percent relapsed to addiction within the first year and about 12 percent within three years, most of them without formal treatment. The most important variable was not pharmacological, it was the radical change in environment. The drug was the same; the context was different; the behavior changed.

This finding, combined with the Rat Park data, supports the general claim that social disconnection is a major driver of addiction. But the phrase 'the opposite of addiction is connection' obscures an important nuance: the Vietnam veterans were not simply getting more connection at home. They were getting a different set of environmental affordances, work, family, housing, purpose, that made drug use both less necessary and less available. 'Connection' is a partial description of a richer social ecology.

The pharmacological critique of Hari's strong formulation is that opioid withdrawal is a genuine physiological process that does not reverse simply because a person feels more connected. George Koob and Nora Volkow's framework, which emphasizes the neuroadaptive changes that chronic drug use produces in reward, stress, and executive function circuits, shows that the brain changes measurably with sustained use, and that these changes persist after environmental improvement.
