Jack Herer published The Emperor Wears No Clothes in 1985 with a specific political economy in mind. Cannabis legalization would distribute economic power to small farmers, local processors, and community businesses. Industrial hemp would replace petrochemical products, paper pulp, and synthetic fibers. The decriminalization of cannabis would restore dignity and economic opportunity to communities destroyed by a century of racially targeted prohibition.

The legal cannabis industry that actually emerged is measurable. By 2025, the combined US legal cannabis market, medical and recreational, was valued at approximately $40 billion annually. Employment in the legal cannabis industry exceeded 400,000 full-time equivalent positions. Tax revenue from cannabis sales across legal states exceeded $15 billion cumulatively since 2014.

These are large numbers. They do not describe Herer's political economy.

Consolidation has proceeded rapidly in every state that has legalized recreational cannabis. The initial wave of small operators, often the activists and advocates who drove legalization, has been largely displaced by multi-state operators (MSOs) with access to capital markets, real estate, and regulatory expertise. California's cannabis market, the largest in the US, consolidated so aggressively that by 2024 most small dispensaries were operating at a loss or had closed. The craft cannabis sector, analogous to craft brewing, exists in some markets but at a small fraction of industry revenue.

Equity provisions in legal cannabis markets have been systematically underfunded. Illinois passed one of the most ambitious social equity frameworks, allocating a percentage of cannabis tax revenue to communities disproportionately impacted by prohibition. By 2024, the program had distributed a fraction of its intended funding due to administrative bottlenecks and legal challenges from non-equity operators.

The racial equity gap has not closed. The ACLU's 2023 analysis found that Black Americans continued to be arrested for marijuana possession in legal states at higher rates than white Americans despite equivalent use rates, the disproportion narrowed but did not disappear. The communities most targeted by the drug war have not received proportionate economic benefit from legalization.

The hemp market, which Herer identified as the most important industrial opportunity, has developed in a different direction from his vision. The 2019-2020 CBD extraction bubble overproduced massively, crashed prices, and eliminated most small hemp farmers. By 2024, the hemp market had restabilized around larger operators with processing infrastructure. Hempcrete is a real product used in some construction projects. Hemp textiles are a small but growing market. Hemp biofuel has not scaled.

The honest assessment: Herer was right that cannabis prohibition was unjust, that the scheduling was scientifically unjustified, and that industrial hemp had commercial potential. He was wrong that legalization, when it came, would empower the communities and create the distributed economic model he envisioned. The industry that emerged is substantially corporate, substantially concentrated, and substantially failing to deliver the social equity that provided the political momentum for legalization in the first place.

pieces.title: Island and Its Limits: Huxley's Utopia Evaluated
pieces.pullQuote: Island is Huxley's answer to Brave New World: the same pharmacological tools used for liberation rather than control. The novel's failure as fiction is part of its value as argument.
pieces.body:
Aldous Huxley published Island in 1962, his final novel, eleven months before his death. It is widely considered his weakest novel and his most important philosophical document. The two judgments are related.

Pala, the island of the title, is a small nation that has integrated Eastern contemplative practice with Western science and Tantric sexuality into a genuinely functional society. The moksha-medicine, a psilocybin-like substance derived from a local mushroom, is used by Palanese at key life transitions: adolescence, serious illness, death. The drug is not recreational. It is sacramental in precisely the sense Huxley meant by 'gratuitous grace': a tool for opening the reducing valve at moments when the reduction is most costly.

The novel fails as fiction because Huxley cannot sustain the dramatic tension required. Pala is too good; the protagonist's cynicism converts too readily; the ending, Indonesian invasion destroys the utopia just as the protagonist achieves enlightenment, arrives as an imported tragedy rather than one grown from the novel's own logic.

But Island is doing something different from what novels usually do. It is a worked example: if you actually designed a society around the principles Huxley developed in The Perennial Philosophy (1945) and The Doors of Perception (1954), what would it look like? How would childhood education work? How would dying work? What would the relationship between science and contemplative practice look like? How would the sacramental use of consciousness-expanding substances be integrated into ordinary life?

These questions are not answered by The Doors of Perception, which describes an experience, not a social structure. Island is the social structure. Its failure as a novel is the price of its success as a thought experiment, characters who exist to demonstrate social arrangements cannot also be psychologically complex in the way that dramatic fiction requires.

The correspondence in Moksha contains Huxley's own uncertainty about whether Island was achieving what he wanted. He writes to Osmond about the difficulty of dramatizing states of consciousness that are, by definition, not reducible to the dramatic. The letters around Island's composition are more philosophically interesting than most of the novel.

pieces.title: The Basel Years: How a Pharmaceutical Company Handled a Sacred Drug
pieces.pullQuote: The manufacturer distributed LSD to researchers worldwide at minimal cost from 1947 to 1966. This was pharmaceutical generosity without precedent. What it meant about the manufacturer's understanding of what it had synthesized is worth examining.
pieces.body:
In 1947, the Basel drug company released LSD under a trade name, as tablets and an injectable solution, as a tool for psychiatric research. The pricing was minimal: the manufacturer supplied LSD to qualified researchers at essentially no cost, treating it as a contribution to science rather than a commercial product.

This decision shaped everything that followed. Because LSD was freely available to researchers, the 1947-1966 period produced over 1,000 scientific papers, treated approximately 40,000 patients in clinical programs, and established a research base that, despite the 1968 scheduling, could not be fully erased. The knowledge existed in published form.

Hofmann's memoir reveals his ambivalence about this period. He was proud of LSD's research applications and troubled by its counterculture appropriation. He understood that the manufacturer's generous distribution had enabled both.

In 1963, under pressure from the US Food and Drug Administration, the manufacturer began restricting distribution, requiring institutional affiliation and research protocols. In 1966, facing the US Congressional hearings on LSD and the wave of negative publicity driven by Leary's public advocacy, the manufacturer withdrew its LSD product from the market entirely and ceased distribution.

The withdrawal ended the clinical research program. It also ended the period in which a pharmaceutical company had voluntarily restrained commercial impulses in the belief that a substance required special handling. Hofmann consistently praised this restraint. He argued that LSD needed to be treated as a sacred drug, carefully, with appropriate protocols, without commercialization, and that the company had, for nearly twenty years, honored this requirement.

The contrast with the current psychedelic industry is stark. Dozens of companies have built commercial pipelines around psychedelic compounds. The manufacturer's model, provide it freely, don't commercialize it, restrict access to qualified researchers, has no analog in the 2020s landscape. Whether this represents necessary adaptation to regulatory reality or a failure of the field's founding values is a question Hofmann's memoir raises implicitly throughout.

pieces.title: The Australian Model: What Happens When a Country Actually Approves
pieces.pullQuote: Australia approved psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression and MDMA for PTSD in February 2023. It is the only country to have done so. The implementation has revealed problems the approval process did not anticipate.
sources: TGA Australia, MDMA and Psilocybin Approval (February 2023)
Therapeutic Goods Administration, Authorized Prescriber Scheme Reports (2024-2025)
Australian Healthcare & Hospitals Association, Psychedelic Therapy Implementation (2025)
pieces.body:
On February 3, 2023, the Australian Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) amended the Poisons Standard to allow authorized psychiatrists to prescribe MDMA for post-traumatic stress disorder and psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression. Australia became the first country in the world to approve psychedelic-assisted therapy as standard of care rather than experimental intervention.

The approval created a framework: licensed psychiatrists could apply for Authorized Prescriber status from the TGA, allowing them to prescribe these substances to eligible patients outside a clinical trial. The framework required that sessions be conducted with trained therapists present and that patients receive appropriate preparation and integration support.

Implementation has been slower and more complicated than the approval announcement suggested. By mid-2024, fewer than 100 psychiatrists had received Authorized Prescriber status nationally. The compound costs, legally produced pharmaceutical-grade psilocybin and MDMA, were high: a full treatment course cost between AUD $25,000 and $35,000 per patient, with no Medicare coverage. Patients were primarily wealthy and privately funded.

A 2025 report from the Australian Healthcare and Hospitals Association identified the central equity problem: the world's first legal psychedelic therapy program was accessible almost exclusively to people with significant private means. The communities with the highest rates of treatment-resistant depression and PTSD, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, veterans, people with histories of trauma, were the least likely to access the approved treatment.

The Australian experience is the most important policy evidence available for what happens after approval. The lesson: approval of the treatment does not solve the access problem. A regulatory framework that permits prescription by authorized psychiatrists at unsubsidized cost produces a boutique treatment for the wealthy. The Australian government is aware of this and working on Medicare coverage pathways; as of mid-2026, coverage has not been established.

For the US approval process: the Australian experience suggests that FDA approval of synthetic psilocybin psilocybin, when it comes, will produce an initial market serving a narrow population. Whether the equity framework develops from there, or whether the Australian model of expensive boutique treatment becomes the US default, is the most important downstream policy question.

pieces.title: The Students of Schultes: What the Next Generation Found
pieces.pullQuote: Schultes trained a generation of ethnobotanists who went back to the communities he had documented. What they found was a race against time that Schultes had warned about and no one had adequately funded.
sources: Plotkin, Tales of a Shaman's Apprentice (1993)
pieces.body:
Richard Evans Schultes trained more than the 3,000 undergraduates who passed through his Harvard Economic Botany course. He trained a generation of field ethnobotanists who took his methods and his urgency into the field: Wade Davis, Mark Plotkin, Glenn Shepard, William Milliken, among others. Their fieldwork, conducted primarily in the 1980s and 1990s, extended Schultes's documentation project into the period when the race he had described in 1967 was visibly being lost.

Mark Plotkin's Tales of a Shaman's Apprentice (1993) documented his work with the Tirio people of Suriname and Brazil. What Plotkin found was Schultes's aspirin-pill problem in acute form: young Tirio men were choosing to train as health workers in the Western medical system rather than as traditional plant medicine practitioners. The knowledge was not being transmitted. The healer Plotkin had apprenticed himself to had no successor in the traditional sense.

Wade Davis's One River (1996) reconstructed Schultes's Amazon expeditions through Davis's own fieldwork in the same regions, twenty years later. What Davis documented was both the persistence of the knowledge and its precarity, specific villages still had healers with specific knowledge, but the healers were old, the apprentices were fewer, and the botanical contexts were under pressure from agricultural expansion, mining, and road development.

The Amazon Conservation Team, founded by Plotkin in 1996, developed a documentation methodology, community-controlled mapping projects that recorded traditional knowledge in formats the communities themselves owned, that has become a model for ethnobotanical preservation. By 2025, the ACT had supported territory mapping and knowledge documentation projects in more than 70 indigenous communities across the Amazon basin.

What the students of Schultes found, collectively, is that documentation is necessary but not sufficient. The knowledge does not survive in an archive, it survives in people, and people survive in communities, and communities survive on territories. The ethnobotanical preservation project is inseparable from the land rights project.

pieces.title: The Peyote Exemption: How Indigenous Rights Shaped Drug Law
pieces.pullQuote: The 1994 AIRFA amendments created a specific federal exemption for NAC peyote use. This is the only federally recognized right to use a Schedule I substance for religious purposes that was not created by litigation.
sources: American Indian Religious Freedom Act Amendments (1994)
Peyote Way Church of God v. Thornburgh (5th Cir. 1991)
pieces.body:
The Native American Church's use of peyote in religious ceremonies has been legally protected since the 1994 amendments to the American Indian Religious Freedom Act, but the road to that protection was neither simple nor complete.

In 1990, the Supreme Court in Employment Division v. Smith held that the First Amendment does not require religious exemptions from neutral laws of general applicability. The case involved Alfred Smith and Galen Black, Native American members of the NAC who were fired from drug counseling jobs and denied unemployment benefits after testing positive for peyote following a religious ceremony. The Smith decision effectively removed constitutional protection for peyote use in NAC ceremonies.

Congress responded with the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (1993) and then specifically with the 1994 AIRFA amendments, which added a provision explicitly protecting the use, possession, transportation, and sale of peyote for bona fide religious ceremonies of the Native American Church. This created a statutory exemption, not a constitutional right, for NAC peyote use.

The exemption is NAC-specific. Non-Native practitioners who use peyote for spiritual purposes do not receive the same protection, even within the same ceremony. The Peyote Way Church of God, a predominantly non-Native organization that uses peyote sacramentally, challenged this restriction and lost in the Fifth Circuit in 1991: the court held that the racial classification of the NAC exemption served the compelling government interest of protecting Native American culture.

Colorado's Proposition 122 (2022) navigated this history by decriminalizing mescaline but explicitly excluding peyote from the decriminalization. The drafters made a deliberate choice: the conservation status of peyote and the specific interests of the NAC warranted keeping the plant outside a broader decriminalization framework.

Schultes documented the Huichol peyote pilgrimage with care and respect. The legal history of peyote's status reveals how complicated the relationship between indigenous plant medicine rights and broader drug policy reform has been, and continues to be.

pieces.title: The Archive and the Fire: Ethnobotany in the Extinction Era
pieces.pullQuote: We are losing knowledge faster than we can document it. The documentation projects are real and insufficient. What Schultes called urgency in 1967 is now crisis.
sources: Brondizio et al., IPBES Global Assessment (2019)
pieces.body:
In 1967, Richard Evans Schultes told the NIMH symposium in San Francisco that ethnopharmacological research was racing against time. The aspirin pill was arriving. The mission school was transmitting different values. The road was bringing the market. The race to document indigenous plant knowledge before it disappeared was urgent.

Fifty-seven years later, the race he described has not been won. The question is whether it can still be won in meaningful form, or whether the knowledge systems Schultes dedicated his career to documenting are now too damaged to restore.

The evidence: the global language extinction rate, relevant because language is the primary carrier of traditional ecological knowledge, has accelerated. David Harmon and Jonathan Loh's work (for example The Index of Linguistic Diversity, Language Documentation & Conservation, 2010) found that languages and biodiversity are correlated geographically and decline together. The regions with the greatest biological diversity contain the most linguistic diversity; both are under the most pressure. A widely repeated estimate holds that one language is lost every two weeks (Source not found; under review), each taking with it specific knowledge of local ecology, plant uses, and the social context in which that knowledge was transmitted.

The IPBES Global Assessment (2019), the most comprehensive scientific review of biodiversity loss, found that indigenous and local knowledge is declining rapidly alongside the biodiversity it describes. The assessment identified indigenous-managed territories as the most effective conservation units on the planet while documenting the legal and economic pressures that are displacing indigenous peoples from those territories.

The documentation response has been substantial: the Biodiversity Heritage Library has digitized over 60 million pages of botanical literature. The Global Biodiversity Information Facility aggregates millions of specimen records. Ethnobotanical databases at Kew, the Missouri Botanical Garden, and Harvard contain structured records of plant uses across cultures. Schultes's own 24,000 specimens are curated and accessible.

What these archives cannot preserve is what Schultes's colleague Paul Alan Cox called 'the living laboratory of indigenous medicine': the dynamic, context-dependent, community-embedded knowledge that determines when a plant is appropriate, how it is prepared for a specific condition, what spiritual or ceremonial context surrounds its use, and what contraindications experienced practitioners recognize. This knowledge is transmitted person-to-person, in specific landscapes, over years of practice. No database can hold it.

Mark Plotkin's Amazon Conservation Team developed community-controlled knowledge mapping as a partial response: the communities themselves decide what is documented, in what format, and with what access restrictions. The mapped knowledge stays with the community; the ACT provides technical support and legal protection for the territories in which the knowledge is embedded. This approach has documented knowledge in 70+ communities over 30 years.

The limitation: documentation preserves a record of what was known. It does not preserve the capacity to use that knowledge, the trained practitioner who can apply it, the ecological context in which the plants grow, the social institutions that structured its transmission. Schultes's herbarium is one of the most valuable botanical collections in the world. The communities that helped him fill it are smaller, more fragmented, and under more pressure than when he visited them.

The honest assessment of where ethnobotany stands in 2026: the field has done more than Schultes could have imagined in 1967 to document what exists. The forces he identified as threatening, the aspirin pill, the road, the market, have accelerated beyond what the documentation projects can match. The knowledge is being preserved in archives at roughly the same rate as it is being lost from communities. This is not sufficient, and everyone in the field knows it.

pieces.title: Who Owns the Pharmacopoeia: Intellectual Property and Sacred Plants
pieces.pullQuote: Schultes documented 24,000 specimens. The communities who guided him have no legal claim to the 78 pharmaceutical compounds derived from his work. The Nagoya Protocol covers new exploitation. It does not remedy old exploitation.
sources: Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979)
Swanson, Biotechnology and the Problem of Property (1994) [Source not found; under review]
Global Health Innovation Center, Traditional Knowledge and IP (2025)
pieces.body:
Richard Evans Schultes's Amazon herbarium represents one of the world's most valuable repositories of traditional botanical knowledge in Western scientific format. The 24,000 specimens he collected, the detailed field notes, the chemical analyses conducted with Hofmann and others, this archive has been the foundation for botanical, pharmacological, and ethnopharmacological research for fifty years.

Seventy-eight pharmaceutical compounds have been derived from or developed in response to plants documented in the ethnobotanical tradition that Schultes represented. The communities whose knowledge guided the documentation have received no systematic benefit from these compounds.

The intellectual property framework that governs this situation has two parts. The first part, historical exploitation, is outside the reach of any current international agreement. The Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit-Sharing covers new commercial exploitation of genetic resources and traditional knowledge, not exploitation that occurred before its entry into force in 2014. The debt to the communities whose knowledge produced the pharmacopoeia has no legal mechanism for remediation.

The second part, new exploitation, is theoretically covered by Nagoya, but implementation is weak. A 2025 Global Health Innovation Center analysis found that the majority of pharmaceutical companies with products derived from traditional plant knowledge had not conducted the prior informed consent and benefit-sharing negotiations Nagoya requires. Enforcement is left to national authorities who frequently lack the capacity or political will to pursue multinational pharmaceutical companies.

The psychedelic industry presents a specific current case. Psilocybin is derived from mushrooms documented extensively by Schultes and others from indigenous Mexican traditions. Ibogaine is derived from the iboga shrub of the Gabonese Bwiti tradition. Both are now the subject of commercial pharmaceutical development programs with patent portfolios and investor backing. Neither program has established benefit-sharing relationships with the communities of origin that would meet the Nagoya standard.

Schultes's work was conducted in the colonial scientific tradition, take specimens, take knowledge, publish in Western journals, build careers at Western institutions. He was personally respectful of the communities he worked with and documented their knowledge with more care than most of his contemporaries. But the structural arrangement was extractive regardless of his personal intentions. The communities remain outside the benefit stream.

pieces.title: MDMA After the Rejection: What the 2024 FDA Decision Actually Means
pieces.pullQuote: The FDA rejected the first psychedelic NDA in August 2024. The reasons were methodological, not efficacy-based. Whether this is regulatory caution or regulatory failure is the most important contested question in the field.
sources: FDA advisory committee briefing documents, MDMA-assisted therapy application (June 2024)
Yaden et al., Nature Mental Health (2024) [Source not found; under review]
pieces.body:
In June 2024, the FDA's Psychopharmacologic Drugs Advisory Committee voted 10-1 that the evidence did not support approval of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD. In August 2024, the FDA issued a Complete Response Letter declining to approve the sponsor's MDMA application, the first formal application to approve a psychedelic-assisted therapy.

The data: the Phase 3 trials (MAPP1 and MAPP2) enrolled 263 participants with severe PTSD. In MAPP1, 67% of the MDMA group no longer met PTSD diagnostic criteria at follow-up, compared to 32% of placebo. In MAPP2, 71% versus 48%. The treatment differences were statistically significant. The effect sizes were large by psychiatric standards.

The FDA's concerns were not about whether MDMA helped participants. They were about whether the trials demonstrated that MDMA specifically, independent of the intensive psychotherapy surrounding it, was responsible for the benefit, and whether the safety characterization was adequate.

The unblinding problem: participants who receive active MDMA know they've received it, the phenomenological effects are unmistakable. This breaks the double-blind standard that FDA drug approvals depend on. If participants know they've received the active drug, therapist and patient expectancy effects cannot be controlled. The measured treatment difference might be partly or largely attributable to expectancy rather than pharmacology.

The committee was also concerned about therapist boundary violations: reports of therapists engaging in inappropriate conduct with MDMA-treated patients during sessions, including the high-profile accusations against therapists at several trial sites. The FDA found that the safety monitoring for therapist behavior was inadequate.

The FDA's position, as expressed in the Complete Response Letter, was not that MDMA doesn't help people with PTSD. It was that the current trial design cannot demonstrate what specifically causes the benefit in a way that meets FDA standards for drug approval.

David Yaden and colleagues at Johns Hopkins are cited as publishing a 2024 perspective in Nature Mental Health (Source not found; under review) arguing that the FDA's methodological standards were appropriate and that the field needed to develop better trial designs, including active placebos that mimic some phenomenological features of MDMA without the therapeutic effects, and more careful separation of drug and psychotherapy components.

MAPS and others have argued the opposite: that the FDA's standards are impossible to meet for a drug whose mechanism of action involves the subjective experience itself, and that the unblinding problem is a feature of the treatment rather than a methodological flaw to be designed around.

Jay Stevens wrote in Storming Heaven about a research program ended not by scientific failure but by political conditions. The MDMA situation is structurally different: the political conditions in 2024 are more favorable to psychedelic therapy than they were in 1968. The challenge is methodological, not political. But the result, a promising clinical program unable to achieve approval despite positive efficacy data, has structural similarities.

As of mid-2026, the sponsor is working on the design of an additional Phase 3 trial that addresses the FDA's methodological concerns. Whether an adequate design is possible, and whether the company can fund it, are open questions. MDMA remains Schedule I in the US while Australia has approved it for clinical use. The gap between the evidence and the approval will persist until the methodological problem is solved or the approval standard is revised.

pieces.title: Rick Strassman's DMT Trials: The First Controlled Research
pieces.pullQuote: Strassman administered IV DMT to 60 participants in 400 sessions at the University of New Mexico from 1990 to 1995. He documented entity contact in the majority of sessions. He didn't know what to do with the data.
sources: Strassman et al., Arch. Gen. Psychiatry (1994)
pieces.body:
Rick Strassman's DMT research program at the University of New Mexico was the first controlled clinical study of a classic psychedelic in the United States in over twenty years. From 1990 to 1995, working under DEA Schedule I researcher registration and IRB approval, Strassman administered intravenous DMT to 60 participants in approximately 400 sessions.

The primary published findings concerned dose-response relationships, cardiovascular safety, endocrine effects, and subjective experience ratings (using the Hallucinogen Rating Scale). These findings, published in Archives of General Psychiatry in 1994 and subsequent journals, established that IV DMT produced rapid, intense, brief (15-30 minute) experiences with a manageable safety profile across the range of doses tested.

What the published papers did not fully capture, and what Strassman's 2001 book DMT: The Spirit Molecule communicated to a general audience, was the consistency of entity contact across participants. In the majority of high-dose sessions, participants reported encountering autonomous entities: beings who seemed to be present in a real place, who sometimes communicated, who were experienced as independent rather than as products of the participant's imagination.

Strassman describes his own disorientation at this finding: his training had not prepared him to take entity contact seriously as a phenomenon requiring explanation, yet the consistency of the reports across participants with no prior psychedelic experience, and the specificity of their descriptions, made dismissal difficult.

The 2023 Imperial College fMRI study (Timmermann et al., PNAS 120(13)) mapped DMT's global brain effects, large increases in global functional connectivity, network disintegration and desegregation, and compression of the principal cortical gradient. It did not isolate entity contact as a distinct neural signature, and no published imaging study yet has: the phenomenology is well documented, the neural specificity is not. The reports are real as reports; no neural correlate specific to entity contact has been identified. Strassman spent twenty years wondering what it meant. The interpretation remains open.

pieces.title: The Ayahuasca Churches: From Brazil to the Supreme Court
pieces.pullQuote: The União do Vegetal won at the Supreme Court in 2006. The case was unanimous. The opinion was written by Chief Justice Roberts. It is the most important legal precedent for psychedelic religious freedom in American history.
sources: Gonzales v. O Centro Espirita Beneficente Uniao do Vegetal (2006)
pieces.body:
The União do Vegetal (UDV) is a Brazilian syncretic religion founded in 1961 by José Gabriel da Costa, known as Mestre Gabriel, in Porto Velho. Its sacrament is hoasca, ayahuasca, consumed in ritual ceremonies presided over by trained mestres. The UDV has approximately 20,000 members in Brazil and several thousand in the United States.

In 1999, DEA agents raided the UDV's New Mexico temple and seized hoasca, charging the organization with violation of the Controlled Substances Act. The UDV sued, arguing that the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA) protected their sacramental use of hoasca.

The case reached the Supreme Court as Gonzales v. O Centro Espirita Beneficente Uniao do Vegetal. On February 21, 2006, the Court ruled unanimously in favor of the UDV. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote the opinion: the government had not demonstrated a compelling interest that overrode the UDV's sincere religious use of hoasca under RFRA. The government's arguments, that DMT is Schedule I and that allowing UDV use would undermine drug control generally, were rejected as insufficient to meet RFRA's compelling interest standard.

The Gonzales ruling is the bedrock of American psychedelic religious freedom law. It established that RFRA protects sincere religious psychedelic use from the Controlled Substances Act, and that the government must demonstrate a compelling interest by least restrictive means before overriding such use.

As of 2026, four US organizations have DEA exemptions for ayahuasca: the UDV (SCOTUS 2006), Santo Daime (9th Circuit 2009), the Iowaska Church of Healing (DEA settlement 2024), and the Church of Gaia (first non-litigation DEA approval, May 2025). All other ayahuasca ceremonies in the US operate without federal legal protection, though prosecution is rare. McKenna's DMT visions, which he described in True Hallucinations, are the experiential territory these legal battles have been fought over.

pieces.title: Psychedelic Science 2025: The Field Comes Back Together
pieces.pullQuote: Psychedelic Science 2025 drew 12,000 attendees to Denver in June 2025. It was the largest psychedelic conference in history. The field that had been underground for fifty years assembled publicly.
pieces.body:
The Psychedelic Science 2025 conference, held in Denver in June 2025, drew approximately 12,000 attendees over five days, researchers, clinicians, policymakers, advocates, facilitators, investors, journalists, and curious members of the public. It was the largest gathering in the history of psychedelic science.

The content spanned the full range of the field: Phase 3 clinical results, regulatory strategy, indigenous knowledge and ethics, harm reduction, business development, veteran advocacy, religious freedom law, and the political coalition that had produced $50 million in Texas ibogaine research funding. Colorado Governor Jared Polis announced pardons for people convicted of state psychedelic possession charges.

The conference captured the field's current character: genuinely bipartisan, genuinely complex, and in some tension with itself. The researchers presenting Phase 3 clinical data were sharing space with advocates for decriminalization and with indigenous leaders arguing that commercialization of plant medicines without benefit-sharing was a continuation of colonial extraction.

Rick Perry, former Republican Governor of Texas, Secretary of Energy under Trump, was there, speaking about ibogaine for veterans. Rick Doblin, MAPS founder, psychedelic activist for forty years, was there, still arguing for the therapeutic framework after the FDA rejection of MDMA. Shipibo-Conibo healers were there, expressing concern about the commodification of their traditions.

This is the world McKenna was trying to describe when he talked about the Archaic Revival: a moment when psychedelic plant knowledge returned to public discourse, when the institutions that had suppressed it could no longer ignore it, when the culture was reconsidering its relationship to consciousness. Whether the conference represented the Archaic Revival or its co-optation is the question McKenna's framework asks, and which Psychedelic Science 2025 did not resolve.

pieces.title: Scheduling Endogenous Compounds: The DMT Paradox
pieces.pullQuote: The human body produces DMT. The compound is detectable in blood and urine under normal physiological conditions. Its Schedule I status, 'no accepted medical use, high abuse potential', applies to a compound the body makes.
sources: Strassman et al., Arch. Gen. Psychiatry (1994)
Barker, McIlhenny & Strassman, Drug Testing and Analysis (2012)
pieces.body:
Dimethyltryptamine is Schedule I under the US Controlled Substances Act. It has been since the Controlled Substances Act of 1970. Schedule I status means: high potential for abuse, no currently accepted medical use, lack of accepted safety for use under medical supervision.

DMT is also produced by the human body. Barker, McIlhenny and Strassman's 2012 review in Drug Testing and Analysis collected reports of DMT detected in human blood, urine and cerebrospinal fluid, while noting inconsistent methods across studies. It is produced by the lung, retina, and likely other tissues from the amino acid tryptophan through the enzyme aromatic amino acid decarboxylase. The human body manufactures a Schedule I controlled substance as part of normal metabolism.

This creates a legal paradox that has no clean resolution. The Controlled Substances Act schedules chemical compounds; it does not create an exception for endogenous production. The DEA's enforcement focus is on the manufacture, distribution, and possession of DMT in quantities and forms associated with deliberate use, not on the trace amounts found in blood under normal conditions. But the legal distinction between endogenous and exogenous DMT is not written into the law.

The clinical significance: Rick Strassman's hypothesis, that the pineal gland produces elevated DMT during near-death experiences, deep meditation, and REM sleep, has not been confirmed. Strassman documented the hypothesis in DMT: The Spirit Molecule (2001) and has advocated for research to test it. The specific claim about pineal production is disputed; the broader claim about endogenous DMT as a component of altered states remains an active research area.

Colorado's Proposition 122 decriminalized personal possession of DMT alongside psilocybin, ibogaine, and mescaline. The decriminalization applies to the compound as it appears in plant preparations, ayahuasca, for example, and in synthetic form. It does not change the federal Schedule I status. McKenna's account of DMT experiences in True Hallucinations describes encounters with the Schedule I version. Whether they engaged the same system the body uses endogenously is a question the law cannot answer and science has not yet resolved.

pieces.title: The Hemp Economy Herer Predicted: Industrial Cannabis in 2026
pieces.pullQuote: Herer was right that hemp had substantial industrial potential. He was wrong that it would undercut petrochemicals, synthetic fibers, and timber paper. The market that emerged is real and modest. It is not the revolution he described.
sources: Herer, The Emperor Wears No Clothes (1985)
Cannabis market research firm, Hemp Market Report (2024)
pieces.body:
Jack Herer's 1985 argument rested on a specific empirical claim: that industrial hemp, Cannabis sativa grown for fiber, seed, and stalk rather than cannabinoid content, was the most versatile industrial crop in agricultural history, capable of replacing petrochemical plastics, synthetic fibers, timber paper, and fossil fuels if prohibition were lifted. He documented this claim with historical sources, scientific studies, and the 1942 US government film Hemp for Victory, which had urged American farmers to grow hemp for the war effort before prohibition resumed afterward.

The Agricultural Improvement Act of 2018, the Farm Bill, removed hemp from the Controlled Substances Act, defining hemp as Cannabis sativa with THC content below 0.3% by dry weight. This ended eighty years of federal prohibition on hemp cultivation in the United States. By 2025, hemp was being grown commercially in approximately 35 states.

The hemp economy that emerged is real. It is not the one Herer described.

The 2018-2020 CBD extraction bubble was the first major commercial wave. Farmers planted hemp for CBD extraction, the cannabidiol compound extracted from the flowers, responding to a perceived consumer demand for CBD wellness products. The market overproduced massively. By 2020, CBD hemp was selling for less than the cost of processing it. Thousands of farmers lost money. The CBD extraction market has since stabilized at a smaller scale, dominated by larger operators with processing infrastructure rather than the small family farms Herer's vision implied.

Industrial hemp fiber and seed markets have developed more steadily. Hemp textiles are a growing category, with brands including an outdoor clothing company and Levi's incorporating hemp fiber blends. Hempcrete, a building material combining hemp hurds (the woody core of the stalk) with lime, is used in a small number of construction projects and has attracted architectural interest for its carbon-sequestering properties. Hemp seed oil and hemp seed protein are established food market categories. Hemp-derived CBD gummies are available in gas stations across America.

What has not developed: hemp biofuel at commercial scale. Hemp-derived plastic replacing petroleum plastic at commercial scale. Hemp paper replacing timber paper at commercial scale. The industrial hemp economy Herer described, in which hemp's superior yield per acre would make it economically irresistible as a replacement for less efficient crops and petrochemical products, has not materialized in the seven years since re-legalization.

The reasons are structural. Industrial hemp processing requires infrastructure, decorticators for separating fiber from stalk, retting facilities, specialized equipment, that was dismantled or never built during the prohibition decades. Rebuilding that infrastructure requires capital investment that takes time and carries risk. Petrochemical supply chains are deeply embedded with cost structures that hemp cannot undercut in the near term even with equivalent performance. Timber paper production has its own entrenched infrastructure.

Herer's claim about hemp's potential was not fabricated. The historical record he documented, hemp as a significant American agricultural product before prohibition, capable of producing fiber, fuel, paper, and medicine, is accurate. His claim that re-legalization would produce rapid industrial transformation underestimated the structural inertia of existing supply chains and the infrastructure gap created by eighty years of prohibition.

The honest assessment in 2026: industrial hemp is a real and growing market, probably reaching $10-15 billion annually within the next decade. It is a specialty agricultural category, not an industrial revolution. Herer was right about the prohibition being unjust and right about the agricultural potential. He was optimistic about the pace and scale of the transformation.

pieces.title: The Ayahuasca Science Since Narby: What Twenty-Five Years of Research Has Found
pieces.pullQuote: Narby published in 1998, when there was almost no controlled research on ayahuasca. There is now. The combinatorial problem he posed remains open. Everything else is better understood.
sources: Dos Santos et al., Ther Adv Psychopharmacol (2016)
pieces.body:
When Jeremy Narby published The Cosmic Serpent in 1998, controlled clinical research on ayahuasca was essentially nonexistent in Western scientific literature. He was writing about a phenomenon, the pharmacological effects and cultural context of ayahuasca, that had been documented by ethnobotanists and anthropologists but not studied in clinical settings. The Hoasca Project (1993), a collaboration between Brazilian and American researchers studying União do Vegetal members, was the first controlled study of long-term ayahuasca use, and it had only recently been published.

Twenty-five years later the research landscape is substantially different. The mechanism is well characterized. The therapeutic applications are actively studied. The phenomenology has been measured in hundreds of subjects. The combinatorial problem Narby posed remains open. Everything else is better understood.

THE PHARMACOLOGY

Ayahuasca is a brew prepared from Banisteriopsis caapi (a vine containing β-carboline alkaloids, harmine, harmaline, tetrahydroharmine) and Psychotria viridis or Diplopterys cabrerana (leaves containing N,N-dimethyltryptamine). The β-carbolines are monoamine oxidase inhibitors that prevent the gut and liver from metabolizing DMT before it reaches the central nervous system. Without MAO inhibition, orally ingested DMT is pharmacologically inactive. The combination produces 4-6 hour psychedelic experiences with a characteristic phenomenology.

The specific 5-HT2A receptor binding that drives the psychedelic effects is now characterized at atomic resolution. The contribution of each alkaloid to the overall experience, harmine's mild stimulant effect, tetrahydroharmine's serotonin reuptake inhibition, DMT's primary hallucinogenic action, is reasonably well understood at the receptor level.

THERAPEUTIC RESEARCH

Rafael Guimarães dos Santos and colleagues at the University of São Paulo reviewed studies of ayahuasca, psilocybin and LSD for depression, anxiety and addiction (Therapeutic Advances in Psychopharmacology, 2016). They found promising antidepressant, anti-anxiety and anti-addictive effects, mostly from small or uncontrolled studies. The neuroplasticity mechanism, BDNF upregulation, dendritic spine growth, provides a pharmacological explanation for both the rapid onset and the lasting duration.

A 2019 review in Current Neuropharmacology by Hamill and colleagues summarized ayahuasca research in addiction and mental illness and reported generally positive but preliminary findings. The evidence base is substantially weaker than for psilocybin (fewer RCTs, smaller samples, more heterogeneous preparation) but points in the same direction.

THE ENTITY CONTACT QUESTION

Narby's specific focus, the consistency of serpentine imagery and entity contact across shamanic traditions, has been documented further in surveys, though not explained. Timmermann et al.'s 2023 PNAS paper, using simultaneous EEG-fMRI during IV DMT administration, mapped DMT's global brain effects, large increases in global functional connectivity, network disintegration and desegregation, and compression of the principal cortical gradient. It did not isolate entity contact as a distinct neural signature, and no published imaging study yet has: the phenomenology is well documented, the neural specificity is not. Similar reports are well documented in self-selected surveys. Neural correlates specific to entity contact have not been identified. The interpretation, whether entities are produced by the brain or perceived through the brain, is not settled by neuroscience.

THE COMBINATORIAL PROBLEM

Narby's core puzzle, how Amazonian peoples identified the specific combination of these two plants from 80,000 candidate species in the absence of any obvious single-session discovery mechanism, remains without an accepted scientific explanation. No controlled research has addressed the acquisition question. The pharmacological interaction is understood; its discovery by human beings without the tools of Western pharmacology is not. This remains the most genuinely open question Narby raised.

pieces.title: Peyote Under Pressure: Conservation, Native Rights, and the Psychedelic Industry
pieces.pullQuote: Peyote is not a recreational drug that happens to be used ceremonially. It is a sacrament under ecological pressure from the same forces that benefit financially from other psychedelics becoming legal. This is the most acute ethical contradiction in the current psychedelic moment.
sources: Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979)
Labate & Cavnar, Peyote: History, Tradition, Politics, and Conservation (2016)
Gehr, Drugs of the Dreamtime (2021) [Source not found; under review]
Native American Church of North America, Conservation Statement (2023)
pieces.body:
Richard Evans Schultes documented peyote ceremonies with the Huichol (Wixáritari) people of central Mexico in the 1930s and 1940s, the weeks-long pilgrimage to Wirikuta, the sacred desert where peyote grows; the careful harvesting protocol that leaves the root system intact; the prayers that accompany each cut. He was observing a practice continuous for at least 5,000 years, possibly much longer. Peyote use is documented in the archaeological record of northeastern Mexico at least from 3780-3660 BCE.

As of 2026, Lophophora williamsii, peyote, is listed as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. Its range in Texas and northern Mexico has contracted by more than 30% since the 1970s due to habitat loss, agricultural expansion, ranching, and overharvesting. The conservation crisis Schultes warned about has materialized.

The NAC DIMENSION

Approximately 250,000-500,000 members of the Native American Church use peyote ceremonially in the United States. The legal protection for this use, established by the 1994 AIRFA amendments after the Supreme Court's 1990 Employment Division v. Smith decision removed constitutional protection, is specific to Native American Church members and bona fide ceremonial use. Non-Native ceremonial use of peyote is not federally protected.

The NAC does not buy peyote from commercial distributors. It sources it from licensed distributors in Texas, the only US state where peyote grows commercially, who harvest from private ranchlands under DEA license. The supply is constrained by the limited range, the slow growth rate of the plant (it takes 10-20 years to reach harvestable size), and the increasing demand from a growing NAC membership base.

The NAC has explicitly requested that peyote be excluded from psychedelic decriminalization and legalization measures. Colorado's Proposition 122 honored this request, it decriminalized mescaline while specifically excluding peyote. Oregon's Measure 109 does not address peyote. The NAC's concern is straightforward: any expansion of legal access to peyote beyond current NAC ceremonial use will increase harvesting pressure on a plant already under conservation threat, and will appropriate a sacred practice without the cultural context that gives it meaning.

THE INDUSTRY CONTRADICTION

The psychedelic industry's relationship to peyote is the most acute ethical contradiction in the current moment. Mescaline, the active compound in peyote, is of commercial interest as a therapeutic compound. Several companies have filed patents for mescaline derivatives and synthetic mescaline production processes. Synthetic mescaline, produced in a laboratory, would not require peyote harvesting and would not raise conservation concerns. The NAC has not objected to synthetic mescaline research.

The objection is to the cultural context: the use of peyote or its derivatives in therapeutic or recreational frameworks that extract the pharmacological compound from the ceremonial tradition that developed it, stewarded it, and protected it through a century of criminalization. From the NAC's perspective, the psychedelic industry's interest in mescaline-derived compounds is another form of the extraction that has characterized Indigenous-Western relations for five centuries, taking the useful part without acknowledging the source.

Schultes's documentation of the Huichol peyote pilgrimage in Plants of the Gods was careful and respectful. He understood that the ceremony was inseparable from the plant's meaning. The current psychedelic industry's engagement with mescaline and peyote derivatives is largely divorced from that understanding, focused on the pharmacological mechanism, not the cultural context.

THE CONSERVATION PATH

Several conservation projects are attempting to address the peyote shortage. The Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies (MAPS) has supported peyote cultivation research. The Cactus Conservation Institute documents peyote populations. Some NAC members and affiliated organizations have established small-scale cultivation operations. The growth rate of the plant, the same characteristic that Schultes documented in Huichol harvesting protocols, makes scaling cultivation difficult. A peyote cactus planted today will not be harvestable for a decade.

The conservation problem and the cultural appropriation problem are connected: the resolution that serves both is synthetic mescaline for non-Native therapeutic use, combined with legal protection for NAC ceremonial use of natural peyote, combined with funded conservation of wild peyote populations. This framework has been articulated by the NAC and has not been implemented at policy level.

pieces.title: April 19, 1943
pieces.pullQuote: Everything in my field of vision wavered and was distorted as if seen in a curved mirror.
sources: Preller et al., Changes in global and thalamic brain connectivity in LSD-induced altered states of consciousness are attributable to the 5-HT2A receptor, eLife (2018)
Grinspoon, L. LSD Reconsidered: Should clinical research be resumed? The Sciences (January 1981)
Krebs & Johansen, Lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) for alcoholism: meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, J Psychopharmacol (2012)
Strassman & Qualls, Dose-response study of N,N-dimethyltryptamine in humans I, Arch Gen Psychiatry (1994)
Griffiths et al., Psilocybin can occasion mystical-type experiences having substantial and sustained personal meaning and spiritual significance, Psychopharmacology (2006)
Gasser et al., Safety and efficacy of lysergic acid diethylamide-assisted psychotherapy for anxiety associated with life-threatening diseases, J Nerv Ment Dis (2014)
Albert Hofmann (1906 to 2008), University of Zurich Department of Chemistry symposium page
pieces.body:
Albert Hofmann's laboratory journal for April 19, 1943 holds three short entries. In his later account of that day he says the notes end there, and that he managed the last words only with great effort.

Hofmann was a chemist at a Basel drug company, working on ergot alkaloids. In 1938 he had made the twenty-fifth compound in a series of lysergic acid derivatives, LSD-25, hoping for a circulatory and respiratory stimulant. The pharmacologists recorded a strong effect on the uterus and noted that the test animals grew restless, but they showed no special interest, and testing stopped. Five years later, in the spring of 1943, a hunch that the substance might have properties the first tests had missed led him to make it again.

On Friday, April 16, in the middle of the afternoon, he had to stop work. He felt restless and slightly dizzy, went home and lay down. In the report he sent to Professor Stoll at the company, he described an "uninterrupted stream of fantastic pictures, extraordinary shapes with intense, kaleidoscopic play of colors." The state faded after about two hours. He suspected that a trace of the solution had touched his fingertips during crystallization and been absorbed through the skin.

Three days later, on Monday, April 19, Hofmann decided to test that guess with a deliberate self-experiment. The date is now marked by enthusiasts as Bicycle Day. He chose what he believed was the smallest amount that could produce any effect, judging by what was then known about ergot alkaloids, and took it at 4:20 in the afternoon, diluted in water. It proved too much. The volunteers Werner Stoll tested in Zurich a few years later received substantially less, and Hofmann himself wrote that the grave side effects of his session came from overdosage.

Forty minutes later his journal records "dizziness, feeling of anxiety, visual distortions, symptoms of paralysis, desire to laugh." A supplement dated April 21 adds that he went home by bicycle and that the worst of the crisis ran from six to about eight that evening. He asked his laboratory assistant to escort him, and with no automobile available because of wartime restrictions, they rode. His field of vision wavered as if seen in a curved mirror. He felt unable to move from the spot, although the assistant told him afterward that they had traveled very fast.

At home he could barely ask his companion to summon the family doctor and to ask the neighbors for milk, which he chose as a general antidote for poisoning. The neighbor who brought it was, to him, "a malevolent, insidious witch with a colored mask." He feared he was going insane. He asked himself, "Was I dying?"

By the time the doctor arrived, the worst had passed. The doctor found extremely dilated pupils and nothing else abnormal. Pulse, blood pressure and breathing were normal. Slowly the terror gave way, and Hofmann began to watch the colors and shapes behind his closed eyes. This was the first documented deliberate LSD experience, and for several hours it was frightening.

He slept, and woke refreshed. Walking in the garden after a spring rain, he wrote, "everything glistened and sparkled in a fresh light. The world was as if newly created."

Hofmann could only guess at the mechanism. After serotonin was identified in the brain, early researchers suspected that LSD acted through it. David Nichols's 2016 review in Pharmacological Reviews reports a consensus that psychedelics act as agonists or partial agonists at the serotonin 5-HT2A receptor, with particular importance for receptors on pyramidal cells in layer V of the cortex. In a 2018 study, Preller and colleagues gave LSD to 24 healthy volunteers. It changed connectivity across the brain, including the thalamus, and a drug that blocks the 5-HT2A receptor fully blocked those effects. Huxley, writing in 1954 about mescaline, described the brain as a "reducing valve" that filters what reaches awareness, borrowing the image from C. D. Broad's reading of Bergson. The thalamus findings can be read as consistent with that picture. That reading is an interpretation, and the picture remains a metaphor.

Hofmann lived to 102 and died in 2008. He named his memoir LSD: My Problem Child, and in it he describes how his joy at having fathered the compound was tarnished when it spread as an inebriant. He asked himself, "Would LSD become a blessing for humanity, or a curse?"

Werner Stoll published the first scientific description of its effects in 1947, in a Swiss neurology and psychiatry journal. Psychiatrists in Switzerland, Germany, Britain, Czechoslovakia and the United States then used it in therapy. Lester Grinspoon wrote in 1981 that between 1950 and the mid-1960s more than a thousand clinical papers discussed 40,000 patients, with problems that included alcoholism and obsessional neurosis. Hofmann also describes its use with dying patients. The 40,000 figure is a retrospective count, and the evidence is uneven. A 2012 meta-analysis by Krebs and Johansen pooled six randomized trials of LSD for alcoholism, with 536 participants, and found a beneficial effect on alcohol misuse.

The law closed in during the 1960s. On August 23, 1965, the company announced it would stop producing and distributing LSD, citing misconceptions spread by publicity, the absence of adequate legislation, and wider availability after the last patent expired in 1963. Licensed researchers could still obtain it by special permit, and Hofmann wrote that the paperwork discouraged many of them. Public Law 90-639, signed on October 24, 1968, raised the penalties for unlawful acts involving LSD and extended the federal possession offense to it. The Controlled Substances Act of 1970 later placed it in Schedule I, a category defined by high potential for abuse and no currently accepted medical use in treatment in the United States. Grinspoon attributed the end of most clinical work to legal and financial obstacles as much as to any loss of interest.

Hofmann lived to see human research with psychedelics resume. Strassman and Qualls published dose-response studies of DMT in 1994, and a Johns Hopkins group led by Griffiths published a psilocybin study in 2006. A Swiss pilot study of LSD-assisted psychotherapy, by Gasser and colleagues, appeared in 2014, six years after his death.

The journal stops after those few lines. The literature that followed has now run for more than eight decades.

pieces.title: The Man in the Garden Chair
pieces.pullQuote: In the garden, Huxley found himself facing 'a Last Judgment which, after a long time and with considerable difficulty, I recognized as a chair', and on the brink of panic.
sources: Carhart-Harris & Friston, REBUS and the Anarchic Brain, Pharmacological Reviews (2019)
Husserl, Phenomenology (Encyclopaedia Britannica article), trans. Palmer, Journal of the British Society for Phenomenology (1971)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Edmund Husserl
pieces.body:
The flowers are the scene The Doors of Perception is best known for. Huxley took his pill at eleven on a May morning in 1953, and an hour and a half later he was sitting in his study, looking at a small glass vase that held a rose, a carnation and an iris. He writes that he was no longer looking at an unusual flower arrangement. He was seeing 'what Adam had seen on the morning of his creation', which he calls 'the miracle, moment by moment, of naked existence.' He asks himself whether Istigkeit was the word Meister Eckhart liked to use, and he translates it as 'Is-ness.' That passage is beautiful and famous. The scene that matters most to me comes later, after he has listened to music, when the investigator suggests a walk in the garden.

Huxley goes out through the French window and under a pergola. Sun comes through its laths and throws zebra-like stripes of shadow across the seat and back of a garden chair. He gazes at the chair for what seems an immensely long time. At any other time, he says, he would have seen a chair barred with light and shade, but that day 'the percept had swallowed up the concept.' The sight is so wonderful that it comes close to terrifying him, and he writes that he suddenly had an inkling of what it must feel like to be mad. Two paragraphs later comes the sentence this piece is about. Confronted by a chair that looked like the Last Judgment, or, to be more accurate, by 'a Last Judgment which, after a long time and with considerable difficulty, I recognized as a chair', he found himself all at once 'on the brink of panic.'

Huxley names the emotion. Looking back, he says the fear was of being overwhelmed, of disintegrating under a pressure of reality greater than a mind used to living among symbols could bear. He adds that the going was toward greater beauty and deeper significance, and that it still felt like going too far. He sets the fear beside religious writing. The literature of religious experience, he says, is full of the terrors of people who come too suddenly face to face with the Mysterium tremendum, and he points to The Tibetan Book of the Dead, where the departed soul shrinks in agony from the Pure Light of the Void.

The chair also tests the theory Huxley had laid out earlier in the essay. Quoting the Cambridge philosopher C. D. Broad on Bergson, he proposes that the brain and nervous system work mainly to eliminate, shutting out most of what we might perceive and leaving a small selection useful for survival. He calls the filter the 'reducing valve' and what lies behind it 'Mind at Large.' Mescaline, in his view, impairs the efficiency of the valve and lets more through. He is explicit that a temporary by-pass does not abolish the valve. What arrives is more than usual and different from usual, and Huxley allows that some of it can be terrifying. His account of how the drug loosens the valve, by lowering the sugar supply to the brain, is not the mechanism the current consensus describes, which is action as an agonist or partial agonist at serotonin 2A receptors (Nichols, 2016). Researchers have also discussed reduced sensory gating, with the thalamus as one candidate site, and Carhart-Harris and Friston mention that proposal in their 2019 REBUS paper. These remain hypotheses. The valve was a metaphor, and nothing in Huxley's essay measures a thalamus.

The essay also makes a larger claim. Near its close Huxley writes that being shaken out of the ruts of ordinary perception is 'an experience of inestimable value to everyone and especially to the intellectual.' In the pages around the chair he asserts that the drug brings hell and purgatory only to people with a recent case of jaundice, periodic depression or chronic anxiety, and that a reasonably healthy person goes in without fear. In those pages these are Huxley's assertions, offered without data. Both statements are in the book, and so is his report of reaching the brink of panic.

Phenomenology offers a vocabulary for what he describes. Edmund Husserl, who laid out his method in an article for the Encyclopaedia Britannica, taught a deliberate suspension of the 'natural attitude' in which we take the world's reality for granted. He called it the epoché, often glossed as bracketing. Huxley does not mention Husserl in the essay, and the epoché is a discipline practiced by a person who is awake and working at it. The resemblance to a percept swallowing a concept is worth noticing. It does not show that mescaline performs the epoché.

The self does not vanish in the garden. On the way out, Huxley reports that it felt odd that 'I' was not the same as his arms and legs. At the chair, someone is still there to be frightened, someone who afterward analyzes the fear and who spent that long time working to recognize what he was looking at. The self is thinner than usual and it is present.

He does not describe working his way through the fear. 'None too soon', he writes, he was steered away from the disquieting splendors of the chair. The ivy on the hedge shone with a jade-like radiance, a clump of red hot pokers seemed to strain upward into the blue, and a large pale blue automobile at the curb made him laugh until the tears ran down his cheeks. The episode ends because he was steered away from it, in his words.

The book holds all of it: the vase and the chair, the Is-ness of the flowers and the Last Judgment in the garden. Huxley wrote down the panic along with the bliss, and a reader who quotes only the flowers has read part of his account. In his account, the doors of perception did not sort what came through by whether it was pleasant.

pieces.title: The Scream at the Start of Everything
pieces.pullQuote: Nixon told Congress on June 17, 1971: "If we cannot destroy the drug menace in America, then it will surely in time destroy us."
sources: Hari, The Hunting of Billie Holiday, Politico Magazine (January 2015)
Harwood, One Thing You Can Say for the War on Drugs Is We Gave It a Fair Shot (interview with Hari), ACLU (April 23, 2015)
Biography.com, Billie Holiday: How the Government Targeted the Strange Fruit Singer with Drug Arrests
Porter, Billie Holiday: There was Never a Federal Campaign against Strange Fruit, Part 2, Substack (October 31, 2022)
DEA Museum, Harry Jacob Anslinger exhibit, Narcotics Enforcement in the 1930s
U.S. Sentencing Commission, Mandatory Minimum Penalties in the Federal Criminal Justice System, ch. 2 (2011)
Nixon, Special Message to the Congress on Drug Abuse Prevention and Control (June 17, 1971)
Nixon, Remarks About an Intensified Program for Drug Abuse Prevention and Control (June 17, 1971)
Baum, Legalize It All, Harper's Magazine (April 2016)
Marlan, Beyond Cannabis: Psychedelic Decriminalization and Social Justice. Lewis & Clark Law Review 23(3):851 (2019)
Seddon, Prescribing heroin: John Marks, the Merseyside clinics, and lessons from history. Int J Drug Policy 78:102730 (2020)

Christian Science Monitor, Mexico activists vow to press ahead after mother seeking justice is murdered (December 22, 2010)
pieces.body:
In Johann Hari's telling, the American war on drugs began with one man's fixation, and the fixation hardened into law.

Harry Anslinger became the first commissioner of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics when it was founded in 1930, and he held the post until 1962. The bureau was created to take over enforcement of the Harrison Narcotics Act from a narcotics division inside the Treasury's Prohibition Unit, where a corruption scandal had broken. Prohibition ended in 1933. Hari argues that Anslinger inherited men who had spent years fighting alcohol and a bureau that needed a new mission, and that he found it in drugs.

The book's title comes from a story Hari tells about Anslinger as a boy in Altoona, Pennsylvania. A farmer's wife was screaming, the boy was sent to the pharmacy for opiates, which were legal then, and the screaming stopped. Hari treats that memory as the root of a career spent chasing the scream, and he says the chase produced many more screams. No independent record of the incident has been located.

Hari's first long case is Billie Holiday, one of the best-known jazz singers in the country, who used heroin. She was arrested in 1947 on a narcotics charge and sentenced to a year in a federal prison in West Virginia, and she lost the New York cabaret card that let her sing in clubs serving alcohol. In Hari's account, Anslinger assigned an agent named Jimmy Fletcher to follow her, and Hari ties the pursuit to her refusal to stop singing "Strange Fruit." The jazz historian Lewis Porter, who has examined that claim, says no federal campaign against the song has been documented. The drug arrests are on record. Their motive is the disputed part.

In 1959 Holiday collapsed and was admitted to Metropolitan Hospital in New York with liver and heart disease. Narcotics agents arrested her in her hospital room on a heroin charge, and she was placed under police guard. Hari reports that she was handcuffed to the bed, that friends were kept out, and that a doctor brought in by her friends prescribed methadone, which was stopped after about ten days. She died on July 17, 1959, at forty-four.

Hari also draws on Bureau memos that described jazz in racist terms, and he quotes an instruction from Anslinger to his agents to prepare marijuana cases against musicians, which he takes from the journalist Larry Sloman. In his account the Treasury Department told Anslinger the jazz world could not be broken, and Anslinger narrowed his attention to Holiday.

What the era left in law is easier to document. The Boggs Act of 1951 and the Narcotics Control Act of 1956 set mandatory minimum sentences for drug offenses. Congress repealed nearly all of those minimums in 1970, in the Comprehensive Drug Abuse Prevention and Control Act, whose Title II is the Controlled Substances Act. Anslinger had left office eight years earlier. The Controlled Substances Act sorts drugs into five schedules. Schedule I covers drugs with a high potential for abuse, no currently accepted medical use in treatment in the United States, and a lack of accepted safety under medical supervision. It lists heroin alongside marijuana, LSD, psilocybin, mescaline and peyote. Methamphetamine and fentanyl are in Schedule II.

On June 17, 1971, Richard Nixon called drug abuse "public enemy number one," and in his message to Congress that day he said, "If we cannot destroy the drug menace in America, then it will surely in time destroy us." Dan Baum reported in Harper's Magazine in 2016 on a 1994 interview with John Ehrlichman, Nixon's domestic policy adviser. Baum quotes Ehrlichman as saying the White House knew it "couldn't make it illegal to be either against the war or black," but that by getting the public to associate hippies with marijuana and Black people with heroin, it could disrupt those communities. The account rests on Baum's notes of a single interview, and it appeared after Hari's book. Ehrlichman died in 1999. His family and three former Nixon aides have disputed it.

Dustin Marlan's 2019 article in the Lewis & Clark Law Review starts from this legal inheritance. He argues for decriminalizing psychedelics on social justice and neurodiversity grounds, notes that psychedelics have long sat in Schedule I, and repeats Ehrlichman's remarks to support his statement that the drug war was a politically motivated effort to discredit the antiwar and hippie movements and to oppress racial minorities. He relies on secondary sources for that and presents no arrest data of his own. He does quote an advocacy group saying that people arrested for psychedelics are more likely to be young, non-white and economically marginalized than other users.

Hari says the book draws on more than 200 interviews, and it follows many lives beyond Holiday's. John Marks was a psychiatrist who prescribed heroin to patients in Liverpool and two neighboring towns from 1982 to 1995, until political pressure closed the clinics. Bud Osborn, a Vancouver poet and a founding member of the drug users' group VANDU, died in 2014. Marisela Escobedo campaigned in Ciudad Juárez for justice for her murdered daughter and was shot dead outside the state government building in December 2010. Parts of the book's sourcing have been challenged, and Hari answers readers on a corrections page.

The scream of the title belongs to the farmer's wife in Altoona, as Hari tells it. Holiday's last weeks, a sick woman under arrest and guard in a hospital room, are among the first cases he sets beside it. His argument is that a chase begun to silence one scream produced many more.

pieces.title: The Secret That Lasted Two Thousand Years
pieces.pullQuote: Whatever happened in the telesterion, the people who wrote about it tied it to death and hope. What the Mysteries contained is still an open question.
sources: Wasson, Hofmann & Ruck, The Road to Eleusis (1978)
Homeric Hymn to Demeter, trans. Evelyn-White (1914)
Plutarch, How the Young Man Should Study Poetry, in Moralia I (Loeb, trans. Babbitt, 1927)
Plutarch, Life of Alcibiades 22 (Loeb, trans. Perrin, 1916)
Hippolytus, Refutation of All Heresies 5.8 (early 3rd century CE)
Bizzotto, J. The hypothesis on the presence of entheogens in the Eleusinian Mysteries. Medicina Historica 2(2):85-93 (2018)
Ott & Neely, Entheogenic (hallucinogenic) effects of methylergonovine. J Psychedelic Drugs 12(2):165-166 (1980)
Hofmann et al., Psilocybin, ein psychotroper Wirkstoff aus dem mexikanischen Rauschpilz Psilocybe mexicana Heim. Experientia 14(3):107-109 (1958)
Wasson, R.G. Seeking the Magic Mushroom, Life magazine (1957)
Wasson, Soma: Divine Mushroom of Immortality (1968)
Native American Church peyote exemption, 42 U.S.C. 1996a (1994)
Marlan, D. Beyond Cannabis. Lewis & Clark Law Review, 23(3):851 (2019)
pieces.body:
The initiates at Eleusis, the ancient Greek mystery cult on the plain west of Athens, were bound by an oath of silence about what happened in the telesterion, the great hall where the culminating ceremony took place. The Homeric Hymn to Demeter, usually dated to around the seventh century BCE, calls the rites something no one may pry into or utter, because awe of the gods checks the voice. Athens enforced the silence. In 415 BCE the city charged Alcibiades with mimicking the Mysteries at a private house, and it condemned him to death in his absence. Livy reports that two uninitiated Acarnanian youths who wandered into the sanctuary around 200 BCE were put to death for it.

The rites were celebrated until the end of the fourth century CE, when Theodosius I banned pagan cult and the sanctuary was later wrecked, traditionally by Alaric's Goths. If the sanctuary's Mycenaean origins are counted, that is a span close to two thousand years.

Several writers said what the ceremony meant to them, though none described it. The Hymn calls anyone who has seen the rites happy, and says the uninitiated will fare worse in the darkness below. Pindar wrote of the initiate in a line Martin Nilsson rendered as "he knows the end of life and he knows its god-sent beginning." Plutarch preserves lines of Sophocles calling those who have seen the rites thrice blessed, because for them alone there is life in Hades. In Cicero's dialogue On the Laws, a speaker named Marcus says that of everything Athens gave the world, nothing was better than the Mysteries, which taught people "to die with a better hope." His companion Atticus speaks of the rites as ones into which they themselves had been initiated. This is literary praise and contains no eyewitness description, and none of it mentions a drug. It does show that educated Greeks and Romans connected the Mysteries with death.

In 1978 three men published The Road to Eleusis. R. Gordon Wasson was a New York banker and amateur mycologist whose 1957 Life magazine article, "Seeking the Magic Mushroom," brought Mexican sacred mushrooms to a mass audience. Albert Hofmann was the Swiss chemist who first synthesized LSD in 1938 and isolated psilocybin from Mexican mushrooms in the late 1950s. Carl Ruck was a classicist at Boston University. They proposed that the kykeon, the drink initiates consumed, contained psychoactive ergot alkaloids. The Hymn describes the kykeon as barley meal, water and mint. The hypothesis supposes the barley carried ergot, a fungus (Claviceps purpurea) that infests rye and other grains and wild grasses, and whose alkaloids are derivatives of lysergic acid, the starting point for Hofmann's synthesis of LSD. The surviving descriptions of the drink do not mention the fungus.

Hofmann's chapter supplied the chemistry. Some kinds of ergot contain alkaloids such as lysergic acid amide and ergonovine, which dissolve in water, alongside the toxic ergotamine-type alkaloids, which do not. Hofmann argued that a water-based drink could carry the first group and leave the second behind, so priests with ancient tools could have prepared a psychoactive extract. The book also reports that he tried ergonovine on himself. Later self-experimenters described effects dominated by bodily sensations and a dreamy, drowsy state, unlike LSD. A trial of one pure compound does not show what a kykeon would have done.

Wasson supplied the comparative frame. He had documented sacred mushroom use among the Mazatec of Mexico, and he later argued that the Vedic Soma was the fly agaric mushroom. He saw the Mysteries as another case of one pattern: a plant or fungus taken inside a ritual to produce an experience understood as contact with the divine. Ruck's chapter went through the ancient evidence. Many scholars read the culminating rite as a ritual enactment of the myth of Demeter and her daughter, with sacred objects shown to the initiates. Ruck argued that the testimony pointed to a vision produced by a drug.

The hypothesis has not won general acceptance. Walter Burkert, the leading historian of Greek religion of his generation, rejected it in Ancient Mystery Cults and looked to the ritual itself for the explanation. One 2018 review of the debate describes scholars as divided between enthusiastic supporters and flat rejection. Botanical objections have hit parts of Hofmann's case. Giorgio Samorini, who supports a role for ergot, and Francesco Festi showed that the Paspalum ergot Hofmann floated as an alternative is not known in Europe before modern times.

Even the secret was not kept perfectly. Two Christian writers hostile to the cult claimed to expose parts of it. Clement of Alexandria reports a password in which the initiate says they fasted and drank the kykeon. Hippolytus, in the early third century, says the highest rite showed initiates an ear of grain reaped in silence, in the course of describing a Gnostic sect's teaching. Neither names a drug.

Eleusis also turns up in modern legal argument about psychedelics. In 2006 the Supreme Court held in Gonzales v. O Centro that, under the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, the federal government had not yet shown a compelling interest in stopping a church from using hoasca, a tea also called ayahuasca, in its ceremonies. Federal law has protected traditional ceremonial peyote use by Indians since 1994. Dustin Marlan's 2019 law review article on psychedelic decriminalization cites Eleusis as an early psychedelic ritual and surveys these exemptions.
