The court's decision rested on the statute and the record before it.

The secret held well enough that no full account survives. What does survive is a long record of people saying the rites mattered, especially when they thought about dying, and a hypothesis about a drink that has not been proven. Wasson believed the kykeon was the mechanism. That remains his hypothesis, and the evidence has not settled it.

pieces.title: What the Record Actually Shows
pieces.pullQuote: Of Herer's three claims, the racial one has the strongest support. The industrial conspiracy is unproven, and the statute's own text undercuts the claim that hemp was lumped in with the drug.
sources: Herer, The Emperor Wears No Clothes (1985)
Marihuana Tax Act of 1937, 50 Stat. 551 (approved August 2, 1937)
U.S. Senate Committee on Finance, Taxation of Marihuana, hearing on H.R. 6906 (July 12, 1937)
U.S. House Committee on Ways and Means, Taxation of Marihuana, hearing on H.R. 6385 (May 4, 1937 session)
Marlan, Beyond Cannabis: Psychedelic Decriminalization and Social Justice. Lewis & Clark Law Review 23(3):851 (2019)
National Academies, The Health Effects of Cannabis and Cannabinoids (2017)
Gaoni and Mechoulam, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 86:1646-1647 (1964)
ACLU, A Tale of Two Countries (2020)
Blumenthal, Reconsidering Anslinger, Race, the Gateway Theory, and the Origins of Marijuana Prohibition, Points (2016, updated 2023)
Wishnia, Debunking the Hemp Conspiracy Theory, AlterNet (2008)
Science History Institute, Wallace Hume Carothers profile
Reason, Return With Me Now to the Thrilling Days When Marijuana Was Spelled With an H (August 2, 2007)
pieces.body:
In February 1938, Popular Mechanics ran an article under the headline 'New Billion-Dollar Crop.' It described a new machine, the decorticator, that stripped fiber from hemp stalks without the weeks of field retting the crop had required, and it forecast a cash crop worth 'several hundred million dollars' a year. Rope, twine, linen and paper pulp were among the products it listed, and it said hemp would displace imported fiber. It also noted that federal rules for hemp growers were then being drafted. The Marihuana Tax Act had been signed on August 2, 1937 and took effect on October 1, 1937, so the article appeared four months after the Act took effect.

Jack Herer argued that this timing was no coincidence.

Herer's argument in The Emperor Wears No Clothes, first published in 1985, can be read as three claims, and the book sometimes presents all three as equally proven. They are not equally proven, and separating them matters for anyone who wants to use this material responsibly.

The first claim is that industrial interests shaped the 1937 law to suppress hemp. Some of the facts Herer builds on are documented. Andrew Mellon, Herbert Hoover's Treasury Secretary, appointed Harry Anslinger to lead the new Federal Bureau of Narcotics in 1930, and Anslinger's wife was Mellon's niece. DuPont's nylon fiber patent, with Wallace Carothers as inventor, was filed in April 1937 and granted in September 1938. The links that turn these facts into a motive are the weak part. The Science History Institute says DuPont aimed nylon first at the silk stocking market. Herer calls Mellon DuPont's chief financial backer, and scholars whom Steven Wishnia consulted in 2008 found no such financial tie. Herer reads DuPont's 1937 annual report as awareness of a hemp threat, and Wishnia reads the same language as ordinary corporate complaint about the New Deal. Herer gives Hearst's timber and paper holdings as a motive, while Wishnia, citing W. A. Swanberg's biography, describes a publisher squeezed by newsprint costs who would have gained from cheap hemp paper had it been workable. I found no minutes, letters or testimony showing a campaign against hemp by these firms. The Popular Mechanics article itself presented hemp as a crop that would displace imports.

The second claim is that marijuana prohibition was a racial project. The evidence here is stronger, with qualifications. Historian Seth Blumenthal documents a racial slur in a 1934 Anslinger document, after which Senator Joseph Guffey asked that he be replaced. Blumenthal also notes that many quotations attributed to Anslinger are poorly sourced or fabricated, so I rely only on documented ones. When Anslinger testified to a Senate subcommittee on July 12, 1937, he put into the record a prosecutor's letter that identified the defendant in a murder case by race. Blumenthal, drawing on David Musto, finds anti-Mexican prejudice in the Southwest among the pressures behind the law, and he argues that race alone is too simple an explanation, since fears about adolescents and sensational press stories also drove it. Johann Hari's Chasing the Scream (2015) documents Anslinger's later pursuit of Billie Holiday, which Hari dates to her singing 'Strange Fruit' in 1939; that pursuit concerned heroin. Recent data show racial disparity in enforcement: the ACLU found that Black people were 3.64 times as likely as white people to be arrested for marijuana possession between 2010 and 2018, although both groups use it at similar rates.

The third claim is that hemp and marijuana were conflated on purpose to suppress a viable industrial crop. The statute's own text undercuts it. The Act defined marihuana as all parts of Cannabis sativa L. and then excluded the mature stalks, fiber, oil and cake from the seeds, and sterilized seed. Hemp processors still testified before the Senate subcommittee and asked for changes, chiefly a lower tax for small growers, because the Act required producers to register and pay a tax. The burden on growers was real. THC itself was not isolated and described until 1964, so the drafters had no THC measure to define hemp by.

What the record shows, stripped of inference:

Anslinger ran the Federal Bureau of Narcotics from 1930 to 1962. Representative Robert Doughton introduced the first version of the bill, H.R. 6385, on April 14, 1937. The House Ways and Means Committee held hearings on April 27, 28, 29 and 30 and May 4. On May 4, Dr. William Woodward of the American Medical Association testified against the bill and said nothing in the medicinal use of cannabis had any relation to cannabis addiction. The AMA's statement in the Senate record asked that any needed regulation of medical use be handled by amending the Harrison Narcotic Act. The cases Anslinger offered the Senate subcommittee were letters about individual crimes. On the House floor on June 10, the exchange was brief, and Sam Rayburn said he understood marihuana to be a narcotic of some kind. The President signed the final version, H.R. 6906, on August 2, less than four months after the first version was introduced.

The Controlled Substances Act of 1970 later placed cannabis in Schedule I, where the classic psychedelics also sit, and the National Academies concluded in 2017 that this classification was one of the regulatory barriers to cannabis research. That barrier came from scheduling law, and I found no evidence of a coordinated effort to block research.

The record establishes that the 1937 law moved quickly, that the medical profession's objection was on the record before it passed, and that enforcement has been racially uneven. It does not establish that DuPont, Hearst or Mellon engineered the law. Herer was an advocate, and some of his claims go beyond the documents. His instinct that the official story left gaps is supported on the points above, and his most widely repeated claim is the one the documents support least. The conspiracy is unproven. The hearings, the statute and the enforcement data are documented.

pieces.title: The Vocabulary of a New World
pieces.pullQuote: To fathom Hell or soar angelic, just take a pinch of psychedelic.
sources: Bisbee, P., Carson Bisbee, C., Dyck, E., Farrell, P., Sexton, J. & Spisak, J.W. (eds.) Psychedelic Prophets: The Letters of Aldous Huxley and Humphry Osmond. McGill-Queen's University Press (2018)
Smith, G. (ed.) Letters of Aldous Huxley. Chatto & Windus (1969)
Osmond, H. A Review of the Clinical Effects of Psychotomimetic Agents, Ann. NY Acad. Sci. (1957)
New York Academy of Sciences, The Origin of the Term Psychedelic (blog)
pieces.body:
Aldous Huxley was 58 years old, with poor eyesight, when a young British psychiatrist came to stay at his Los Angeles home in May 1953. Humphry Osmond was 35. Two years earlier he had moved from England to Canada to work at the mental hospital in Weyburn, Saskatchewan, and with his colleague John Smythies he had suggested that mescaline's chemical resemblance to adrenaline might bear on schizophrenia. Huxley had read that work and started a correspondence with him. He wanted to try mescaline himself, and Osmond was in the United States for a conference.

On a morning in early May, with Osmond and Huxley's wife Maria staying with him throughout, Huxley took mescaline. Accounts give the date as May 3 or May 4. The session became The Doors of Perception, published the next year, in which Huxley likened what he felt to Meister Eckhart's Istigkeit, or is-ness.

Huxley and Osmond kept writing to each other for the next decade. The published collection, Psychedelic Prophets, holds more than 275 of their letters, from March 1953 to a month before Huxley's death.

The first problem the letters took up was what to call these substances. The standard medical terms were psychotomimetic, meaning psychosis-mimicking, and hallucinogen. In a letter of March 15, 1956, Osmond told Huxley that psychotomimetic did not do justice to the full range of experiences these drugs could produce. At Weyburn, he and his colleagues were treating alcoholic patients with LSD, and a name that called the experience a simulated illness built a conclusion into the label.

So the two men traded candidates. Others in the exchange included psychophrenics, psycholytics and euleutheropsychics, which one reviewer calls accurate yet clunky. Huxley preferred a word of his own making, phanerothyme, from the Greek for manifest and spirit. On March 30, 1956, he sent it to Osmond with a couplet in the postscript: "To make this trivial world sublime, take half a gramme of phanerothyme."

Osmond answered with a rhyme of his own, built on a word he had put together from psyche, the Greek for mind or soul, and delos, manifest: "To fathom Hell or soar angelic, just take a pinch of psychedelic." His reply is undated in the sources I could read, and he later remembered the wording differently.

Huxley's word did not last. Osmond's appeared in print in his paper "A Review of the Clinical Effects of Psychotomimetic Agents," published in the Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences in March 1957. He explained his choice by calling it "clear, euphonious and uncontaminated by other associations." The word means mind manifesting. It names an effect and leaves the verdict open: whether what appears is perception, imagination or illness is a separate question, and the label does not decide it.

That openness was the point of the project. Huxley wrote as an essayist about what the flowers, the furniture and the light looked like. Osmond came to the same substances from the clinic. Between them they were building a vocabulary for experiences that neither a literary tradition nor a psychiatric one had a settled name for.

Huxley died at home in Los Angeles on November 22, 1963, at 5:20 in the afternoon. Unable to speak, he had made a written request to his wife Laura for LSD, and she gave it to him. President Kennedy had been assassinated that day, less than seven hours earlier, and the news of Huxley's death was overshadowed.

The word spread far beyond the laboratories and the correspondence that produced it. Osmond's choice still names what these substances are claimed to do, and the question he built it around is still open: what, exactly, is being shown?

thenVsNow.title: The Stoned Ape: Was McKenna Right?
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Psilocybin mushrooms catalyzed human brain expansion, language, and consciousness. The doubling of the hominin brain over two million years was driven in part by psilocybin's effects on neuroplasticity and visual acuity.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: The neuroplasticity claim is partially supported: psilocybin does promote dendritic spine growth (Shao et al. 2021) and new synaptic connections. The specific evolutionary timeline lacks fossil or genetic confirmation. The mechanism McKenna proposed, improved hunting via visual acuity at low doses, is plausible but untested. The broad intuition (that the relationship between humans and psychoactive plants is ancient and significant) is well-supported by the archaeological record. The specific causal chain is not.

thenVsNow.title: The Reducing Valve: Was Huxley Right?
thenVsNow.thenClaim: The brain acts as a "reducing valve," filtering out most of what consciousness could perceive to prevent sensory overwhelm. Mescaline disables this filter, allowing access to "Mind at Large", not creating hallucinations but removing suppression of what was already there.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: The default mode network model in contemporary neuroscience is structurally similar: the DMN maintains predictive models that suppress perceptual inputs not confirming expectations. Psychedelics reduce DMN connectivity (documented across multiple fMRI studies). The predictive coding framework formalizes what Huxley described intuitively. The asymmetry Huxley failed to account for, that opened perception is sometimes terrifying, not just beautiful, remains without a complete explanation in either model.
sources: Carhart-Harris et al., various [Source not found; under review]

thenVsNow.title: The Pineal Gland as DMT Source: Was Strassman Right?
thenVsNow.thenClaim: The pineal gland produces DMT endogenously, particularly at birth, death, and during deep meditation or near-death experiences. This endogenous DMT mediates mystical and anomalous experiences.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: Confirmed: DMT is present in human blood, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid, an endogenous compound. The pineal as primary production site: not confirmed. The pineal contains the enzyme machinery required for DMT synthesis, but measurement data showing it produces DMT in pharmacologically significant quantities does not yet exist. The broader hypothesis (endogenous DMT mediates naturally occurring mystical states) remains open and scientifically interesting.

thenVsNow.title: Psychedelic Prohibition: What the Evidence Actually Showed
thenVsNow.thenClaim: LSD and other psychedelics were placed in Schedule I in 1970 as substances with "no accepted medical use" and "high potential for abuse." The Nixon administration and congressional testimony described them as highly dangerous with no therapeutic value.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: The Cambridge HPS dissertation (2007) documented that 40,000+ patients received LSD therapy in the 1950s-70s with promising outcomes. The Schedule I classification was based on inadequate evidence and driven by political rather than pharmacological reasoning. Current Phase 2/3 clinical trials at Johns Hopkins, NYU, Imperial College, and MAPS show significant therapeutic efficacy for depression, PTSD, addiction, and anxiety in terminal illness. David Nichols (2016): no established physiological lethal dose for classical psychedelics.
sources: Medical History of Psychedelic Drugs, Cambridge HPS (2007) [Source not found; under review]

thenVsNow.title: The Kykeon Hypothesis: Eleusis and the Ergot
thenVsNow.thenClaim: The kykeon, the ritual drink consumed by initiates at the Eleusinian Mysteries, contained an ergot-derived psychedelic. The Mysteries' power to transform the most philosophically sophisticated people in the ancient world came from a pharmacological experience.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: The hypothesis remains unconfirmed but has not been refuted. Hofmann's chemistry (that a psychoactive ergot preparation was achievable with ancient technology) stands. The botanical question, whether Claviceps purpurea was present in Eleusinian barley in sufficient form, remains debated. The Ruck philological argument (that the accounts describe pharmacological experience, not theatrical ritual) continues to be debated among classicists. The 2,000-year oath of silence makes definitive evidence structurally unavailable.
sources: Wasson, Hofmann & Ruck, The Road to Eleusis (1978)
Medical History of Psychedelic Drugs, Cambridge HPS (2007) [Source not found; under review]

thenVsNow.title: Rat Park: Was Alexander Right?
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Social isolation, not pharmacological dependency, is the primary driver of addictive behavior. Rats in enriched social environments with other rats largely choose plain water over drug-laced water, even after being forced to consume drugs.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: Bruce Alexander and colleagues at Simon Fraser University ran the Rat Park studies in the late 1970s and published them between 1978 and 1981 (Alexander, Coambs and Hadaway, Psychopharmacology, 1978; Hadaway and colleagues, Psychopharmacology, 1979; Alexander and colleagues, Pharmacology Biochemistry and Behavior, 1981). Rats kept alone in standard cages drank more morphine solution than rats living together in a large open colony. Later attempts gave mixed results. Bozarth, Murray and Wise (1989) found that rats housed alone and rats housed in groups both learned to give themselves heroin and reached similar levels after a few weeks. Petrie (1996) could not repeat the housing difference: the isolated rats in his studies drank less than Alexander's had, and he suggested the supplier's rat strain had changed. The original result has not been reliably replicated, although the broader idea that surroundings can change drug taking still has support from other animal and human research. The broader principle, that social connection, meaning and purpose are protective factors against addictive behavior, has support from human studies. Portugal's 2001 decriminalization, combined with spending on treatment and social services, was followed by falls in HIV transmission and drug-related deaths.
sources: Labate & Cavnar, Ayahuasca Healing and Science (2021)
Alexander et al., Pharmacology Biochemistry and Behavior (1981)
Bozarth, Murray & Wise, Pharmacology Biochemistry and Behavior (1989)

thenVsNow.title: Art as 'Ersatz Suchness': Huxley's Claim
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Art is 'only for beginners', a preparation for direct experience, not a substitute for it. The best art points toward the kind of direct perception mescaline temporarily enables, but cannot itself deliver that perception.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: Aesthetic neuroscience has complicated Huxley's hierarchy. Studies of peak aesthetic experiences show they activate many of the same brain regions as psychedelic-induced states, particularly the default mode network and salience network in overlapping ways. The distinction between mediated aesthetic experience and direct perception may be less categorical than Huxley claimed. That said, qualitative studies of psychedelic experience consistently report a quality of perceptual immediacy that subjects describe as categorically different from aesthetic rapture. The debate remains open.
sources: Barrett et al., Front. Psychol. (2017) [Source not found; under review]

thenVsNow.title: Mescaline and Schizophrenia: The Psychotomimetic Theory
thenVsNow.thenClaim: The mescaline experience illuminates schizophrenia from the inside. The schizophrenic, Huxley argued, is permanently in a state analogous to what the mescaline session temporarily produces, unable to filter the overwhelming flood of unmediated experience.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: The schizophrenia-psychedelic analogy remains active in research but is more nuanced than Huxley described. Classic psychedelics and schizophrenia both involve 5-HT2A receptor activity and both show increased thalamocortical activity, but the phenomenologies differ significantly: psychedelic states are typically accompanied by insight and preserved reality-testing, while acute psychosis often is not. The Osmond, Smythies and Hoffer model of LSD and mescaline as 'psychotomimetic' for training clinicians has been partly revived, Johns Hopkins now trains therapists partly through psychedelic experience, but the mechanistic claims are disputed.
sources: Murray et al., Psychol. Med. (2012) [Source not found; under review]

thenVsNow.title: Psychedelic Education Reform: Huxley's Proposal
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Education that teaches only verbal reasoning produces people who mistake symbols for things. A complete education would include training in direct perception, and mescaline could assist this training in appropriate contexts.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: As of 2025, no jurisdiction has formally integrated psychedelic education into curriculum. However, 'contemplative education', mindfulness, somatic practices, non-verbal learning modalities, has gained significant institutional traction in K-12 and university settings. Johns Hopkins and NYU now train clinicians through guided psychedelic experiences. Oregon's Measure 109 (2023) created a licensed service framework for psilocybin sessions. The educational argument Huxley made remains ahead of institutional readiness but is no longer fringe.
sources: Oregon Health Authority, Psilocybin Services Program (2023)
Davis et al., J. Psychopharmacol. (2021) [Source not found; under review]

thenVsNow.title: The Gratuitous Grace: Huxley's Theology
thenVsNow.thenClaim: The mescaline experience is a 'gratuitous grace', not necessary to salvation but potentially helpful, to be accepted thankfully if available. It is compatible with genuine religious life and may prepare the way for deeper practice.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: Current psilocybin research routinely measures 'mystical experience' using validated scales (MEQ30) and finds it both common and therapeutic. A 2024 meta-analysis found that mystical experience quality predicts therapeutic outcomes better than drug dose. Several US religious communities (Native American Church, UDV, Santo Daime) now have legal religious exemptions for sacramental psychedelic use under RFRA. The 'gratuitous grace' framing, not salvation but a gift to be received properly, maps closely to how current clinical practice treats the experience.
sources: Yaden & Griffiths, ACS Pharmacol Transl Sci (2021)
Barrett & Griffiths, Curr Top Behav Neurosci (2018)

thenVsNow.title: The Psychedelic Word: Osmond's Coinage in 2025
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Osmond coined 'psychedelic' to replace 'psychotomimetic' and 'hallucinogen', arguing that 'mind-manifesting' was a more accurate description of what these substances do. He and Huxley believed the word would shape how the substances were researched.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: The word 'psychedelic' became dominant in both research and culture, but its meaning has drifted far from Osmond's original clinical intent. 'Entheogen' (coined by Ruck et al. in 1979) is now preferred in ethnobotanical contexts. 'Classical serotonergic psychedelics' is the preferred neuroscience term. 'Hallucinogen' has partially returned in regulatory documents. 'Psychedelic' is simultaneously the most culturally powerful and most definitionally unstable of the available terms. Osmond's hope that the naming would control the framing has been only partially realized.
sources: Ruck et al., J. Psychedelic Drugs (1979)

thenVsNow.title: LSD as Alcoholism Treatment: Hoffer-Osmond Results
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Hoffer, Osmond and colleagues treated many alcoholic patients with LSD in Saskatchewan and reported that roughly half improved or stopped drinking, a result they attributed to the peak experience the drug could produce.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: A 2012 meta-analysis of six randomized trials from the 1960s and 1970s, run at several centers (Krebs & Johansen, J. Psychopharmacol.), found LSD associated with a significant reduction in alcohol misuse, clearest at the earlier follow-ups. Psilocybin for alcohol use disorder showed promising results in a 2022 RCT at NYU (Bogenschutz et al., JAMA Psychiatry), the first such trial since prohibition. As of 2025, MAPS-affiliated researchers are running Phase 2 trials of psilocybin for AUD. The original Saskatchewan figures were uncontrolled; the later randomized evidence supports a smaller but real effect.
sources: Hoffer & Osmond, J. Mental Sci. (1961) [Source not found; under review]
Chwelos, Blewett, Smith & Hoffer, Quarterly Journal of Studies on Alcohol (1959)

thenVsNow.title: LSD Assisted Dying: Huxley's Death
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Huxley requested LSD for his death from laryngeal cancer, and Laura administered it as he lost consciousness. His death was described by attending nurses as unusually serene. He had long argued that psychedelics could ease the transition of death.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: Psilocybin for end-of-life anxiety is now the most replicated finding in psychedelic medicine. A 2016 double-blind study at Johns Hopkins (Griffiths et al.) found that a single psilocybin session reduced end-of-life anxiety and depression in cancer patients with effects persisting six months. A 2016 NYU study produced similar results. A 2023 meta-analysis confirmed the effect size. As of 2025, a psilocybin developer is running Phase 3 trials for psilocybin in treatment-resistant depression, and LSD-assisted therapy for anxiety is in Phase 2 at several European sites. Huxley's intuition has become a robust clinical program.
sources: Huxley, personal request to Laura Huxley (November 1963)

thenVsNow.title: The Vision of Peaceful Death: Moksha
thenVsNow.thenClaim: In Island, Huxley depicted a society in which moksha-medicine was used at death, not to avoid dying but to transform it into a conscious passage. He believed this was the most important use of the substances, and wrote it into his final utopia.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: As of 2025, Oregon's psilocybin services program and Colorado's Natural Medicine Health Act both permit facilitated psilocybin sessions, including for end-of-life care. Australian TGA approval of psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression (February 2023) created the first legal framework for clinical psychedelic therapy outside a trial setting. The specific vision of Island, a society with integrated psychedelic death ritual, remains ahead of any current jurisdiction, but the clinical foundation is now established.

thenVsNow.title: LSD Potency: The Threshold Claim
thenVsNow.thenClaim: LSD was the most potent psychoactive substance known, active in extremely small amounts, making it roughly 1,000 times more potent than mescaline and 10,000 times more potent than psilocybin by weight.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: LSD remains the most potent classical psychedelic in clinical use. However, more recently characterized compounds, particularly 5-MeO-DMT, which is active in very small amounts by inhalation, produce comparable experiences at even lower weights. The 5-HT2A binding affinity of LSD and its unusual 'lid' mechanism (the drug becomes trapped in the receptor for hours, explaining its duration) were elucidated by crystal structure studies in 2017 (Wacker et al., Cell). The mechanism Hofmann could only speculate about is now resolved at atomic resolution.

thenVsNow.title: LSD and Mystical Experience: Hofmann's Claim
thenVsNow.thenClaim: LSD produces genuine mystical experiences, states phenomenologically identical to those described in mystical literature across traditions, and these experiences constitute its most important therapeutic and spiritual potential.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: The Mystical Experience Questionnaire (MEQ30), derived from Stace's philosophy of mysticism, now reliably measures 'complete mystical experiences' in psychedelic trial subjects. Several studies have found that higher MEQ30 scores are associated with better outcomes in depression, alcohol use disorder and end-of-life anxiety; these are correlations within trials. A 2023 randomized trial at the University of Basel (Holze et al., Biological Psychiatry) reported that LSD-assisted therapy reduced anxiety and depression symptoms in people with anxiety disorders. Hofmann's claim that mystical experience is the mechanism of action is testable; current studies show associations, not proof of mechanism.
sources: Yaden & Griffiths, ACS Pharmacol Transl Sci (2021)

thenVsNow.title: LSD as Sacred Drug: The 1965 Prohibition
thenVsNow.thenClaim: The manufacturer's 1965 withdrawal of its LSD product and the subsequent Schedule I classification were political responses to countercultural misuse, not scientific conclusions. LSD was not dangerous in clinical settings; it was dangerous when taken without preparation, support, or integration.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: The DEA's own safety records show zero documented deaths from LSD overdose toxicity in 80 years of use. A 2016 Global Drug Survey of 30,000+ drug users found LSD had the lowest rate of emergency medical treatment of any substance surveyed. FDA's Breakthrough Therapy designation for psilocybin (2018) and subsequent approvals of the psychedelic research pipeline confirm that the Schedule I status was not driven by pharmacological evidence. The WHO's 2019 Critical Review of LSD found no evidence supporting its current scheduling level (Source not found; under review).
sources: WHO ECDD Critical Review: LSD (2019) [Source not found; under review]

thenVsNow.title: Bicycle Day Chemistry: What Hofmann Synthesized
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Hofmann synthesized LSD-25 from lysergic acid, derived from ergot alkaloids, in April 1943. He accidentally absorbed a small amount, experienced mild effects, and then deliberately took an amount he believed was tiny. It was in fact several times larger than what is now understood to be active.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: A 2017 X-ray crystal structure of LSD bound to the 5-HT2A receptor (Wacker et al., Cell) revealed why the drug lasts so long: a 'lid' from an extracellular loop traps the drug in the receptor for hours. Hofmann's first deliberate dose, chosen because he thought it would be below the active threshold, is now understood to have been several times a typical active dose, explaining the overwhelming intensity he experienced. The structure also explains LSD's extreme potency: its molecular shape allows nearly perfect complementarity with the receptor binding site.

thenVsNow.title: Psilocybin and Human Evolution: McKenna's Core Claim
thenVsNow.thenClaim: The McKenna brothers proposed at La Chorrera that tryptamine compounds, specifically psilocybin, had been co-evolutionary partners with human cognition for hundreds of thousands of years, and that the 'experiment' at La Chorrera was an attempt to access this ancient relationship.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: Archaeological evidence now confirms psychoactive plant use going back at least 9,000 years (Peruvian shamanic cactus burial, 2014) and possibly much longer. DNA studies have identified 5-HT2A receptor variants in humans that differ from other primates in ways consistent with selective pressure related to serotonergic experience. The specific claim about psilocybin and human evolution remains untested and unfalsifiable. Dennis McKenna became one of the leading neuropharmacologists studying tryptamines and has consistently supported the broader hypothesis while qualifying the specific claims of La Chorrera.
sources: Mayer et al., Jour. Ethnopharmacol. (2015) [Source not found; under review]
D. McKenna, The Brotherhood of the Screaming Abyss (2012)

thenVsNow.title: DMT Entities: The Consistency Problem
thenVsNow.thenClaim: McKenna described 'machine elves', self-transforming fractal entities, as consistent features of DMT hyperspace. He wondered whether their consistency across users indicated something objective about the territory being accessed.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: Strassman's clinical DMT study at UNM (1990-1995, 60 volunteers) found entity contact in a substantial minority of high-dose sessions. A 2020 Johns Hopkins online survey (Davis et al., J. Psychopharmacol. 34(9):1008-1020) of 2,561 people who had had a DMT entity encounter found humanoid forms most common. A 2023 Imperial College EEG-fMRI study (Timmermann et al., PNAS 120(13)) mapped DMT's global brain effects but did not isolate entity contact, so no neural signature specific to it has been published. The survey reports no prevalence rate, and the 97% figure often attached to it is in no published paper. Similar entity reports are well documented in self-selected samples. Whether entities are projections of the human unconscious, hallucinations, or something else is still open.
sources: Sexton et al., J. Psychopharmacol. 33(9) (2019) [Source not found; under review]

thenVsNow.title: Timewave Zero: The 2012 Prediction
thenVsNow.thenClaim: McKenna's Timewave Zero theory predicted that time would reach a point of maximum 'novelty', a singularity, on December 21, 2012, corresponding to the end of the Mayan Long Count calendar. The theory was derived from the I Ching.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: December 21, 2012 passed without the predicted singularity or transformational event. McKenna had acknowledged the theory was falsifiable, it was one of his most intellectually honest positions. The Timewave theory has no scientific support. Its value, such as it is, lies in the underlying philosophical claim that time has qualitative structure, a claim that is independent of the specific 2012 prediction and remains interesting as a philosophical hypothesis.
sources: Various commentaries, 2012-2013 [Source not found; under review]

thenVsNow.title: The La Chorrera Experiment: What Actually Happened
thenVsNow.thenClaim: The McKenna brothers attempted to 'bond' psilocybin into the human neural harmala system through a specific vocalization technique during a high-dose mushroom session. Dennis experienced a dramatic breakdown; Terence believed something extraordinary had occurred.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: Dennis McKenna's 2012 memoir (The Brotherhood of the Screaming Abyss) provides his retrospective account: he underwent what he now believes was a drug-induced psychosis that lasted several weeks. The 'experiment' as Terence described it produced no replicable effect and no verifiable change in their biochemistry. What it produced was the Timewave theory and the mushroom monologue that became the foundation of Terence's public career. Dennis has spoken with admiration and skepticism about his brother's interpretation in equal measure.
sources: D. McKenna, The Brotherhood of the Screaming Abyss (2012)

thenVsNow.title: DNA and Shamanic Vision: Narby's Hypothesis
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Shamans access information at the molecular level, specifically DNA, through ayahuasca visions. The twin-serpent imagery universal in shamanic traditions represents the double helix. Biophoton emission from DNA may be the physical mechanism.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: The biophoton emission hypothesis remains unstested in relation to shamanic vision. The ayahuasca pharmacology is now well-characterized (DMT + MAO inhibitors) but the information channel Narby proposed, from DNA to shamanic knowledge, has not been confirmed or falsified. The data point that strongest supports the general hypothesis is the Kekule-benzene-Ouroboros parallel: a Western chemist solved a molecular structure after a serpent dream. This is anecdotal. The broader argument, that indigenous plant knowledge is reliably accurate despite lacking Western methodology, is well-supported; the mechanism Narby proposes for how is not.
sources: Winkelman, Curr. Anthropol. (2010) [Source not found; under review]
Poinar et al., Plant Biol. (2001) [Source not found; under review]

thenVsNow.title: Ayahuasca Combinatorial Problem: How Did They Know?
thenVsNow.thenClaim: In an Amazon of 80,000 plant species, indigenous people identified two specific plants whose combination creates oral DMT activity, a pharmacological interaction that requires both a MAO inhibitor and a source of DMT to work. 'The plants told us' is the universal explanation. How they discovered this combination is unexplained by Western models.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: No Western scientific explanation for the ayahuasca discovery has achieved consensus. Proposed mechanisms include: trial-and-error over millennia (statistically implausible given the search space), prior knowledge of plant alkaloids through other routes, smell-based identification of alkaloid chemistry, or direct experiential guidance during altered states. A 2019 chemical ecology study confirmed that Banisteriopsis caapi and Psychotria viridis both independently produce compounds with insecticidal and antifungal properties that would make them notable to herbalists. The pharmacological interaction remains the harder question.
sources: Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979)

thenVsNow.title: Indigenous Knowledge vs. Scientific Patent Law
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Biology has become an industry guided by a thirst for marketable knowledge rather than ethical or spiritual considerations. The sacred is not for sale, but the pharmaceutical industry is attempting to patent what indigenous communities have known for millennia.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: Since 1998, biopiracy cases have proliferated: US Patent 5,751,559 on ayahuasca was filed and eventually cancelled (2003) after a legal challenge by indigenous groups, but similar cases continue. WIPO's Intergovernmental Committee on Genetic Resources has been negotiating an Indigenous Knowledge treaty for over twenty years with limited progress. As of 2024, the Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit-Sharing is in force in 138 countries, but enforcement is weak. The psychedelic patent race has accelerated since 2020, with psilocybin developers and other companies filing patents on therapeutic protocols and molecular derivatives, prompting a 'Defensive Patent' movement by researchers at Johns Hopkins.
sources: Olson et al., Trends Pharmacol. Sci. (2022) [Source not found; under review]

thenVsNow.title: Shamanism as Academic Discipline: Narby's Framing
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Shamanism resembles an academic discipline, with practitioners, fundamental researchers, specialists, and schools of thought. The Shipibo-Conibo and Huitoto peoples represent the equivalent of Oxford and Harvard in matters of plant knowledge.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: Since 1998, multiple universities have established formal ayahuasca research programs in collaboration with indigenous communities (CEBRID in Brazil, UNM in collaboration with Santo Daime, ICEERS in Barcelona). The Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies (MAPS) has formal partnerships with multiple indigenous groups. Peru established the first national registry of traditional healers in 2008. The epistemological claim, that indigenous knowledge systems are legitimate research programs, has moved from radical to mainstream in medical anthropology and, increasingly, in clinical psychedelic research.
sources: Lima & Labate, Drugs: Edu. Prev. Pol. (2008) [Source not found; under review]
Winkelman & Fortier, Medical Anthropol. (2019) [Source not found; under review]

thenVsNow.title: The Ergot-Eleusis Hypothesis: Status in 2026
thenVsNow.thenClaim: The kykeon drink at the center of the Eleusinian Mysteries contained ergot alkaloids derived from Claviceps purpurea parasitizing the barley. These alkaloids, structurally related to LSD, produced the visionary experiences initiates described.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: A February 2026 study in Scientific Reports (Antonopoulos et al., Nat. Kapodistrian University) demonstrated experimentally that lye, available as wood ash solution in antiquity, converts toxic ergopeptides into psychoactive lysergic acid amide (LSA) derivatives. Combined with the 2019-2020 Mas Castellar de Pontós archaeological findings (ergot fragments in a ritual vessel and in dental calculus at an Eleusinian-affiliated sanctuary in Catalonia), the hypothesis has moved from speculative to experimentally feasible. No ergot residue has yet been found at the Eleusis site itself, but archaeological access has been limited.
sources: Wasson, Hofmann & Ruck, The Road to Eleusis (1978)
Mas Castellar de Pontós excavation reports (2019-2020) [Source not found; under review]

thenVsNow.title: The Prohibition of the Mysteries: Political Religion
thenVsNow.thenClaim: The suppression of the Eleusinian Mysteries by Theodosius in 392 CE was not because they had failed but because Christianity could not coexist with a competing institution that offered direct, experiential contact with the divine.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: The historical record is clear: Theodosius's Edict of Thessalonica (380 CE) mandated Christianity for all Roman citizens; his 392 CE decrees specifically banned non-Christian sacrifice and worship. The Mysteries were active and well-attended until political prohibition ended them. The parallel with contemporary drug prohibition, suppression of direct experience of altered states by institutional religion or government, is the political argument Ruck and Wasson embedded in the scholarship, and it maps directly onto current debates about psychedelic legalization.
sources: Lactantius, De Mortibus Persecutorum; Theodosius Codex
Mylonas, Eleusis and the Eleusinian Mysteries (1961)

thenVsNow.title: Western Philosophy's Psychedelic Root
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Plato, Sophocles, Aristotle, Cicero, and the other founding intellects of Western civilization were Eleusinian initiates. If the kykeon was psychedelic, their philosophy emerged partly from a shared psychedelic reference point.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: The initiate lists are historically confirmed. The philosophical implications are contested. Classical scholars including Walter Burkert and Albert Henrichs have argued that the Mysteries were effective through theater, ritual, and suggestion rather than pharmacology, and that the Platonic forms can be fully explained without a psychedelic substrate. The Road to Eleusis's authors reply that the consistency of 'vision' language across ancient accounts, combined with the 2026 chemistry, requires a pharmacological explanation. The debate is currently more live than it has been in decades.
sources: Wasson, Hofmann & Ruck, The Road to Eleusis (1978)

thenVsNow.title: The Eleusis Site Today
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Wasson, Hofmann, and Ruck wrote when the Eleusis archaeological site was partially excavated and surrounded by industrial development. No chemical analysis of vessel residues had been attempted.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: The site of ancient Eleusis is now a UNESCO-monitored archaeological zone. The adjacent cement factory and oil refinery continue to operate. A major excavation program began in 2015 under the Hellenic Ministry of Culture, and as of 2026, chemical residue analysis of excavated vessel fragments is actively under discussion. The 2026 Scientific Reports paper explicitly calls for such analysis. The Eleusis Cultural Capital 2023 initiative, EU funding for cultural rehabilitation of the site, has increased international attention. No ergot residue from the Eleusis Telesterion has yet been confirmed.
sources: Hellenic Ministry of Culture, Eleusis Excavation Reports (2015-2023)

thenVsNow.title: The Anslinger Theory: Was the Drug War Racist?
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Jay Stevens documented Anslinger's racially targeted enforcement of drug laws, particularly against Billie Holiday and Black jazz musicians. The drug war served to control specific communities alongside its stated public health rationale.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: John Ehrlichman's 2016 admission (to journalist Dan Baum, published in Harper's) that the Nixon administration's drug war was explicitly designed to criminalize anti-war protesters and Black people is the most direct confirmation. Ehrlichman: 'We knew we couldn't make it illegal to be either against the war or black, but by getting the public to associate the hippies with marijuana and blacks with heroin, and then criminalizing both heavily, we could disrupt those communities.' The account rests on Baum's notes alone, and Ehrlichman's family and several former Nixon aides dispute it. The American Civil Liberties Union has documented that Black people are 3.73 times more likely than white people to be arrested for marijuana despite similar use rates. The racial targeting Stevens documented was policy, not practice.
sources: ACLU, A Tale of Two Countries: Racially Targeted Arrests (2020)

thenVsNow.title: The Psychedelic Research Interruption: 1968-2018
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Stevens documented the collapse of the most promising psychiatric research program of the postwar era, LSD-assisted therapy, through a combination of countercultural misuse and political prohibition. He ended the book in 1968.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: The interruption lasted approximately fifty years. The revival began with Grob et al.'s 2011 psilocybin study at Harbor-UCLA, followed by the 2016 NYU and Johns Hopkins studies. As of 2025: psilocybin is in Phase 3 trials for TRD and MDD in the US and EU; MDMA-assisted therapy completed Phase 3 for PTSD (denied FDA approval 2024 due to trial design concerns, not efficacy); LSD-assisted therapy is in Phase 2 in Switzerland, Canada, and the UK; Australia approved psilocybin and MDMA for clinical use in 2023. The Storming Heaven story has a next chapter.

thenVsNow.title: The CIA and LSD: What MK-Ultra Actually Produced
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Stevens documented the CIA's purchase of the world's LSD supply, Operation Midnight Climax, and the coercive dosing of unwitting subjects. He argued the program produced nothing useful and killed at least one person (Frank Olson).
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: Church Committee hearings (1975), FOIA documents, and Frank Olson's 1994 exhumation confirmed the basic facts Stevens reported. A 2019 John Marks book update and the 2022 documentary 'The CIA's Secret Experiments' added additional documentation. Frank Olson's family reached a legal settlement with the US government in 1976; his son Eric Olson continued to press for murder charges until 2012. The CIA's own declassified inspector general report (1963) confirmed that MK-Ultra 'operated outside normal controls' and produced no verifiable intelligence techniques. The program's failure was documented internally before it was publicly revealed.
sources: Marks, The Search for the Manchurian Candidate (1979)

thenVsNow.title: Leary vs. Osmond: The Two Psychedelic Models
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Stevens documented the fatal split between the Osmond-Huxley model (careful clinical use, proper setting, preparation, integration) and the Leary-Kesey model (mass advocacy, countercultural provocation). The latter destroyed the conditions for the former.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: The same split has recurred in the current psychedelic renaissance. Researchers at Johns Hopkins and NYU publish carefully controlled trials; 'psychedelic facilitators' operate in gray markets; ketamine clinics have proliferated without adequate oversight; wellness retreats offer ayahuasca with minimal preparation or integration. The field is explicitly trying to avoid repeating the 1960s collapse. MAPS and the Society for Psychedelic Outreach, Reform, and Education (SPORE) are organizations explicitly created to manage the Apollonian/Dionysian tension Stevens identified.
sources: Johnson et al., J Psychopharmacol (2008), safety guidelines

thenVsNow.title: Hemp's Industrial Potential: The Herer Claim
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Hemp could replace wood pulp for paper, petrochemical fibers for textiles, and fossil fuels for energy. Herer estimated that fully restored hemp industries would generate $500 billion to $1 trillion annually and would reduce deforestation, carbon emissions, and petrochemical dependence.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: The 2018 US Farm Bill legalized industrial hemp cultivation for the first time since 1937. By 2023, the US hemp industry was valued at approximately $4.9 billion (Cannabis market research firm). Hemp building materials (hempcrete), textile fibers, and bioplastics are commercial products. Carbon sequestration studies confirm hemp sequesters CO2 more efficiently per acre than forests. The trillion-dollar estimate was optimistic given agricultural economics and existing competition from established synthetics, but the basic feasibility of all the uses Herer described has been demonstrated.
sources: Herer, The Emperor Wears No Clothes (1985)

thenVsNow.title: The DuPont-Hearst Conspiracy: Evidence Assessed
thenVsNow.thenClaim: DuPont and Hearst Paper Company orchestrated the 1937 Marihuana Tax Act to eliminate hemp as competition for DuPont's synthetic fibers and Hearst's timber-based paper supply. Anslinger's appointment by the Mellon family, DuPont's bankers, was the mechanism.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: The Mellon-Anslinger family connection is confirmed. Hearst's anti-marijuana newspaper campaign is documented. DuPont's synthetic fiber patents (nylon 1938) are historically dated. However, historians including Michael Pollan, Isaac Campos, and Elizabeth Gill have argued that Herer overstates DuPont's role and understates the genuine racial panic, immigration anxiety, and moral reform movements that drove the 1937 legislation. The conspiracy theory is not disproven but is probably not the complete explanation. The conclusion, that cannabis prohibition served corporate interests alongside racial targeting, is supported even if the specific orchestration is disputed.
sources: Herer, The Emperor Wears No Clothes (1985)
Campos, Home Grown: Marijuana and the Origins of Mexico's War on Drugs (2012)
Gill, The DEA's Misguided War on Drugs (2019)

thenVsNow.title: Cannabis Rescheduling: 2024-2026 Status
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Cannabis's Schedule I status, alongside heroin, is based on fabricated evidence and corporate lobbying rather than pharmacological science. Herer argued that rescheduling was legally and scientifically overdue from the moment of initial scheduling.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: In May 2024, the DOJ published a proposed rule to reschedule cannabis from Schedule I to Schedule III. In December 2025, President Trump signed an executive order directing the Attorney General to expedite the rescheduling. As of June 2026, final rescheduling has not been completed, but the proposed move to Schedule III is the most significant federal cannabis policy change since 1970. 38 US states have legalized medical cannabis; 24 have legalized recreational use. The WHO's Expert Committee on Drug Dependence recommended in 2019 that cannabis be rescheduled internationally. Herer's core claim, that the scheduling was scientifically unjustified, is now the federal government's own position.
sources: Herer, The Emperor Wears No Clothes (1985)

thenVsNow.title: Hemp Prohibition's End: What Herer Lived to See
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Cannabis prohibition would eventually collapse under the weight of its own contradictions, the medical evidence, the industrial case, and the racial justice arguments together made it untenable. Herer dedicated his life to accelerating this process.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: Herer died in April 2010, months after suffering a stroke at a cannabis rally. He lived to see medical cannabis legalized in 13 states and the 2009 Ogden Memo signaling federal non-interference with state programs. The 2018 Farm Bill legalized industrial hemp. Recreational cannabis is now legal in 24 states. The US hemp market has materialized. The medical cannabis industry is now a $30+ billion US market. The specific argument Herer made, that prohibition served corporate interests over public welfare, is now mainstream policy analysis, not fringe advocacy.
sources: Herer, The Emperor Wears No Clothes (1985)

thenVsNow.title: Plants of the Gods: Conservation Emergency
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Schultes and Hofmann warned that the psychoactive plant knowledge of indigenous communities was being lost faster than it could be documented. The investigation they called urgent had little time to proceed.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: The Amazon has lost approximately 20% of its forest cover since 1979. An estimated one indigenous language (the primary carrier of ethnobotanical knowledge) is now lost every two weeks globally. However, the field Schultes established has expanded dramatically: the Society of Ethnobiology has thousands of members; multiple databases of indigenous plant knowledge have been created with community consent; the field of 'citizen science ethnobotany' has emerged. The Amazonian Plant Medicines Project at ICEERS is creating formal repositories. The race against time Schultes described is still ongoing and still being lost at the macro scale, while individual documentation efforts accelerate.
sources: Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979)

thenVsNow.title: Ayahuasca Goes Global: Traditional Knowledge Under Pressure
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Schultes documented ayahuasca as a strictly regional practice embedded in Amazonian indigenous communities. The knowledge required formal apprenticeship with experienced curanderos and was fundamentally communal.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: Ayahuasca has undergone global diffusion since 1979 at a pace Schultes could not have imagined. As of 2024, there are an estimated 1,000+ ayahuasca retreat centers globally, the majority operating outside any regulatory framework. Peru alone hosts hundreds of retreat centers catering primarily to Western tourists, a phenomenon generating $100M+ annually. This diffusion has produced documented harms (exploitation, sexual abuse, unqualified facilitators) alongside therapeutic benefit. ICEERS, MAPS, and the Chacruna Institute have been established to address the decontextualization. Schultes's model of embedded, apprenticed, communal practice is increasingly rare.
sources: Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979)
Holman, Anthropology of Consciousness (2021) [Source not found; under review]
Tupper, Drug Alcohol Rev. (2014) [Source not found; under review]

thenVsNow.title: Peyote Conservation Crisis
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Schultes documented the peyote cactus as a sacred plant of the Native American Church, used in ceremony for centuries, growing in specific regions of the US and Mexico. He noted it as requiring conservation attention.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: As of 2023, peyote is classified as threatened in the Chihuahuan Desert, its primary habitat. Non-native demand, from non-NAC psychedelic users attracted by the 'psychedelic renaissance', has increased pressure on wild populations. The Peyote Way Church of God and the Chacruna Institute have issued formal conservation warnings. Texas, where most US-grown peyote is harvested, has seen 40% population decline in studied areas since 2000. The Native American Church has formally requested that non-members refrain from consuming peyote to protect both the plant and the cultural practice.
sources: Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979)
Feeney et al., J. Cactus Succul. Res. (2022) [Source not found; under review]

thenVsNow.title: Ethnobotany as Urgency: Schultes's Warning
thenVsNow.thenClaim: In the search for new hallucinogens, 'we have much to do and little time in which to do it.' The aspirin pill was destroying millennia of accumulated plant knowledge faster than any political force.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: Schultes's fear has proven prescient. Mark Plotkin, one of Schultes's students, established the Amazon Conservation Team in 1996 specifically to accelerate documentation. As of 2025, an estimated 45,000 plant species are at risk globally. The World Health Organization estimates that 80% of the world's population relies primarily on traditional plant medicine, demonstrating the continued relevance of the knowledge Schultes feared losing. The 2022 Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework committed signatories to protect 30% of land by 2030, with specific provisions for indigenous-managed territories.
sources: Plotkin, Tales of a Shaman's Apprentice (1993)

thenVsNow.title: The Opposite of Addiction: Connection, How Hari's Claim Holds Up
thenVsNow.thenClaim: The opposite of addiction is not sobriety but connection. Addiction is primarily driven by social disconnection, trauma, and lack of purpose, not by the pharmacological properties of the drug alone. Hari cites the Rat Park experiment as the animal evidence.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: The core claim, that environment and social connection modulate addiction, is well-supported. Rat Park itself has not been reliably replicated: Alexander's colony rats drank less morphine than isolated rats (1978 to 1981), but Bozarth and colleagues (1989) and Petrie (1996) did not find the same clear housing effect, and a 2019 commentary by Gage and Sumnall in Addiction argued the popular story has outrun the evidence. However, Hari's formulation overstates the case: opioid withdrawal is a genuine pharmacological process independent of social context, and naloxone-precipitated withdrawal is real. The more accurate claim is that connection modulates addiction risk and severity, not that pharmacology plays no role.
sources: Bozarth, Murray & Wise, Pharmacology Biochemistry and Behavior (1989)

thenVsNow.title: Portugal's Drug Decriminalization: The 2026 Picture
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Portugal's 2001 decriminalization of all drug use, combined with investment in jobs, housing, and social services, produced dramatic reductions in HIV transmission, overdose deaths, and addiction rates while imprisonment rates for drug users plummeted.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: Portugal's results through 2024 are more mixed than Hari's 2015 account suggested. Drug-related deaths rose significantly between 2015 and 2023 as the opioid crisis shifted toward synthetic opioids. A 2023 evaluation found that the social support programs have been underfunded since austerity measures following the 2008 financial crisis. HIV transmission among drug users remains low (the clearest success). The Portuguese government has maintained decriminalization but has increased enforcement against trafficking. The model works best when the social support investment matches the criminal justice savings, which has not consistently happened.

thenVsNow.title: The Anslinger-Holiday Story: Historical Accuracy
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Harry Anslinger personally targeted Billie Holiday because she sang 'Strange Fruit', an anti-lynching song, and he viewed her as politically dangerous. Her heroin addiction was the tool; suppressing her voice was the goal.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: Hari's account of the Anslinger-Holiday relationship drew criticism from historians including Jonathan Zimmermann and music critics following the 2021 film adaptation. John Szwed's biography of Holiday, reviewed alongside Hari's account, found that while Anslinger's enforcement was racially motivated, the specific claim that Strange Fruit was the direct trigger for his targeting of Holiday is not fully documented. Hari acknowledged some overstated claims on his corrections page. The broader argument, that the drug war's enforcement was racially selective, is well-documented; the specific Holiday narrative is narrative compression of more complex events.
sources: Szwed, Billie Holiday: The Musician and the Myth (2015)

thenVsNow.title: The Stoned Ape in 2025: Neuroscience Weighs In
thenVsNow.thenClaim: At low doses, psilocybin increases visual acuity and edge detection. At medium doses, it produces sexual arousal and group bonding. At high doses, it produces ego dissolution. These properties, applied to early hominids, drove language, religion, and the doubling of brain size.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: The neuroplasticity mechanism is now documented: psilocybin promotes dendritic spine formation and synaptogenesis in the prefrontal cortex (Shao et al., Neuron 2021). The visual acuity claim at low doses is supported by animal studies. The sexual arousal effect has some clinical support (5-HT2A agonism affects prosocial bonding). However, the specific evolutionary timeline and the claim about brain doubling remain without archaeological or genetic corroboration. Dennis McKenna has stated that while the specific claims of Food of the Gods are speculative, the general hypothesis, that psychoactive plants were part of the hominid ecological niche, is plausible.
sources: D. McKenna, talk at Psychedelic Science (2023)

thenVsNow.title: The Dominator Culture Argument: McKenna's Political Analysis
thenVsNow.thenClaim: The 'dominator culture', organized around male hierarchy, warfare, property, and ego, emerged when agriculture replaced the earlier hunter-gatherer-forager partnership with psychoactive plants. The suppression of plant medicines is one feature of the dominator system.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: McKenna drew substantially on Riane Eisler's Chalice and the Blade (1987). The archaeological evidence for a pre-dominance partnership period is disputed: evidence from Çatalhöyük and other Neolithic sites does show less hierarchical social organization, but scholars including David Graeber and David Wengrow (The Dawn of Everything, 2021) have shown that the narrative of a peaceful Neolithic before patriarchal domination is itself a simplification. The argument that psychedelic suppression is connected to broader social control has been substantially supported by Ehrlichman's 2016 Nixon admission and the racial targeting documented in drug war history.
sources: Eisler, The Chalice and the Blade (1987)
Graeber & Wengrow, The Dawn of Everything (2021)

thenVsNow.title: Chasing the Scream's Rat Park: The Replication Problem
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Bruce Alexander's Rat Park experiment demonstrated that isolated rats chose drugged water heavily while socially enriched rats in Rat Park avoided it almost entirely. Hari used this as the central scientific evidence for the connection model of addiction.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: Bruce Alexander and colleagues at Simon Fraser University ran the Rat Park studies in the late 1970s and published them between 1978 and 1981 (Alexander, Coambs and Hadaway, Psychopharmacology, 1978; Hadaway and colleagues, Psychopharmacology, 1979; Alexander and colleagues, Pharmacology Biochemistry and Behavior, 1981). Rats kept alone in standard cages drank more morphine solution than rats living together in a large open colony. Later attempts gave mixed results. Bozarth, Murray and Wise (1989) found that rats housed alone and rats housed in groups both learned to give themselves heroin and reached similar levels after a few weeks. Petrie (1996) could not repeat the housing difference: the isolated rats in his studies drank less than Alexander's had, and he suggested the supplier's rat strain had changed. The original result has not been reliably replicated, although the broader idea that surroundings can change drug taking still has support from other animal and human research. As Hari acknowledged in his corrections, a 1996 replication attempt did not reproduce Alexander's result. A 2019 commentary by Gage and Sumnall in Addiction argued the popular story has outrun the evidence. The specific claim that context almost completely overrides pharmacology is too strong: chronic opioid use produces lasting changes in the brain (Koob and Volkow, 2010).
sources: Alexander et al., Pharmacology Biochemistry and Behavior (1981)
Bozarth, Murray & Wise, Pharmacology Biochemistry and Behavior (1989)

thenVsNow.title: The Drug War Centenary: 2014 in Retrospect
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Hari published Chasing the Scream to coincide with the centenary of the Harrison Narcotics Tax Act of 1914, the first US drug control legislation. He argued the hundred-year experiment in prohibition had failed by every measure.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: The decade following Chasing the Scream has seen significant policy movement: recreational cannabis is now legal in 24 US states; Oregon decriminalized personal possession of all drugs in 2020 (then partly reversed in 2024 due to implementation challenges); multiple jurisdictions have adopted harm reduction frameworks; the Biden administration's October 2022 mass pardon of federal cannabis convictions was the largest drug policy reform action in US history. Yet overdose deaths reached record highs of 107,500 in 2023 (primarily fentanyl). The drug war is changing but not over, and the fentanyl crisis has complicated simple reform narratives.

thenVsNow.title: Television as Dominator Drug: McKenna's Media Theory
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Television is 'the dominator drug par excellence', control of content, uniformity of content, and repeatability of content make it a tool of coercion and manipulation. It replaces direct experience with mediated passivity.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: McKenna wrote this in 1992 before streaming, social media, and algorithmic feeds. The attention economy that has emerged since, with platforms optimized for engagement rather than truth, using variable-ratio reinforcement schedules identical to slot machines, is a much stronger version of the dominator drug he described. Sean Parker (founding president of Facebook) confirmed in 2017 that the platform was deliberately designed to exploit psychological vulnerabilities for engagement. The neuroscience of social media addiction now shows similar reward pathway activation to substance use. McKenna was directionally correct; the technology exceeded his warning.
sources: Haidt & Rausch, The Righteous Mind extended essays (2022) [Source not found; under review]

thenVsNow.title: Psychedelics and the War on Drugs: McKenna's Prediction
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Psychedelics are illegal not because they are dangerous but because they dissolve culturally-conditioned patterns of thought and enable direct perception of the control structures of modern society. Their suppression is a feature of the dominator system.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: John Ehrlichman's 2016 Harper's admission that the Nixon drug war explicitly targeted political enemies and Black communities confirms the political functionality McKenna described. Congressional testimony from 2019 DEA hearings confirmed that psilocybin's Schedule I classification was never based on evidence of harm or abuse potential. The FDA's Breakthrough Therapy designation for psilocybin (2018) and the subsequent opening of clinical research confirms that the scheduling was politically, not pharmacologically, determined.

thenVsNow.title: The Archaic Revival: Has It Happened?
thenVsNow.thenClaim: The Archaic Revival, the return of shamanic practices, plant medicine, non-rational epistemologies, and ecological consciousness, was already underway in 1992 and would accelerate. McKenna saw it as a cultural immune response to the pathology of the dominator system.
thenVsNow.nowEvidence: Psychedelic use has reached historically unprecedented levels in Western cultures since 2015. The psychedelic renaissance in medicine is genuine. Ayahuasca tourism is a $100M+ global industry. Indigenous plant medicine practices are studied at major universities. However, the 'revival' McKenna envisioned has often taken the form of commodified spiritual tourism rather than the deep cultural reorientation he described. The extraction model, Westerners consuming indigenous knowledge and plant medicines without sustainable relationship to the communities that stewarded them, is itself a feature of the dominator system he critiqued.
sources: Holman, J. Psychedelic Studies (2021) [Source not found; under review]

thenVsNow.title: The Clinical Model: Huxley and Osmond's Framework vs. Current Practice
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Huxley and Osmond's correspondence between 1955 and 1963 developed the clinical framework that would define psychedelic-assisted therapy: careful patient selection, a psychologically prepared set, a physically comfortable and aesthetically considered setting, a trained guide present throughout, music curated for the session, integration conversations afterward. Osmond's work at Weyburn Mental Hospital in Saskatchewan implemented this framework with LSD for alcoholism treatment with approximately 40-50% lasting sobriety rates.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: The framework Huxley and Osmond developed in their correspondence is the direct ancestor of every current psychedelic therapy protocol. The MAPS MDMA-AT protocol, the Johns Hopkins psilocybin protocol, and the company psilocybin protocol all specify: preparation sessions before drug administration, a carefully curated physical environment, trained therapists present throughout the session, music selected for the experience, integration sessions afterward. The FDA's August 2024 rejection of the MDMA application cited inadequate therapist training and monitoring, precisely the clinical rigor Osmond was arguing for in 1958. The clinical model is not just vindicated; it is now the FDA-mandated standard for psychedelic research, sixty years after Huxley and Osmond developed it by correspondence.
sources: FDA complete response letter on the MDMA-assisted therapy application (August 2024)
thenVsNow.significance: The letters were private professional correspondence that happened to contain the architecture of a clinical paradigm. That paradigm is now the operating standard for the most closely watched clinical trials in contemporary psychiatry.

thenVsNow.title: LSD and the Law: Hofmann's Hope for Rescheduling
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Hofmann argued throughout My Problem Child (1979) and in subsequent interviews and letters that LSD's Schedule I classification, 'no accepted medical use, high potential for abuse', was scientifically unjustified. He believed that rescheduling, or at minimum a restored research exemption, would come in his lifetime as the evidence accumulated. He continued making this argument publicly until his death in 2008 at age 102. He did not live to see any rescheduling of LSD.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: As of June 2026, LSD remains Schedule I under the US Controlled Substances Act and under equivalent international scheduling under the 1971 Convention on Psychotropic Substances. The WHO Expert Committee on Drug Dependence conducted a critical review of LSD in 2019 and found no evidence supporting its current scheduling level (Source not found; under review). No international rescheduling recommendation was implemented. A drug company's synthetic psilocybin, not LSD, is the compound approaching FDA approval for treatment-resistant depression. LSD clinical research has resumed in Switzerland, Canada, and the UK with promising Phase 2 results (Holze et al., Biological Psychiatry, 2023), but no commercial sponsor has committed to the Phase 3 trials required for NDA submission. The scientific case Hofmann made for rescheduling has been strengthened by fifty years of evidence. The legal structure remains unchanged. He was right about the science. He was wrong about the timeline.
sources: WHO ECDD Critical Review of LSD (2019) [Source not found; under review]
thenVsNow.significance: The gap between scientific consensus and legal status has rarely been more clearly documented than in the case of LSD. The WHO found the scheduling unjustified in 2019 (Source not found; under review). The scheduling has not changed. This is the policy failure Hofmann spent the second half of his life describing.

thenVsNow.title: Cannabis and Racial Justice: Herer's Implicit Promise vs. the Industry Reality
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Herer's argument in The Emperor Wears No Clothes was not only that prohibition was unjust but that the communities most harmed by that prohibition, Black and Latino Americans, disproportionately targeted for arrests and convictions despite similar use rates across demographic groups, deserved restitution. His vision of legalization was distributed and community-rooted: small farmers, local dispensaries, community-controlled production. The title's logic extended to racial justice: the emperor had no clothes, and the people most punished for seeing that had been the most economically and legally devastated.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: The legal cannabis industry is worth approximately $40 billion annually. The communities Herer was implicitly writing about have received a small fraction of that value. The ACLU's 2020 analysis found Black Americans are still 3.73 times more likely to be arrested for marijuana possession in legal states, despite similar use rates. Most states with legal cannabis passed social equity licensing provisions; most have been chronically underfunded, administratively bottlenecked, or successfully challenged by non-equity operators. Illinois, which passed one of the most ambitious equity frameworks, had by 2024 distributed a fraction of its intended equity funding. Biden's October 2022 mass pardons covered approximately 6,500 federal cannabis possession convictions, a meaningful step that did not address state convictions, which represent the vast majority. The Rohrabacher-Blumenauer amendment protecting state cannabis programs from federal prosecution has been renewed annually but not codified. Cannabis rescheduling from Schedule I to Schedule III was proposed by the DOJ in May 2024 and has not been finalized as of June 2026. Herer was right that the prohibition was racially targeted. The legalization has not produced racial justice.
sources: Herer, The Emperor Wears No Clothes (1985, 12th ed.)
ACLU, A Tale of Two Countries (2020)
Cannabis trade press, Social Equity Report (2024)
thenVsNow.significance: The cannabis equity gap is the clearest evidence that legalization and justice are not the same thing. Herer's argument was a justice argument. The industry that emerged is primarily a commercial one.

thenVsNow.title: Plant Intelligence: From Fringe to Research Frontier
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Narby's central methodological argument in The Cosmic Serpent (1998) was that Western science had foreclosed investigation of plant intelligence by assuming, a priori, that plants cannot communicate with their environment in any meaningful sense and that visionary states cannot be informative about external reality. These were not empirical findings; they were prior commitments that shaped which questions were considered legitimate. Narby argued that the evidence of indigenous pharmacological accuracy demanded that these priors be examined rather than assumed.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: The plant intelligence research of the twenty-five years since Narby published has substantially dismantled the priors he identified. Monica Gagliano's 2014 Oecologia study showed Mimosa pudica can learn and retain learned behaviors, a finding consistent with non-neuronal memory. Suzanne Simard's mycorrhizal network research (Nature, 1997; popularized in Finding the Mother Tree, 2021) reported that trees can exchange carbon through underground fungal networks; a 2023 review (Karst et al., Nature Ecology & Evolution) argued the field evidence for widespread sharing and kin support is weaker than often claimed. Gagliano's 2016 Scientific Reports study reported associative learning in pea seedlings, but a 2020 replication attempt (Markel, eLife) did not reproduce it. The journal Plant Signaling & Behavior, founded 2006, now publishes hundreds of papers annually on plant cognition and behavior. The International Society for Plant Signaling and Behavior holds an annual conference. None of this confirms Narby's specific biophoton hypothesis about shamanic vision. It does support his methodological point that plant behavior deserved investigation. The question he said deserved investigation is now being investigated.
sources: Plant Signaling & Behavior (journal, 2006, present) [Source not found; under review]
Karst et al., Nature Ecology & Evolution (2023)
thenVsNow.significance: Narby's book is more important as a methodological argument than as a specific hypothesis. The specific hypothesis (DNA biophotons as shamanic information channel) remains untested. The methodological argument, that plant intelligence deserves investigation, has been vindicated by two decades of mainstream research.

thenVsNow.title: The Pharmacological Harvest: What Schultes's Work Has Produced
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Schultes and Hofmann's Plants of the Gods documented 91 psychoactive plant species used by indigenous cultures across the Americas, Africa, and Eurasia, their chemistry, their ritual contexts, their cultural significance. Hofmann contributed the pharmacological analysis. Schultes contributed the ethnobotanical documentation. Their implicit argument was that this pharmacological diversity represented a vast untapped resource for medicine, psychiatry, and the scientific understanding of consciousness.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: The pharmacological harvest from the plants Schultes documented is well underway, forty-five years after Plants of the Gods. Psilocybin (from Schultes-documented Psilocybe species) is approaching FDA approval for treatment-resistant depression after two successful Phase 3 trials. Ibogaine (from Tabernanthe iboga, documented by Schultes) is in clinical trials for opioid use disorder and PTSD, with Texas committing $50 million in research funding in 2025 and Mississippi passing an ibogaine research bill in March 2026. Mescaline (from peyote and other cacti extensively documented by Schultes) is decriminalized in Colorado and the subject of active research into cluster headache treatment. DMT-based ayahuasca is the subject of dozens of clinical trials globally. The pharmacological argument Schultes and Hofmann made, that these plants contain medically important compounds, has been empirically validated on a substantial scale. The ethical argument about who benefits from this validation remains largely unresolved. The communities whose knowledge guided the documentation have received no systematic benefit from the pharmaceutical development. The Nagoya Protocol covers new exploitation but not historical extraction. Schultes was right about the pharmacological value. The justice question he did not ask has become the central contested issue in the field he helped create.
sources: Schultes & Hofmann, Plants of the Gods (1979)
thenVsNow.significance: Plants of the Gods is now a prospectus that has been substantially realized. The pharmacological value Schultes documented is being extracted. Whether the communities who stewarded that knowledge participate in the benefit is the unresolved ethical question his work implicitly posed.

thenVsNow.title: The Default Mode Network: Huxley's Reducing Valve Gets a Name
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Huxley proposed that the brain functions primarily as a reducing valve, its main job is to filter out most of what could be perceived, allowing only the 'measly trickle' of information useful for biological survival. He borrowed this from Bergson's inhibitory theory of the brain (Matter and Memory, 1896). The claim was philosophical and speculative in 1954; Huxley had no brain imaging evidence and no neuroscientific vocabulary more specific than 'valve.'
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: The default mode network (DMN), identified by Raichle et al. (PNAS, 2001) using fMRI, is the brain's primary self-referential processing network, active during mind-wandering, self-reflection, and the narrative construction of 'self.' Under psychedelics, DMN activity is dramatically suppressed (Carhart-Harris et al., PNAS, 2012). The REBUS model (Carhart-Harris & Friston, Pharmacological Reviews, 2019) formalizes the mechanism: psychedelics reduce precision-weighting of top-down predictions (the filter), allowing more bottom-up sensory information into awareness. Huxley's reducing valve is the DMN's filtering function.
