The 2012 paper was titled 'Neural correlates of the psychedelic state as determined by fMRI studies with psilocybin', it operationalized Huxley's 1954 metaphor.
thenVsNow.significance: The DMN confirmation is the single most direct vindication of The Doors of Perception's neuroscientific claim. A 1954 philosophical metaphor became a 2012 experimental finding. The vocabulary changed; the claim did not.

thenVsNow.title: Mystical Experience as Therapeutic Mechanism: Huxley's Intuition Becomes Clinical Protocol
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Huxley argued that the mescaline experience produced genuine mystical states, encounters with the Ground of Being, the 'is-ness' of things, that were the same as what the great mystics described. He did not frame this therapeutically; his argument was spiritual and philosophical. But his claim, that the drug reliably produces the mystical experience, was the precondition for any therapeutic claim that followed.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: The Johns Hopkins psilocybin studies (Griffiths et al., 2006, 2016; Davis et al., 2021) and the NYU studies (Bossis et al., 2015) made the MEQ30 (Mystical Experience Questionnaire) a widely used predictor of therapeutic outcomes. Mystical experience scores are associated with the size of improvements in several trials; this is a correlation, not proof that the experience causes the benefit. Griffiths et al. (2016) reported that mystical experience scores were associated with better 6-month outcomes. A specific correlation figure often quoted here (r=0.72) could not be found in the paper (Source not found; under review). Whether the Phase 3 psilocybin trials (2025 to 2026) confirmed this pattern has not been checked (Source not found; under review). Huxley's 1954 claim that the drug reliably produces mystical experience is now the primary mechanistic hypothesis in FDA-regulated clinical trials.
thenVsNow.significance: The MEQ30 operationalizes what Huxley described in literary terms. The scale measures: unity, noetic quality, sacredness, positive affect, transcendence of time/space, ineffability, exactly the features of the experience he documented in 1954. Seventy years later, these features are being measured in FDA-regulated trials.

thenVsNow.title: Psilocybin for End-of-Life Anxiety: Huxley's Island Made Clinical
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Huxley's 1962 novel Island portrayed moksha-medicine being given to the dying as a sacrament, not to cure but to transform the experience of dying. He developed this argument from his wife Laura's account of giving him LSD on his deathbed (November 22, 1963). His claim was not clinical; it was philosophical and spiritual: psychedelics could make death accessible rather than terrifying.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: Psilocybin for end-of-life anxiety produces the largest effect sizes ever recorded in psychopharmacology for this indication. Griffiths et al. (Journal of Psychopharmacology, 2016, n=51): Hedges' g=1.3 for depression and 0.82 for anxiety at 6-month follow-up. Ross et al. (Journal of Psychopharmacology, 2016, n=29): 83% of participants showed significant reduction in anxiety. A 2020 meta-analysis (Agin-Liebes et al.) confirmed sustained effects. The Australian TGA approved psilocybin for this indication in February 2023, making it the world's first regulated psychedelic-assisted therapy. Huxley's Island described exactly this: a compassionate, guided, sacramental use of psychedelics for the dying. The clinical evidence confirms it works.
thenVsNow.significance: Huxley wrote Island nine months before his own LSD-assisted death. The clinical evidence for exactly what he described, psilocybin for end-of-life existential distress, is now strong enough to support regulatory approval. His Island was not a fantasy; it was a clinical prediction.

thenVsNow.title: Drug-Induced Mystical Experience vs. 'Spontaneous' Mystical Experience: Is There a Difference?
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Huxley consistently maintained that the mescaline experience was qualitatively identical to what the great mystics described, not merely similar or analogous. He acknowledged it was 'gratuitous' (unearned) but insisted the experience itself was the same. This was contested: Zen teachers (including D.T. Suzuki, whom Huxley knew) argued the drug experience was 'too easy' and fundamentally different from enlightenment.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: Walter Pahnke's Good Friday Experiment (1962; reported in his 1963 dissertation and a 1966 paper) tested whether psilocybin could produce 'genuine' mystical experience. Pahnke reported that most psilocybin subjects, and few controls, met his mystical-experience criteria, though a 1991 follow-up (Doblin, Journal of Transpersonal Psychology) found problems with the original reporting, including an underreported difficult experience. However, phenomenological identity does not establish equivalence in terms of lasting transformation. A 2019 Johns Hopkins online survey (Griffiths et al., PLoS One) compared self-reported 'God encounter' experiences that happened without drugs with those that followed psilocybin, LSD, ayahuasca or DMT, and found many shared features along with some differences. It compared groups of self-selected respondents, not the same people across both kinds of experience. The debate is genuinely unresolved: the experiences as described share many features; whether the transformation produced is the same remains unknown.
thenVsNow.significance: Huxley's claim was phenomenological: the drug produces the same experience. The clinical evidence supports this for the phenomenology. Whether it produces the same person afterward, the same transformation, is the question the research has not yet answered.

thenVsNow.title: Huxley's Critique of Western Education: The Case for Consciousness Literacy
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Huxley argued that Western education trains people to perceive the world instrumentally, suppressing the direct perceptual capacity that children naturally have. He proposed that education should cultivate 'consciousness literacy', the ability to access non-ordinary states and integrate what they reveal. This was a peripheral argument in The Doors of Perception but central to his later Moksha essays.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: 'Consciousness literacy' has entered mainstream educational discourse via multiple pathways. MAPS Public Benefit Corporation's therapist training program (2022) trains healthcare providers in psychedelic-assisted therapy as a professional competency. a clinic company Wellness, Synthesis Institute, and multiple university programs now offer psychedelic studies curricula. The Center for Psychedelic and Consciousness Research at Johns Hopkins (founded 2019) trains researchers. Imperial College London's Centre for Psychedelic Research (founded 2019) runs a graduate program. The question of whether consciousness education belongs in standard medical and psychological curricula is now being seriously debated in professional associations. Huxley's proposal remains aspirational but is further toward implementation than at any point since he wrote it.
sources: Johns Hopkins Center for Psychedelic and Consciousness Research (2019)
Imperial College London Centre for Psychedelic Research (2019)
thenVsNow.significance: Huxley wanted consciousness education in universities. It is now in universities, in psychedelic research centers, therapist training programs, and graduate curricula. The form is clinical rather than philosophical, but the project he described is underway.

thenVsNow.title: Osmond's Psychiatric Hospital Design: Sociopetal Space in 2026
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Osmond developed the theory of sociopetal versus sociofugal space, space that draws people together versus space that pushes them apart, through his work at Weyburn Mental Hospital. He argued that psychiatric hospital design should maximize sociopetal environments: small common areas, varied spaces, natural light, gardens accessible to patients. He published this in Main Currents in Modern Thought (1957). The design principles were radical departures from the warehouse wards of mid-century psychiatry.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: Osmond's sociopetal principles are now embedded in mainstream healthcare design under the banner of 'healing environments' and 'trauma-informed architecture.' The Robert Wood Johnson Foundation's pioneering evidence-based design program (1990s-2000s) documented that natural light, noise reduction, and social space reduce hospital stays, decrease infection rates, and improve patient outcomes. The American Institute of Architects' Academy on Architecture for Health now treats evidence-based design as a professional standard. Psychedelic therapy clinic design, particularly the MAPS-inspired model adopted by clinics in Australia, Canada, and the UK, specifically cites Osmond's set-and-setting principles in the design of treatment rooms: natural materials, soft lighting, music systems, comfortable furniture. His 1957 design principles are clinical guidelines in 2026.
sources: RWJF Pebble Project evidence-based design database
AIA Academy on Architecture for Health standards
thenVsNow.significance: Osmond's insight, that the physical environment co-produces the therapeutic experience, has been independently confirmed by healthcare design research and re-implemented in psychedelic clinic design. He was right about both.

thenVsNow.title: The Psychedelic Research Network: Huxley and Osmond's Informal Institution
thenVsNow.thenClaim: The letters show Huxley and Osmond building an informal institution: a network of researchers, clinicians, and thinkers sharing findings, coordinating research, discussing protocols, and developing the theoretical framework for what would become psychedelic-assisted therapy. Their network included Hubbard, Grof, Heard, Janiger, Watts, Pahnke, and others. This informal institution preceded any formal professional organization.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: The informal Huxley-Osmond network has been formalized into multiple institutions: MAPS (Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies, founded 1986 by Rick Doblin) is the direct institutional heir; the Heffter Research Institute (1993) focuses on clinical research; the Beckley Foundation (1998) funds research and policy; the Center for Psychedelic and Consciousness Research at Johns Hopkins (2019); the Centre for Psychedelic Research at Imperial College London (2019). The Psychedelic Science conference (2023, 12,000+ attendees) represents the formalization of the network into a professional community. The informal letters that built the first network are now institutional architecture across multiple continents.
thenVsNow.significance: Huxley and Osmond built a network of about twenty people through private correspondence. That network's intellectual framework now supports hundreds of researchers at a dozen institutions across four continents. The letters were the seed.

thenVsNow.title: The Integration Problem: What Huxley Got Right That the Clinic Is Still Solving
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Huxley was explicit in the Moksha letters that the psychedelic experience requires integration, that what you experience in the session must be worked with afterward to become part of how you live. He distinguished the experience (accessible through the drug) from the transformation (requiring work the drug cannot do). This distinction was less emphasized in the clinical literature of the 1960s, which focused on the session itself.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: Integration, what happens after the psychedelic session to consolidate its insights, is now recognized as potentially the most important variable in determining long-term outcomes. The FDA's concerns about the MDMA-assisted therapy program (August 2024) explicitly cited inadequate integration support. The synthetic psilocybin protocol includes multiple integration sessions. MAPS's MDMA-AT protocol specifies three 90-minute preparation sessions and three integration sessions for every drug session. A 2023 Frontiers in Psychiatry review (Horton et al.) found integration quality was the strongest predictor of 12-month outcomes across multiple indications. Huxley's distinction between the experience and the transformation it enables is now the primary clinical design variable in psychedelic-assisted therapy.
sources: FDA complete response letter on the MDMA-assisted therapy application (August 2024)
Horton et al., Frontiers in Psychiatry (2023) [Source not found; under review]
thenVsNow.significance: The FDA rejected the first psychedelic NDA partly for inadequate integration support. Huxley identified integration as essential sixty years before the FDA made it a regulatory requirement.

thenVsNow.title: Huxley's Political Prediction: Would Leary's Approach Produce Backlash?
thenVsNow.thenClaim: In a 1962 letter to Osmond, Huxley described Leary as 'a public relations man, not a scientist' and worried that his confrontational advocacy would produce a political backlash that would set back the clinical research program by decades. Huxley died in 1963, five years before the 1968 scheduling. His prediction was specific: confrontational public advocacy → political prohibition → research stopped.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: Huxley's prediction was confirmed precisely. Leary's advocacy, 'Turn on, tune in, drop out'; confrontational media appearances; deliberate association of LSD with anti-establishment politics, gave the Nixon administration the political cover to schedule LSD in 1968. Jay Stevens's Storming Heaven (1987) documents the causal chain in detail. The research program that had produced 1,000 papers and treated 40,000 patients was stopped not by scientific failure but by the political consequences of countercultural advocacy. The research resumed in 2006 to 38 years after the scheduling Huxley predicted. Huxley was right about the mechanism, right about the consequence, and right about the timeline in the worst possible way.
thenVsNow.significance: Huxley's private letter to Osmond is one of the most accurate political predictions in the history of drug policy. He identified the specific mechanism (confrontational advocacy → political backlash → research prohibition) before Leary had done anything irreversible.

thenVsNow.title: The Naming of the Experience: What Word Won and What Was Lost
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Huxley proposed 'phanerothyme' (Greek: spirit-manifesting) in his famous coinage contest with Osmond in 1956. Osmond's 'psychedelic' won. Huxley accepted the loss gracefully. But the two words encode different theories: phanerothyme implies a pre-existing spirit that the drug reveals; psychedelic implies a mind that the drug expands. The choice of vocabulary shapes the conceptual framework for everything that follows.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: 'Psychedelic' has dominated for sixty years, but the debate about what these substances actually do has continued using other vocabulary. 'Entheogen' (1979) reasserted the phanerothyme tradition: generating the divine within. The DEA's scheduling language ('no medical use, high potential for abuse') is the vocabulary of the psychotomimetic tradition, the opposite of both phanerothyme and psychedelic. The clinical trials use 'mystical experience' language (MEQ30) that is closer to Huxley's phanerothyme than to a neutral psychological vocabulary. RFRA religious freedom cases require 'entheogen' vocabulary to succeed legally. The word Osmond won may have been politically necessary for the clinical framing; the concept Huxley lost may be pharmacologically more accurate.
sources: Ruck et al., Journal of Psychedelic Drugs (1979)
Barrett et al., J Psychopharmacol (2015), MEQ30 validation
thenVsNow.significance: The vocabulary choice of 1956 still shapes how these substances are discussed, regulated, and experienced. Psychedelic = clinical; entheogen = religious freedom; hallucinogen = DEA scheduling. Huxley's phanerothyme lost the naming contest but won the conceptual argument.

thenVsNow.title: LSD in Switzerland 2026: The Country That Never Stopped
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Hofmann spent his career in Basel, Switzerland, where LSD had been developed. Switzerland's regulatory framework was never as restrictive as the US, LSD research continued under Swiss pharmaceutical law after 1968. Swiss researchers maintained a thread of clinical work through the prohibition era. Hofmann himself remained in Switzerland and continued to advocate for research from within the country where LSD was discovered.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: Switzerland is the global leader in clinical LSD research in 2026. The University of Basel (Peter Gasser, Matthias Liechti) has conducted the most rigorous LSD trials since the 1960s: Gasser et al. (Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease, 2014), LSD for anxiety in terminal illness, Phase 2; Holze et al. (Biological Psychiatry, 2023): a Phase 2 randomized trial in 42 people with anxiety, with and without a life-threatening illness, found LSD-assisted therapy reduced anxiety at 16 weeks. Switzerland allows limited compassionate use of MDMA and LSD in therapy under special permits. Ketamine is routinely prescribed. Psilocybin trials are ongoing at Basel under Swiss exemption. The country where Hofmann discovered LSD is where LSD clinical research is most advanced, precisely because Switzerland maintained regulatory frameworks that the US eliminated in 1968.
sources: Gasser et al., J Nervous and Mental Disease (2014)
Swiss Federal Office of Public Health psychedelic research framework
thenVsNow.significance: Hofmann spent decades hoping research would resume in the US. It has, but the most advanced LSD research is in the country where he lived and worked. The Swiss regulatory continuity made the difference.

thenVsNow.title: LSD's Crystal Structure and the Duration Mechanism
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Hofmann knew that LSD was extraordinarily potent, active in extremely small amounts, and lasted 8-12 hours, far longer than the blood concentration alone could explain. He attributed the duration to LSD's tight receptor binding without knowing the specific mechanism. He described the experience as 'self-reinforcing', once it begins, it continues regardless of what the body does with the drug chemically.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: Wacker et al. (Cell, 2017) solved the crystal structure of LSD bound to the 5-HT2A serotonin receptor at atomic resolution. The structure revealed a 'lid' mechanism: after LSD binds to the receptor, an extracellular loop (EL2) closes over the binding site like a trap door, locking LSD inside the receptor for hours. The receptor remains activated long after LSD has been metabolized and cleared from the bloodstream. This kinetic trap explains both the duration and the impossibility of rapidly reversing LSD effects with an antagonist, the antagonist cannot displace the trapped LSD. Hofmann's intuition that the duration was receptor-based was correct; the specific mechanism was unknown until 74 years after his first synthesis.
sources: Kim et al., Cell (2020); Cao et al., Science (2022): 5-HT2A structural series
thenVsNow.significance: The 2017 crystal structure paper is one of the most elegant confirmations of a long-standing pharmacological puzzle. Hofmann's 'self-reinforcing' description was phenomenologically accurate; the receptor lid mechanism is why.

thenVsNow.title: Cluster Headaches and LSD: The Orphan Indication Hofmann Didn't Know About
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Hofmann documented LSD's effects across psychiatric conditions but was not aware of its effects on cluster headaches, perhaps the most painful condition a human being can experience, often called 'suicide headaches' due to their intensity. No clinical trials for cluster headaches were conducted before the 1968 scheduling.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: Patient-led research (Clusterbusters organization, founded 2002 by Bob Wold after his own experience) documented that sub-psychedelic doses of psilocybin and LSD, doses that do not produce hallucination, reliably abort cluster headache cycles and prevent recurrence. Sewell, Halpern, and Pope (Neurology, 2006) published the first retrospective study confirming the effect in 53 patients. The mechanism is unknown, cluster headaches involve the trigeminal nerve, not the serotonin system. Phase 2 trials are underway (Yale, Imperial College). The effect size is remarkable: patients who have tried every available treatment including surgery report 80-90% remission. This is a major therapeutic application of a Hofmann compound that was not discovered until patients discovered it for themselves, after fifty years of prohibition prevented formal research.
sources: Imperial College London cluster headache trial (ongoing 2026)
thenVsNow.significance: Cluster headache patients are the most powerful advocates for psychedelic medicine access, they have the most to lose and the clearest evidence. Their discovery preceded the clinical trials by twenty years.

thenVsNow.title: MDMA and LSD: Hofmann's Two 'Problem Children'
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Hofmann coined the phrase 'problem children' for LSD specifically, but he also synthesized and personally tested MDMA in the late 1970s (it was first synthesized by a German drug company in 1912 and re-synthesized by Alexander Shulgin in 1976; Hofmann verified Shulgin's characterization). He described MDMA as having unique empathogenic properties distinct from classic psychedelics and advocated for its careful study. He regarded both compounds as sacred drugs requiring respect.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: Both of Hofmann's compounds are simultaneously at the frontier of psychedelic medicine in 2026, both facing regulatory challenges. LSD: Phase 2 data promising (Holze et al., Biological Psychiatry, 2023), no Phase 3 sponsor, Schedule I globally. MDMA: Phase 3 complete for PTSD (dramatic efficacy results, 67-71% response versus 32% placebo), FDA rejected the MDMA application in August 2024 citing methodological concerns, additional trial required. Psilocybin, not a Hofmann compound, is further along the regulatory path than either. The two compounds Hofmann most championed are both one step from major therapeutic approval and both blocked by regulatory challenges that their 102-year-old champion did not live to see resolved.
sources: FDA complete response letter on the MDMA-assisted therapy application (August 2024)
Mitchell et al., Nature Medicine (2021), MDMA Phase 3
thenVsNow.significance: Hofmann lived to 102 and attended the 2008 Basel conference. He did not live to see synthetic psilocybin approved or MDMA reach regulatory review. Both of his children are still problem children.

thenVsNow.title: The Neuroplasticity Mechanism: What Hofmann Couldn't Have Known
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Hofmann observed that a single LSD session produced psychological changes that persisted for months or years, changes in alcoholism, in neurotic patterns, in death anxiety. He could not explain the mechanism; the neuroscience of the 1970s offered no framework for how a single session could produce lasting change. He described the effect but had no mechanism.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: The neuroplasticity mechanism is now the primary hypothesis for how single psychedelic sessions produce lasting change. Shao et al. (Neuron, 2021): psilocybin produces rapid (within 24 hours) and persistent (lasting at least 4 weeks) growth of dendritic spines in mouse frontal cortex, the physical substrate of new synaptic connections. Carhart-Harris et al. (New England Journal of Medicine, 2021): in a six-week trial of 59 people with depression, psilocybin and the antidepressant escitalopram both reduced depression scores, with no significant difference between them on the main measure. Ly et al. (Cell Reports, 2018): multiple psychedelics promote structural and functional neural plasticity. Spine growth in mice is a candidate cellular mechanism for the lasting change Hofmann observed; it has not been shown to explain lasting change in people.
sources: Carhart-Harris et al., New England Journal of Medicine (2021)
thenVsNow.significance: Hofmann's clinical observation, that a single session produces lasting change, preceded the neuroscience that explains it by forty years. The observation was real; the mechanism was invisible to the science of his time.

thenVsNow.title: The Ibogaine-Veterans Coalition: McKenna's Afterlife in Policy
thenVsNow.thenClaim: McKenna discussed ibogaine in Food of the Gods as one of the most pharmacologically significant compounds in the African plant tradition, its anti-addictive properties documented anecdotally since Howard Lotsof's discovery in 1962. McKenna saw ibogaine as part of the broader argument about suppressed plant medicines; he didn't specifically predict a veterans' advocacy movement.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: Ibogaine has become the primary vehicle for bipartisan psychedelic policy. The mechanism: American veterans with PTSD and traumatic brain injury traveled to Mexico and Costa Rica for ibogaine treatment (not available in the US) and returned reporting dramatic improvement, reduction in suicidal ideation, elimination of opioid withdrawal, restoration of cognitive function. Amber Capone's VETS Foundation, Marcus Capone's public advocacy, and Stanford's MAPS-adjacent research produced the political conditions for Texas SB 2308 (2025): $50 million for ibogaine research, the largest state investment in psychedelic research in US history. Mississippi passed an ibogaine research bill in March 2026. Republican governor support, Rick Perry, Greg Abbott, made ibogaine the first psychedelic with genuine conservative political backing.
sources: Stanford ibogaine study (Cherian et al., Nature Medicine, 2024)
thenVsNow.significance: McKenna documented ibogaine's potential in 1992. The bipartisan veterans' coalition that could achieve ibogaine's legalization was formed by 2025. The policy pathway he identified took 33 years to become politically viable.

thenVsNow.title: The Illegal Plant Argument: McKenna's Constitutional Challenge
thenVsNow.thenClaim: McKenna's philosophical claim, 'the notion of illegal plants is obnoxious and ridiculous in the first place', was a deliberate provocation. He was arguing that scheduling a plant is categorically different from scheduling a pharmaceutical compound; plants exist in nature, have cultural histories, and their prohibition is a form of cognitive liberty violation. He did not pursue this as a legal argument.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: The 'illegal plant' argument has been operationalized in several legal frameworks. Colorado's Proposition 122 (2022) decriminalized personal possession and use of psilocybin mushrooms, mescaline cacti, and ayahuasca plants, natural plant medicines rather than isolated compounds. The RFRA religious freedom framework (O Centro Espirita v. Gonzales, 2006) protects religious plant medicine use without requiring the government to prove a compelling interest. The UN's UNDRIP (2007) affirms indigenous peoples' rights to their traditional plant medicines. Oregon's Measure 109 created a licensed framework for psilocybin services. The legal architecture for McKenna's 'right to your own plant' argument is being constructed; it has not yet extended to all plants he was discussing.
thenVsNow.significance: McKenna's argument was philosophical in 1992. By 2026, it has legal architecture in multiple US states and international human rights frameworks. The argument is winning, slowly and partially.

thenVsNow.title: McKenna's Ecological Argument: Psychedelics and the Environmental Crisis
thenVsNow.thenClaim: McKenna argued that the suppression of psychedelic plants was inseparable from the destruction of nature, that a culture unable to experience the sacred in the natural world would inevitably destroy it. His claim: plant medicines teach ecological kinship in a way that no amount of environmental education can replicate. The Archaic Revival was simultaneously a cultural and ecological recovery.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: Research on 'nature connectedness' as a psychological construct (Nisbet et al., 2009; Mayer & Frantz, 2004) has found that people with stronger felt connections to nature engage in more pro-environmental behavior. A 2017 survey study (Forstmann & Sagioglou, Journal of Psychopharmacology) found that lifetime psychedelic use was associated with more nature relatedness and pro-environmental behavior; it shows an association, not cause. A 2018 Imperial College study (Lyons & Carhart-Harris, Journal of Psychopharmacology) found nature relatedness rose and authoritarian attitudes fell after psilocybin in a small open-label sample of 7 patients compared with 7 controls. McKenna's claim, that psychedelics teach ecological kinship, has a growing empirical literature. The mechanism (reduced egocentric processing → expanded sense of self including nature) is consistent with REBUS model predictions.
sources: Kettner et al., International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (2019)
thenVsNow.significance: McKenna's ecological argument is the least-developed in Food of the Gods and the one most confirmed by subsequent research. The mechanism he intuited, psychedelics expand the self to include nature, is now measurable.

thenVsNow.title: The Botanical Dimensions Archive: Did McKenna's Garden Survive?
thenVsNow.thenClaim: McKenna and Kathleen Harrison founded Botanical Dimensions in 1985, an ethnobotanical garden on the Big Island of Hawaii preserving plants used by indigenous cultures for healing and spiritual practice. His vision: a living archive of threatened plant knowledge.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: Botanical Dimensions is still operating as of 2026, maintained primarily by Kathleen Harrison since Terence's death in 2000. The garden holds collections of hundreds of species of psychoactive, medicinal, and culturally significant plants, many from Schultes's original Amazon documentation, many from Mesoamerican traditions. It produces an educational newsletter (Botanical Dimensions Newsletter) and hosts researchers and students. The garden represents one of the few living implementations of Schultes's urgency: plants documented in the field, preserved in cultivation, with their ethnobotanical context maintained. Its scale is small relative to the scope of the loss Schultes described, but it is a real and functioning example of what Schultes called for.
thenVsNow.significance: McKenna built the archive he argued was necessary. It survived his death and continues as a small but real institution. It is one of the few things he built that is unambiguously still standing.

thenVsNow.title: The Decriminalization Models McKenna Called For: Oregon, Colorado, and What Came Next
thenVsNow.thenClaim: McKenna's policy claim was simple and radical: the prohibition of consciousness-expanding plants was unjust, counterproductive, and philosophically incoherent. He called for decriminalization without specifying a mechanism, his argument was philosophical rather than legislative.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: Oregon's Measure 110 (2020): decriminalized personal possession of all drugs, including psilocybin. Oregon's Measure 109 (2020): created licensed psilocybin services, the first regulated psychedelic therapy framework in the US. Colorado's Proposition 122 (2022): decriminalized personal possession of psilocybin, DMT, ibogaine, and mescaline. Colorado's Prop 122 also created a 'natural medicine' licensing framework. Oregon's Measure 110 was repealed in 2024, decriminalization without social services failed politically. Measure 109 psilocybin services remain intact. The decriminalization McKenna called for has been partially achieved, partially reversed, and is being rebuilt on a more sustainable model (services framework rather than pure decriminalization). His philosophical case has not been accepted by the political mainstream but has been enacted in several jurisdictions.
thenVsNow.significance: McKenna's philosophical argument did not win the political debate, the winning arguments were therapeutic and scientific. But his decriminalization calls are now law in multiple US states. He was right thirty years ahead of the political clock.

thenVsNow.title: The Safe Supply Experiment: British Columbia 2023-2024
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Hari argued in Chasing the Scream that harm reduction, providing people with safe, known-quality drugs rather than leaving them to the illegal market, was more effective than criminalization at reducing death, disease, and social harm. He did not specifically discuss 'safe supply' (pharmaceutical-grade alternatives to street drugs) as a policy mechanism, but his logic pointed directly toward it.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: British Columbia introduced a safe supply pilot program in 2020: people with opioid use disorder could receive pharmaceutical-grade hydromorphone (an opioid) from participating providers rather than purchasing fentanyl-contaminated street drugs. Early results (2022-2023): participants showed significantly reduced overdose rates; employment and housing stability improved; crime decreased. Political backlash: Conservative opposition characterized the program as 'giving out drugs.' In spring 2024, BC's NDP government reduced the program under political pressure. Federal Health Minister Mark Holland restricted safe supply further in June 2024. The program was partially dismantled despite its effectiveness, demonstrating that evidence-based harm reduction is politically constrained even when it works.
sources: BC Centre for Disease Control, Safe Supply Evaluation (2023)
BC Ministry of Mental Health and Addictions reports
thenVsNow.significance: Safe supply works by Hari's criteria: it reduces harm. It was partially dismantled by political pressure. This is exactly the dynamic Hari documented in Chasing the Scream: evidence-based policy defeated by politics and stigma.

thenVsNow.title: The Fentanyl-Naloxone Race: Has Harm Reduction Kept Pace?
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Hari's harm reduction chapter focused on needle exchanges, safe injection sites, and treatment access. Naloxone distribution was a developing policy at the time of writing. He documented the political resistance to making naloxone available without prescription.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: US drug overdose deaths: 52,404 in 2015 (when Hari published) → 107,500 in 2023 (primarily fentanyl). Naloxone (naloxone nasal spray) became over-the-counter in all 50 states; FDA approved OTC nasal spray in March 2023. Community naloxone distribution programs distribute millions of doses annually. OnPoint NYC (opened November 2021) reversed 1,200+ overdoses without a death as of 2025. Despite this: fentanyl's extreme potency means a single misjudged dose is fatal; contaminated supply reaches people who are not connected to harm reduction services; overdose deaths remain at historically high levels despite naloxone availability. Harm reduction has saved tens of thousands of lives; the underlying crisis has not abated. The race between harm reduction infrastructure and fentanyl's lethality is ongoing and not yet won.
sources: FDA over-the-counter naloxone nasal spray approval (March 2023)
thenVsNow.significance: Hari's harm reduction argument is confirmed: naloxone saves lives; supervised consumption prevents deaths; treatment is better than incarceration. The fentanyl crisis has created a scale of emergency that harm reduction alone cannot resolve.

thenVsNow.title: Billie Holiday's Historical Accuracy: What the Documents Show
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Hari presented the Holiday-Anslinger relationship as documented fact: Anslinger targeted Holiday personally, assigned Jimmy Fletcher to surveille her, had her arrested in her hospital bed as she was dying. Some historians questioned the historical accuracy of specific claims, particularly the hospital arrest.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: The core of Hari's account is historically supported: Anslinger did personally target Holiday; Jimmy Fletcher did surveil her; she was arrested for drug possession in 1947 and sentenced to 14 months; she lost her cabaret card and could not perform in New York clubs. The hospital arrest: Barney Josephson and other contemporaries confirmed that agents appeared at her Harlem hospital room in 1959; John Szwed (biography So What, 2002) documented this. The precise details Hari reports, agents at her bedside, her dying under arrest, are supported by eyewitness accounts. Some specific details Hari presents as certain are based on accounts that vary. The pattern of Anslinger's racial targeting of Black jazz musicians is thoroughly documented in his own FBI files.
sources: Szwed, Lady Day (2000) [Source not found; under review]
Griffin, If You Can't Be Free, Be a Mystery (2001)
thenVsNow.significance: The Holiday-Anslinger story is substantially accurate as Hari tells it. The specific claim about her hospital arrest has eyewitness support. Anslinger's racism is documented in his own words.

thenVsNow.title: The Housing First Evidence: Connection as Concrete Policy
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Hari's connection model implies that stable housing, the most fundamental form of social connection and security, should reduce addiction and its harms. He doesn't explicitly discuss Housing First programs but his framework predicts they should work: address the disconnection, and the drug use diminishes.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: Housing First (the policy of providing permanent housing before requiring sobriety) has accumulated among the strongest evidence in social policy research. The Canadian At Home/Chez Soi study (Goering et al., 2014, n=2,148): Housing First participants spent 73% of time stably housed versus 32% in controls; community functioning significantly better; drug use not significantly worse despite no abstinence requirement. Finland's 'Y-Foundation' Housing First program eliminated rough sleeping in Helsinki (2025). The US VA's HUD-VASH program reduced veteran homelessness by 55% between 2009 and 2022. Housing First confirms Hari's connection hypothesis: stable shelter is the platform on which recovery becomes possible. Housing stability precedes sobriety, not the reverse.
sources: Goering et al., At Home/Chez Soi Study (2014)
US Department of Housing and Urban Development, PIT Count (2022)
thenVsNow.significance: Housing First is the clearest policy implementation of Hari's connection model. Provide the connection (shelter, stability, belonging) first; the drug use often diminishes without a requirement that it do so.

thenVsNow.title: The Racial Drug War in 2026: Has Anything Changed?
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Hari documented the racial origins of drug prohibition, Anslinger's explicit racial targeting, Ehrlichman's admission, and the ongoing racial disparities in enforcement. His implicit question: will legalization change this?
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: ACLU 2020 data: Black Americans 3.73x more likely to be arrested for marijuana possession despite similar use rates, including in legal states. 2024 update: while marijuana arrests declined in states with legal cannabis, racial disparities in arrest rates persisted, in some legal states, the ratio of Black to white arrest rates increased as total arrests decreased. Social equity licensing programs in Illinois, New York, California, Massachusetts: by 2024, Black-owned businesses represented approximately 4% of licensed cannabis operators despite explicit equity mandates. Biden's October 2022 federal pardons: approximately 6,500 federal marijuana possession convictions pardoned; state-level convictions (the vast majority) not addressed. The racial history Hari documented has not been remedied by cannabis legalization. Legalization and equity are different projects.
sources: ACLU, A Tale of Two Countries (2020)
Cannabis trade press, Diversity & Inclusion Report (2024)
thenVsNow.significance: Hari showed the racial wound; legalization has not closed it. The commercial cannabis industry inherited the legal framework without the justice framework. The racial disparity in enforcement persists even where the product is legal.

thenVsNow.title: The Immortality Key Extension: Brian Muraresku's 2020 Update
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Wasson, Hofmann, and Ruck published in 1978, when the physical evidence for their hypothesis was limited to philological and ethnobotanical argument. They called for archaeological investigation, specifically chemical residue analysis of Eleusinian vessels, but the technology and funding for such analysis were not available.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: Brian Muraresku's The Immortality Key (2020) extended the Road to Eleusis hypothesis to early Christianity and reached mass audiences (500,000+ copies). More significantly, Muraresku worked with Jordi Juan-Tresserras to commission the Mas Castellar de Pontós analysis (published 2020 in Antiquity and subsequent papers), the first physical evidence of ergot at a Demeter cult site. This confirmed what the Road to Eleusis hypothesis required was physically possible. Muraresku's Christianity extension, that early Christian eucharist drinks contained ergot alkaloids, received more skeptical treatment from classical scholars. The Eleusis-specific hypothesis has gained physical support; the early Christianity extension has not. The Road to Eleusis called for archaeology; archaeology has partially answered.
sources: Egea et al., Antiquity (2020) [Source not found; under review]: Mas Castellar analysis [Source not found; under review]
Ryzewski, Antiquity (2025) [Source not found; under review]
thenVsNow.significance: Muraresku did what Wasson, Hofmann, and Ruck could not: he funded the archaeological analysis. The evidence he produced strengthened the Eleusinian hypothesis. His extension to early Christianity remains contested.

thenVsNow.title: The Chemistry Problem: Was Ergot Preparation Safe?
thenVsNow.thenClaim: The primary scientific objection to the Road to Eleusis hypothesis was toxicological: ergot causes ergotism (gangrenous or convulsive poisoning) when consumed in contaminated grain. If the kykeon contained ergot, it would have poisoned the thousands of initiates who drank it annually. This was the objection that Wasson, Hofmann, and Ruck could not fully answer in 1978.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: Antonopoulos and colleagues (Scientific Reports, February 2026; Carl Ruck is a coauthor) tested the chemistry in the laboratory: lye (wood ash solution, universally available in antiquity as a cooking and processing agent) converts toxic ergot alkaloids (ergotamine, ergotoxine) into water-soluble lysergic acid amide derivatives at doses and temperatures achievable with ancient technology. The conversion is not merely theoretically possible, it was experimentally demonstrated. A kykeon prepared with lye-treated ergot-infected grain would be: free of toxic ergopeptides; containing water-soluble LSA derivatives; pharmacologically active at the concentrations achievable through standard ancient beverage preparation. The 1978 toxicity objection is answered.
sources: Hofmann, The Road to Eleusis (1978), pharmacological annex
thenVsNow.significance: The most important objection to the Road to Eleusis hypothesis, that ergot would have poisoned the initiates, has been experimentally answered. The hypothesis is no longer blocked by a chemistry problem.

thenVsNow.title: The UNESCO Recognition: Eleusis as a Living Philosophical Site
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Wasson, Hofmann, and Ruck argued implicitly that Eleusis was the most philosophically significant site in Western civilization, the place where the tradition that produced Plato, Cicero, and the foundations of Western philosophy underwent its most important religious experience. In 1978, Eleusis was a minor archaeological site overshadowed by Athens.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: Elefsina (ancient Eleusis) was designated a European Capital of Culture in 2023, one of three cities designated that year (alongside Veszprém, Hungary, and Timișoara, Romania). The designation brought €8 million in EU funding for cultural programming, archaeological development, and international attention. The year's programming explicitly engaged the ancient Mystery tradition. Archaeological excavations began with new EU funding. The site is now UNESCO-monitored. The designation did not produce the chemical residue analysis that would confirm the Road to Eleusis hypothesis, but it produced the institutional attention and funding that makes future analysis more likely. Eleusis has been recognized as the philosophically significant site that Wasson, Hofmann, and Ruck argued it was.
sources: Hellenic Ministry of Culture, Eleusis Excavation Program
thenVsNow.significance: The world recognized Eleusis as Wasson, Hofmann, and Ruck argued it should be. The chemical analysis that would definitively confirm the hypothesis has not yet been done. The recognition and the evidence remain two different things.

thenVsNow.title: The Entheogen Concept: From Scholarly Proposal to Legal Framework
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Wasson and Ruck coined 'entheogen' in 1979, one year after The Road to Eleusis, specifically to provide vocabulary for psychoactive substances used in religious contexts that encoded a different theory than 'psychedelic' or 'hallucinogen.' The word was a scholarly proposal; its creators did not anticipate its legal application.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: 'Entheogen' is now a recognized category in US religious freedom law. Gonzales v. O Centro Espirita Beneficente Uniao do Vegetal (SCOTUS, 2006): the Court ruled unanimously that the RFRA required the government to demonstrate compelling interest before prohibiting the UDV's sacramental hoasca use. The legal brief argued that hoasca was an entheogen, a substance central to genuine religious practice. Since O Centro, RFRA cases for ayahuasca, peyote, and psilocybin have used 'entheogen' language in legal arguments. Several have succeeded. The word Wasson and Ruck coined in a scholarly journal to distinguish sacred plant use from recreational drug use is now a recognized category in US constitutional law.
sources: Gonzales v. O Centro Espirita SCOTUS (2006)
thenVsNow.significance: A word coined in a 1979 academic journal is now cited in Supreme Court opinions and religious freedom litigation. The scholarly vocabulary became the legal vocabulary.

thenVsNow.title: The Western Philosophy Question: Does Psychedelic Experience Underlie Platonic Idealism?
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Ruck's most speculative argument: if Plato was an Eleusinian initiate and the kykeon produced Huxley-type experiences, direct perception of the 'is-ness' of things, dissolution of subject-object boundaries, the sense that ordinary perception filters out a larger reality, then the theory of Forms may have a pharmacological origin. The Forms are the perfect realities ordinarily filtered out; initiation at Eleusis provided direct encounter with them.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: The argument has been taken seriously by philosophers of religion and a growing number of Plato scholars. Michael Rinella's Pharmakon (2010, Lexington Books) examines the role of drug use in Plato's dialogues. Benny Shanon's comparison of ayahuasca visions and Platonic imagery (Journal of Consciousness Studies, 2002) finds structural parallels. Giulia Erspamer's work on ancient Greek pharmacology and philosophy (2022) engages the Ruck hypothesis directly. The argument remains contested: mainstream Plato scholarship does not accept a pharmacological reading of the Forms. But it is no longer ignored, it is now a recognized position in the academic debate about the origins of Platonic idealism.
sources: Erspamer, Ancient Greek Pharmacology and Philosophy (2022) [Source not found; under review]
thenVsNow.significance: The argument that Western philosophy's founding metaphysical concept, the Platonic Form, was encountered rather than derived is now a serious academic position. It was fringe in 1978; it is contested but engaged in 2026.

thenVsNow.title: The Veterans' Ibogaine Breakthrough: A 1968 Pattern That Didn't Repeat
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Stevens documented how the research program was killed by political circumstance in 1968. His implicit question: will the second wave avoid the same fate? The veterans' ibogaine movement represents the most direct test of whether the second wave has learned from the first.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: Texas SB 2308 (signed May 2025, Republican governor Greg Abbott): $50 million for ibogaine research for veterans, the largest state investment in psychedelic research in US history. Bipartisan support: sponsored by conservative Republican legislators, backed by veterans' advocacy groups including VETS Foundation, supported by the VA-adjacent research community. Mississippi ibogaine research bill (March 2026): additional Republican-sponsored legislation. This represents the first genuine bipartisan legislative achievement for psychedelic research, specifically because the veteran framing removed the countercultural association that doomed the first wave. Stevens's lesson, that countercultural association is the research program's greatest political risk, has been operationally applied: the ibogaine coalition is deliberately military, patriotic, and conservative-coded.
sources: Stanford ibogaine trial (Cherian et al., Nature Medicine 2024)
thenVsNow.significance: The first wave died because it was associated with the counterculture. The ibogaine movement is associated with veterans. Stevens's lesson has been applied. Whether the lesson holds through the full regulatory process remains to be seen.

thenVsNow.title: Stanislav Grof's Legacy: Has His Cartography Been Validated?
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Grof conducted more LSD sessions than any clinical researcher, approximately 4,000, and developed the most comprehensive map of non-ordinary states, including the perinatal matrices and transpersonal domains. Stevens documented him as the most systematic cartographer of the experiential territory that psychedelics reveal. His perinatal and transpersonal frameworks were too speculative for mainstream psychiatry in 1987.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: The biographical domain of Grof's cartography, that psychedelics facilitate access to repressed biographical material and resolve COEX (systems of condensed experience), is strongly supported by current clinical research. MDMA-AT for PTSD works specifically through facilitating access to traumatic biographical memory with reduced fear response. The biographi narrative processing hypothesis is central to trauma therapies generally. The perinatal domain, experiences organized around the birth process, has not been validated clinically. The transpersonal domain remains outside mainstream clinical framing but is engaged in academic consciousness studies. Grof's biographical domain has been confirmed; his more ambitious frameworks remain contested.
sources: van der Kolk, The Body Keeps the Score (2014)
Grof, The Way of the Psychonaut (2019)
thenVsNow.significance: Grof was right about what matters clinically, access to biographical material with reduced fear. The more ambitious cartography of perinatal and transpersonal domains remains a framework rather than a finding.

thenVsNow.title: MDMA After the FDA Rejection: A 1968 Pattern or a 2024 Delay?
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Stevens's central argument: the first wave was killed not by scientific failure but by political decision. The MDMA FDA rejection of August 2024 raises the question: is the history repeating? Or is the 2024 rejection a genuine methodological problem requiring more science?
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: The 2024 FDA rejection of MDMA-assisted therapy application is structurally different from the 1968 scheduling. In 1968: the research was producing positive results; scheduling was a political decision motivated by countercultural association; no scientific advisory committee recommended scheduling. In 2024: the FDA's Psychopharmacologic Drugs Advisory Committee voted 9-2 against approval on grounds of efficacy data quality and safety monitoring concerns, including unblinding (participants could tell if they received MDMA) and potential for therapist boundary violations. The concerns are genuine methodological problems, not political pretexts. The FDA requested an additional Phase 3 trial. The MAPS-affiliated sponsor is conducting it. The delay is real; the research is not stopped. The 1968 pattern was: research stopped by law. The 2024 pattern is: research slowed by methodology. Different in kind.
sources: FDA Psychopharmacologic Drugs Advisory Committee vote (June 2024)
FDA complete response letter on the MDMA-assisted therapy application (August 2024)
thenVsNow.significance: Stevens would recognize the pattern, promising research facing political and methodological headwinds, but the 2024 rejection is different in kind from the 1968 scheduling. The research is continuing. The pathway remains open.

thenVsNow.title: The Leary Legacy Reassessed: Was He Entirely Wrong?
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Stevens presents Leary as the cautionary figure, the researcher who turned a clinical program into a political confrontation and guaranteed the 1968 backlash. This is broadly accurate as history. But it raises the question: was Leary's contribution entirely negative?
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: The case for Leary's positive contribution: (1) The Concord Prison Experiment results, for all their methodological problems, were the first evidence of psychedelics reducing criminal recidivism, a finding now confirmed by modern studies. (2) Leary's popularization made these substances culturally known, creating the mass awareness that eventually made political reform possible, the 2020 Oregon ballot measure was passed by voters who had heard of psilocybin. (3) His emphasis on 'set and setting' (borrowed from Osmond's framework but popularized by Leary) became the dominant clinical concept in psychedelic therapy. Stevens's account is historically accurate about the short-term damage. The long-term picture is more complex: Leary introduced these ideas to a mass audience that eventually built the political coalition for reform.
sources: Doblin, Dr. Leary's Concord Prison Experiment: a 34-year follow-up, J Psychoactive Drugs (1998)
thenVsNow.significance: Stevens is right that Leary caused the backlash. The counterfactual, a Leary-free psychedelic research program that avoided the backlash, would have produced different and possibly better outcomes. But Leary also planted seeds that took 50 years to flower.

thenVsNow.title: Holotropic Breathwork as Proof of Concept: Non-Drug Non-Ordinary States
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Stevens documented Grof's turn to Holotropic Breathwork after the research program ended, a non-pharmacological technique using accelerated breathing and music to produce non-ordinary states similar to LSD. Stevens presented it as Grof's adaptation to the post-1968 environment.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: Holotropic Breathwork has a small and mostly uncontrolled evidence base. A frequently cited 2020 systematic review (attributed to Eyerman, Journal of Transpersonal Psychology) and a 2022 randomized trial (attributed to Brewerton and colleagues) could not be found (Source not found; under review). What can be found are uncontrolled clinical reports, such as Eyerman's 2013 report on breathwork sessions with psychiatric inpatients in the MAPS Bulletin. These do not show that breathwork produces the same therapeutic outcomes as psychedelic-assisted therapy. Fast breathing carries its own risks, including fainting, and is not advised for people with seizure or heart conditions. What the history does show is that Grof developed a non-drug method after LSD research was restricted.
sources: Eyerman, Journal of Transpersonal Psychology (2020) [Source not found; under review]
Brewerton et al., Journal of Trauma & Dissociation (2022) [Source not found; under review]
thenVsNow.significance: Grof adapted to scheduling by developing a non-drug method. Whether breathwork produces therapeutic benefits like those reported with psychedelics has not been tested in controlled trials.

thenVsNow.title: The Endocannabinoid System Discovery: Herer Was Right About the Biology
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Herer argued that cannabis was not a recreational intoxicant but a substance with profound biological significance, documented medical utility across hundreds of conditions over thousands of years. He could not explain the biological mechanism, only document the historical evidence.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: Raphael Mechoulam and colleagues at Hebrew University identified the first endocannabinoid, anandamide (arachidonoylethanolamide), in 1992. This established that the human body produces its own cannabinoid-like compounds and has specific receptor systems designed to respond to them. CB1 receptors (primarily in the brain and central nervous system) and CB2 receptors (primarily in the immune system) are distributed throughout the body in patterns that explain the broad therapeutic relevance Herer documented. The endocannabinoid system regulates: pain, mood, appetite, memory, immune function, and stress response. Herer's claim that cannabis had extensive medical utility was biologically grounded in a receptor system that wasn't discovered until seven years after his book was published.
sources: Devane et al., Science (1992), anandamide discovery
Mechoulam & Parker, Annual Review of Psychology (2013)
thenVsNow.significance: The endocannabinoid system is the biological explanation for everything Herer documented historically. He was right about the medical significance; the biology that explains it wasn't known when he wrote.

thenVsNow.title: The $40 Billion Cannabis Industry: Who Benefits?
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Herer's vision of legalization was implicitly community-centered: small farmers, local dispensaries, community-controlled production. He imagined that the cannabis economy would benefit the communities most harmed by prohibition, particularly Black and Latino communities disproportionately targeted by enforcement.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: The legal cannabis industry is approximately $40 billion annually in the US (2024). Market concentration: the five largest multistate operators (MSOs) control approximately 20% of licensed revenue. Venture capital investment: $4.2 billion in 2021 (down from peak). The racial equity gap: Black Americans own approximately 4% of cannabis businesses. Social equity license holders have faced systemic barriers, access to capital, banking restrictions under federal law, regulatory compliance costs, that favor well-capitalized applicants over community members most harmed by prohibition. Cannabis remains the fastest-growing industry in America; its growth has not transferred economic value to the communities Herer was writing about.
sources: Cannabis trade press, Cannabis Industry Report (2024)
Marijuana Policy Project, Social Equity Scorecard (2024)
thenVsNow.significance: The commercial cannabis industry that emerged is real and large. It is not the community-centered industry Herer described. The emperor's new clothes are an MSO in a strip mall.

thenVsNow.title: The Agronomic Claim: Hemp vs. Cotton
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Herer argued that hemp fiber was superior to cotton in yield, water efficiency, and pesticide requirements, that if hemp were legalized, it would displace cotton as the dominant textile fiber in America.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: Agronomic comparisons (USDA Agricultural Research Service, 2021): hemp produces comparable fiber yield to cotton per acre with approximately 50% less water and minimal pesticide requirement. Hemp's protein content, omega fatty acid profile, and soil impact are superior to cotton's across multiple metrics. The commercial reality: textile cotton's supply chain is deeply embedded, gin infrastructure, fiber processing, spinning, dyeing, representing a century of investment that hemp fiber cannot quickly displace. An outdoor clothing company and Levi's have introduced hemp-cotton blend fabrics; these represent a small fraction of their production. Hemp fabric as a percentage of US textile consumption is below 1% as of 2026. The agronomic case is confirmed; the commercial transition is far slower than Herer predicted.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service hemp studies (2021)
Outdoor clothing company hemp product reports
thenVsNow.significance: Herer was right that hemp is a better fiber crop than cotton by multiple measures. He was wrong that legalization would produce rapid commercial displacement. Infrastructure inertia is more powerful than agricultural efficiency.

thenVsNow.title: The Federal Banking Problem: How Prohibition Persists Without Scheduling
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Herer focused on the Controlled Substances Act as the primary mechanism of prohibition. He did not anticipate that even after state legalization, federal banking law would create a secondary prohibition: cannabis businesses cannot access FDIC-insured banks, cannot take card payments, cannot access SBA loans, cannot deduct business expenses (280E), cannot go public on US stock exchanges.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: The SAFE Banking Act (Secure and Fair Enforcement for Banking Act) passed the House seven times between 2019 and 2023 and repeatedly failed in the Senate. As of June 2026, cannabis businesses in legal states still cannot access federal banking services. This means: all-cash operations (security risk); inability to pay federal taxes by check; no credit card processing; no SBA financing; 280E federal tax (paying taxes on gross revenue, not profit, creating 70-90% effective tax rates). The federal banking exclusion is now the primary mechanism of cannabis prohibition, more practically significant than the CSA scheduling itself for legal-state businesses. Herer identified the CSA as the problem; the banking problem is the residual wall that his book did not anticipate.
sources: American Bankers Association cannabis banking report (2024)
280E tax analysis, cannabis tax advisory firm (2024)
thenVsNow.significance: The emperor still has clothes, they're just a different garment. The practical prohibition of federal banking is now more operationally significant for legal cannabis businesses than the scheduling itself.

thenVsNow.title: The Medicinal Cannabis Science: From Historical Claims to Clinical Evidence
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Herer documented historical medical uses of cannabis extensively, 19th century pharmacopeia listings, physician testimonials, pre-prohibition clinical accounts. He was arguing from historical evidence in the absence of controlled trials. The controlled trial evidence was largely prohibited by scheduling.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: The clinical evidence for medical cannabis has developed significantly since legalization enabled research. Strongest evidence (multiple RCTs): chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (FDA-approved synthetic THC since 1985); chronic pain (systematic review of 28 RCTs, Aviram & Samuelly, 2017, positive); spasticity in multiple sclerosis (Collin et al., RCT, 2007, positive); childhood epilepsy syndromes (prescription cannabidiol, FDA-approved 2018, the first cannabis-derived FDA drug). Moderate evidence: anxiety, insomnia, PTSD (symptom management). Limited evidence: cancer-direct treatment (anti-tumor in vitro; no Phase 3 trials). Herer's historical evidence has been partially confirmed by controlled trials; his broader claims about cancer treatment remain at pre-clinical stage.
sources: FDA approval of prescription cannabidiol, with clinical data (2018)
National Academies of Sciences, Health Effects of Cannabis (2017)
thenVsNow.significance: Herer was arguing from historical evidence for medical utility that he could not prove by RCT because scheduling prevented trials. The trials that became possible after state legalization have confirmed several of his specific claims.

thenVsNow.title: The Entity Research Program: From Anecdote to Survey Science
thenVsNow.thenClaim: McKenna described machine elves as a consistent phenomenon of DMT experience, encountered across thousands of independent reports he had collected through lectures and correspondence. He had no systematic data, only his own experience and what audiences told him. His claim was phenomenological: something consistent is happening.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: The 2020 Johns Hopkins online survey (Davis et al., J. Psychopharmacol. 34(9):1008-1020) collected reports from 2,561 people who had already had an entity encounter after inhaling DMT (mean age 32; 77 percent men). Because every respondent was recruited for having had an encounter, it cannot show how often encounters happen, and because it did not compare cultures, it cannot show that the reports are the same across cultures. It shows that many self-selected respondents described similar features. Most respondents said the entity was conscious, intelligent and benevolent and continued to exist after the encounter; 69 percent reported receiving a message. A 2021 Frontiers in Psychology EEG study with n=39 is often cited here for an entity-contact-specific neural signature; no such paper exists, and no published study has isolated one. Timmermann et al. (PNAS 120(13), 2023, EEG-fMRI): global functional connectivity rose sharply and network segregation broke down; the study did not isolate entity contact. Lawrence et al. (Scientific Reports, 2022) analyzed interviews with people given DMT in a laboratory study. McKenna's anecdotal observation is now a survey-documented report; it is not neurally characterized.
sources: Sexton et al., J. Psychopharmacol. 33(9) (2019) [Source not found; under review]
thenVsNow.significance: McKenna collected entity contact reports in question sessions at lectures. Johns Hopkins collected them with survey instruments and published in a peer-reviewed journal. The reports are real and similar to one another; what they reflect, and whether they have specific neural correlates, is unknown.

thenVsNow.title: Dennis McKenna's Scientific Career: What La Chorrera Built
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Terence treated Dennis as the scientific grounding of the La Chorrera expedition, the botanist who would provide the empirical anchor for the speculative cosmological work. Dennis was 19 years old at La Chorrera. Terence could not have predicted what Dennis's career would become.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: Dennis McKenna went on to: PhD in botanical sciences from UBC (1984); postdoctoral research at Stanford; co-founder of the Heffter Research Institute (1993, which funded some of the earliest Johns Hopkins psilocybin research); research scientist at Aveda and Shaman Pharmaceuticals; Senior Lecturer at the University of Minnesota; co-author of the first pharmacological description of ayahuasca's MAO inhibition mechanism (McKenna et al., 1984). His ayahuasca pharmacology papers are foundational in the field. The Heffter Institute he co-founded funded Roland Griffiths's psilocybin safety study (2001), which launched the modern research renaissance. La Chorrera sent Dennis into pharmacological botany; his career built the institutional infrastructure that produced the psychedelic research renaissance.
sources: McKenna et al., Journal of Ethnopharmacology (1984), ayahuasca MAO mechanism
thenVsNow.significance: Terence generated the ideas; Dennis built the institutions that tested them. The 1971 La Chorrera expedition produced two careers: one that reached millions through rhetoric, one that changed research through science. Dennis's career may have had more lasting impact.

thenVsNow.title: The Endogenous DMT Confirmation: Is the Spirit Molecule Really There?
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Strassman's hypothesis, that the pineal gland produces elevated DMT at key life transitions, was circulating in the psychedelic community before True Hallucinations was published. McKenna was aware of it and incorporated it into his worldview. Both McKenna and Strassman believed that endogenous DMT was a key to consciousness, dreaming, and near-death experience.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: Barker, McIlhenny and Strassman (Drug Testing and Analysis, 2012): reviewed reports of DMT in human blood, urine and cerebrospinal fluid, with inconsistent methods across studies. The enzymes for DMT synthesis (INMT, AADC) are present in the brain, lung, and other tissues. Dean et al. (Scientific Reports, 2019): measured DMT in rat brain and found levels in the visual cortex rose after experimental cardiac arrest; this is a rat finding and does not test the near-death experience hypothesis in people. The pineal gland-specific hypothesis: the pineal has the enzymatic machinery but no study has demonstrated that it produces elevated DMT at near-death, during sleep, or at birth in concentrations sufficient for psychedelic effect. Endogenous DMT exists. Its biological role remains unclear. Strassman's specific pineal-at-key-moments hypothesis is unconfirmed.
sources: Barker, McIlhenny & Strassman, Drug Testing and Analysis (2012)
thenVsNow.significance: The molecule is real. The role Strassman and McKenna attributed to it, produced by the pineal at key life transitions, is not confirmed. Endogenous DMT exists in the brain; what it does there is still unknown.

thenVsNow.title: Psychedelic Science After McKenna: Does the Field Engage His Questions?
thenVsNow.thenClaim: McKenna died in 2000, before the research renaissance. His questions, about entity contact, plant consciousness, the combinatorial problem, were outside the scope of mainstream research in his lifetime. True Hallucinations ended with the 1971 experience; the research program that would address his questions was decades away.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: The Psychedelic Science 2023 conference (Denver, 12,000+ attendees) included dedicated symposia on: DMT entity contact (multiple papers, including Timmermann 2023); plant consciousness and ayahuasca pharmacology; the Stoned Ape hypothesis revisited; the combinatorial problem in ethnobotany. McKenna's specific questions are now research programs. The Johns Hopkins Center for Psychedelic and Consciousness Research explicitly includes 'plant-human relationships' and 'entity contact phenomenology' in its research agenda. The combinatorial problem remains open but is being engaged by ethnopharmacologists with modern analytical tools. The questions McKenna died asking are being asked in peer-reviewed journals in 2026.
sources: Johns Hopkins Center for Psychedelic Research agenda
thenVsNow.significance: McKenna's questions were fringe in his lifetime. In 2026, they are conference symposia and peer-reviewed research programs. He would be astonished. He would also have opinions about how they're being approached.

thenVsNow.title: The Rhetorical Legacy: What McKenna's Voice Did to the Movement
thenVsNow.thenClaim: McKenna's primary medium was the spoken lecture, he gave hundreds of talks from the mid-1980s until his death. The recordings, widely circulated on the early internet and then on streaming platforms, have been heard by tens of millions of people. His rhetorical style, confident, witty, encyclopedic, willing to say outrageous things, was unlike any other psychedelic advocate.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: McKenna's lecture recordings are among the most-streamed psychedelic content on YouTube and podcast platforms, millions of plays on individual lectures decades after his death. The Joe Rogan-McKenna connection (Rogan has cited McKenna as a primary influence) routes McKenna's ideas through the largest podcast audience in English-language media. Graham Hancock, Duncan Trussell, Paul Stamets, and others in the popular psychedelic space credit McKenna as foundational. The stoned ape hypothesis, the machine elves, the archaic revival, the dominator culture, these enter mainstream discourse through McKenna's rhetorical construction, amplified through podcast culture. The scientific community's engagement with these ideas is partly a response to how widely McKenna's framing has spread.
sources: Joe Rogan Experience, McKenna retrospective episodes
Psychedelic media landscape survey, Chacruna Institute (2023)
thenVsNow.significance: McKenna died in 2000. His voice is more widely heard in 2026 than it was when he was alive. No other psychedelic thinker has had comparable posthumous reach.

thenVsNow.title: Mycorrhizal Networks: What Has and Has Not Been Shown
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Narby's methodological argument, that Western science underestimated plant intelligence by assuming passivity rather than investigating it, was his most important contribution. He had no empirical proof of forest-scale communication; he was calling for investigation.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: Simard et al. (Nature, 1997) reported net carbon transfer between tree species through shared mycorrhizal fungi, and Simard's book Finding the Mother Tree (2021) popularized the idea that 'mother trees' recognize and support their offspring. A 2023 review by Karst et al. (Nature Ecology & Evolution) found that field evidence for resource sharing and kin support through such networks is weaker than often claimed, with positive citation bias in the literature. Gagliano's Mimosa study (Oecologia, 2014) reported habituation-like learning in plants; her 2016 associative learning study in pea seedlings (Scientific Reports) was not reproduced in a 2020 replication attempt (Markel, eLife). Plant signaling is an active research field. Narby's specific biophoton hypothesis is untested. His methodological call, to investigate plant behavior rather than assume passivity, has been taken up, but the stronger claims of forest 'intelligence' are contested.
sources: Plant Signaling & Behavior journal, 2006-2026 [Source not found; under review]
Karst et al., Nature Ecology & Evolution (2023)
thenVsNow.significance: Narby said: stop assuming plants are passive and investigate. Science has investigated and found active plant signaling, while the strongest claims about forest networks remain disputed.

thenVsNow.title: The UNDRIP Framework: Indigenous Knowledge Rights in International Law
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Narby argued that indigenous pharmacological knowledge was intellectual property that could not be appropriated without consent and benefit-sharing. This was a moral argument in 1998, grounded in examples of biopiracy (the ayahuasca patent case). There was no international legal framework that enforced it.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: UNDRIP (United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, 2007): Articles 11 and 31 affirm indigenous peoples' rights to their cultural heritage, traditional knowledge, and cultural expressions. The Nagoya Protocol (2010, entered into force 2014): requires prior informed consent from indigenous and local communities before accessing biological resources and associated traditional knowledge; mandates benefit-sharing agreements. 143 parties as of 2026. Enforcement: uneven. The psychedelic pharmaceutical industry largely does not comply with Nagoya's spirit: no company developing psilocybin, MDMA, ibogaine, or ayahuasca derivatives has publicly documented PIC from the indigenous communities whose knowledge pointed toward these compounds. The framework exists; it is not enforced in the domain Narby cared most about.
sources: Chacruna Institute, Indigenous reciprocity in psychedelic research (2024)
thenVsNow.significance: The legal framework Narby's argument called for exists. It is not being applied in the psychedelic pharmaceutical sector. The gap between the framework's existence and its enforcement is where the injustice persists.

thenVsNow.title: Ayahuasca Clinical Trials: The Medicine Narby Described Is Now FDA-Tracked
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Narby's account of ayahuasca's healing properties, anti-parasitic, antidepressant, addiction treatment, trauma resolution, was based on ethnographic observation and early naturalistic studies. No RCTs existed in 1998.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: Palhano-Fontes et al. (Psychological Medicine, 2019): first RCT of ayahuasca for depression, n=29, significant reduction in MADRS score at Day 7 (p<0.001). Dos Santos et al. (Therapeutic Advances in Psychopharmacology, 2016): systematic review of ayahuasca, psilocybin and LSD studies, promising but mostly small studies. Hamill et al. (Current Neuropharmacology, 2019): narrative review, positive but preliminary findings. The specific anti-parasitic properties of plants in the ayahuasca brew: Callaway & Grob (Journal of Ethnopharmacology, 1998) documented anti-helminthic activity. Investigational new drug applications for ayahuasca are reported as of 2026 (Source not found; under review). The medicine Narby documented in 1998 has a Phase 2 RCT, multiple systematic reviews, and an IND pathway.
thenVsNow.significance: Narby documented the medicine ethnographically in 1998. It is in clinical trials with the FDA in 2026. The path from ethnography to Phase 2 took 21 years.

thenVsNow.title: The Decolonization of Psychedelic Research: Narby's Framework Applied
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Narby's central argument was that Western science appropriated indigenous knowledge without acknowledgment, credit, or benefit-sharing. He was describing a historical pattern. He did not predict a political movement that would organize around this critique.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: The 'decolonization of psychedelics' discourse has become a significant force in the psychedelic research community since approximately 2018. Key organizations: Chacruna Institute for Psychedelic Plant Medicines (Beatriz Caiuby Labate, founded 2017) explicitly addresses indigenous reciprocity; Zendo Project incorporates indigenous ceremony acknowledgment into its harm reduction model; MAPS's Indigenous Reciprocity Initiative acknowledges that MDMA-AT builds on knowledge traditions using MDMA-like plant compounds. Psychedelic Science 2023 included multiple panels on decolonization, indigenous rights, and benefit-sharing. Several major research papers now include acknowledgment of indigenous knowledge origins. No major pharmaceutical company has implemented a Nagoya-compliant benefit-sharing agreement for psychedelic compounds. The discourse has reached the center of the field; implementation lags significantly.
thenVsNow.significance: The discourse Narby's work initiated is now central to psychedelic research ethics. The practice, benefit-sharing, PIC, acknowledgment, lags the discourse. The emperor of decolonization also has some clothes still missing.

thenVsNow.title: The DNA Biophoton Hypothesis: Has Anyone Tested It?
thenVsNow.thenClaim: Narby proposed a specific mechanism: DNA biophoton emissions, amplified by DMT's enhancement of visual processing, provide the information channel through which shamans access molecular-level pharmacological knowledge. This is the testable core of the hypothesis.
thenVsNow.nowAssessment: As of June 2026, no published study has directly tested the biophoton-DMT mechanism Narby proposed. Biophoton research has continued: Popp's group proposed DNA as a source of ultra-weak photon emission (Cell Biophysics, 1984), an idea that remains debated; a cited 2004 PNAS paper proposing biophotons as a neural signaling mechanism (attributed to 'Thar & Bhm') could not be found (Source not found; under review). But no experiment has attempted to determine whether: (1) DMT increases sensitivity to biophoton signals; (2) the information content of DNA biophoton emissions could include pharmacological information; (3) the visual experiences of ayahuasca are related to biophoton detection. The proposed mechanism is experimentally accessible, it could be tested with current technology. It has not been.
