previewPack.text:
MODULE 3 PREVIEW PACK, The Science of the Experience
For NotebookLM: generate a 12-15 minute preview podcast.
Format: Two hosts set up the epistemological situation, people described these experiences before science had the tools to measure them. Now science has the tools. Does the map match the territory?

---

THE EPISTEMOLOGICAL SITUATION

Aldous Huxley described what happens to perception under mescaline in 1954 using philosophical vocabulary: the reducing valve, the Mind at Large, the direct perception of Is-ness. He had no fMRI scanner, no way to image what was happening in his brain, no knowledge of the serotonin system.

Albert Hofmann described what happens in an LSD session in 1979 using the vocabulary of a precise chemist who also happened to believe in the sacred: the luminous quality of childhood perception restored, the sacred ground of being made accessible, the mystical experience as the mechanism of therapeutic benefit.

Terence McKenna described the DMT entities in 1993 using every metaphor available to a man who had read everything: merry elfin, self-transforming, machine creatures. He reported what he saw. He did not claim to know what it meant.

None of them had the tools to measure what they were describing.

Now we do.

WHAT THE TOOLS HAVE FOUND

The REBUS model (Carhart-Harris & Friston, 2019): a computational account of what Huxley called the reducing valve. The brain operates as a hierarchical prediction machine. Psychedelics reduce the precision of top-down predictions. More bottom-up sensory information reaches awareness. The valve opens.

The MEQ30 (Mystical Experience Questionnaire): a validated scale measuring what Hofmann called the sacred experience. Six dimensions: unity, noetic quality, sacredness, positive affect, transcendence of time/space, ineffability. MEQ30 score predicts therapeutic outcomes better than drug dose alone.

The DMT entity research: a 2020 Johns Hopkins survey (Davis et al., J. Psychopharmacol. 34(9):1008-1020) recorded 2,561 detailed accounts from people who had had a DMT entity encounter. A 2023 Imperial College EEG-fMRI study (Timmermann et al., PNAS 120(13)) mapped DMT's global brain effects but did not isolate entity contact. The phenomenological report is established. The explanation is not.

THREE THINGS TO WATCH FOR

1. The difference between confirming a mechanism and confirming an explanation. REBUS confirms the mechanism Huxley described. It does not confirm that what floods in when the valve opens is "Mind at Large" in the sense he meant.

2. The MEQ30 is measuring something. The question of what it's measuring, a quality of brain state, or a quality of genuine encounter with something outside the brain, is not settled by the scale.

3. The entity contact data presents the hardest case. The consistency of the report across thousands of independent observers, combined with distinct neural signatures, is not adequately explained by "hallucination" in the dismissive sense. Something consistent is happening. What it is remains open.

MODULE 3 EVIDENCE PACK, The Studies in Detail
For NotebookLM: generate a 18-20 minute evidence-focused episode.
Format: Two hosts work through specific studies. Precise about what each found and what it did not find. Appropriate uncertainty markers throughout.

---

THE NEUROPLASTICITY FINDINGS

Shao et al. (Yale, Neuron, 2021): single psilocybin dose produces rapid and persistent growth of dendritic spines in the medial frontal cortex of mice. The dendritic spine growth was detectable at least one month after a single administration. This is structural neuroplasticity, physical changes in the brain's wiring, from a single experience.

A paper published online in December 2025 (Jiang et al., Cell, 2026) extended this finding in mice: psilocybin triggers activity-dependent rewiring of large-scale cortical networks.

Zhao et al. (2024, Journal of Psychopharmacology): psilocybin promotes neuroplasticity and induces rapid and sustained antidepressant-like effects in mice via activation of the BDNF-mTOR signaling pathway. The BDNF-mTOR pathway promotes dendritic spine growth and synaptogenesis. This is the proposed molecular mechanism linking the psychedelic experience to its lasting antidepressant effects.

A 2025 Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience review confirmed: single oral dose of psilocybin increases dendritic spine density and complexity in both hippocampus and frontal cortex, with effects detectable a week later.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR McKENNA'S STONED APE

The neuroplasticity mechanism McKenna proposed is real. Psilocybin does produce lasting changes in neural architecture from single administrations. This is exactly the kind of change that could, in principle, produce cognitive enhancement over time.

What is not established: any archaeological evidence of psilocybin use by early hominids at the required scale. The specific three-stage dose-response mechanism McKenna described. Any causal chain from mushroom consumption to the cognitive changes he attributed to it.

The honest assessment: the mechanism exists; the specific evolutionary claim is unsupported.

THE ENTITY CONTACT NEUROSCIENCE

Timmermann et al. (Imperial College London, PNAS 120(13), 2023): simultaneous EEG-fMRI during IV DMT found large increases in global functional connectivity and a breakdown of network segregation across the cortex. The study did not isolate entity contact, and no published imaging study yet has. What it did report is global: sharply increased global functional connectivity and a breakdown of network segregation across the whole cortex. It did not separate entity contact from the rest of the experience.

This study does not show whether entity contact has its own neural signature. That question is open.

The interpretation is not settled. The consistent options: entity contact is a product of the brain's pattern-recognition systems applied to an unusually rich and undifferentiated signal. Or: entity contact is the brain's accessing a perceptual register that ordinary consciousness suppresses. The fMRI data is consistent with both interpretations.

THE PHASE 3 CLINICAL DATA

The first (June 2025) and second (February 2026) Phase 3 trials: both met primary endpoints for psilocybin in treatment-resistant depression. A single high dose versus placebo: mean treatment difference -3.6 to -3.8 MADRS points, p<0.001 at Week 6. 25% of high-dose participants showed clinically meaningful response lasting through 26 weeks from one or two doses.

The EPISODE trial (JAMA Psychiatry, May 2026): Phase 2b triple-blind trial at two German university hospitals. High-dose psilocybin showed significantly higher treatment response than active placebo at six weeks. First European Phase 2b psychedelic trial with this level of methodological rigor.

NDA submission for synthetic psilocybin psilocybin targeted Q4 2026. Potential FDA approval decision late 2026 or early 2027.

THE OPEN QUESTIONS

What is the relationship between acute neural changes (the session itself) and lasting structural changes (the dendritic spine growth)?

Why does mystical experience quality predict therapeutic outcomes? Is the mystical experience itself the therapeutic mechanism, or is it a marker for a different underlying process?

What are the DMT entities? Similar reports are documented in self-selected surveys. No neural correlate specific to entity contact has been identified. The ontological question, are they products of the brain or perceptions of something beyond it, is not answerable by current methods.

previewPack.text:
MODULE 4 PREVIEW PACK, The Ancient Question
For NotebookLM: generate a 12-15 minute preview podcast.
Format: Two hosts introduce the Eleusinian Mysteries, the 1978 hypothesis, and the 2019-2026 developments. Narrative, accessible, building toward the central question.

---

THE INSTITUTION

The Eleusinian Mysteries were the most revered religious institution of classical antiquity. They operated continuously for approximately a thousand years, from the pre-Archaic period of Greek religion to their suppression by Emperor Theodosius in 392 CE.

The institution was open to all Greek-speaking people: men, women, slaves, and foreigners could be initiated. The only requirement was that they had committed no murder and could speak Greek. Participation required a multi-day ritual sequence that culminated in an overnight ceremony in the Telesterion, the Hall of Initiation, at the sanctuary of Demeter in Eleusis, approximately 30 kilometers from Athens.

What happened in the Telesterion was protected by the most serious oath in the ancient world: to reveal the contents of the ceremony was punishable by death. The oath held for two thousand years. No initiate ever described what happened.

THE TESTIMONIES

But initiates kept describing what it felt like.

Pindar (5th century BCE): "Blessed is he who has seen these rites before he goes beneath the hollow earth; for he understands the end of mortal life, and the beginning of a new life given of God."

Sophocles (5th century BCE): "Thrice blessed are those mortals who have seen these rites and thus enter into Hades; for them alone there is life, while all others have misery."

Cicero (1st century BCE): "Among the many exceptional and divine things your Athens has produced, nothing is better than those mysteries. For by their means we have been brought out of our barbarous and savage mode of life and educated and refined to a state of civilization."

The vocabulary across five centuries is consistent: seen, not thought; understood from experience, not from argument; a transformation in the understanding of death that was direct and irreversible.

THE HYPOTHESIS

In 1978, R. Gordon Wasson (banker and amateur mycologist), Albert Hofmann (chemist, discoverer of LSD), and Carl Ruck (classical scholar at Boston University) published "The Road to Eleusis."

Their hypothesis: the kykeon, the ritual drink prepared from barley, water, and pennyroyal that initiates received before entering the Telesterion, contained ergot alkaloids. Claviceps purpurea, the ergot fungus endemic to ancient barley fields, produces alkaloids that are structurally related to LSD. Hofmann demonstrated that water-soluble ergot alkaloids could be extracted from ergot through cold-water preparation. These alkaloids are psychoactive. The Eleusinian experience, in the hypothesis, was not produced by theater and suggestion. It was produced by chemistry.

THE 2026 STATUS

In 2019-2020, bioarchaeologist Jordi Juan-Tresserras analyzed material from Mas Castellar de Pontós, an ancient Catalan site associated with the Demeter cult. In dental calculus from a woman buried at the site (3rd-2nd century BCE), he found apparent ergot alkaloids. In a sealed ritual vessel, ergot spores and residues were found in association with beer-making equipment.

In February 2026, Antonopoulos and colleagues at the National Kapodistrian University of Athens published in Scientific Reports demonstrating experimentally that lye, available in antiquity as wood ash solution, converts toxic ergotamine and ergotoxine alkaloids into water-soluble lysergic acid amide derivatives at doses achievable through ancient preparation methods.

The hypothesis has moved from speculative to experimentally feasible and archaeologically evidenced at an affiliated cult site. Direct confirmation at Eleusis itself, ergot residue in the Telesterion, has not yet been found but is now being actively sought.

THREE THINGS TO WATCH FOR

1. The distinction between "vision" and "insight" in the ancient testimonies. Cicero says the Mysteries taught him about life and death. Did he mean he received information? Or had an experience? The answer matters for the pharmacological hypothesis.

2. The 392 CE suppression. Theodosius did not suppress a dying institution. The Mysteries were thriving when they were abolished. Why was a thriving institution abolished? The hypothesis has an answer.

3. The philosophical implication. If the Mysteries were pharmacological, and Plato was an initiate, what is the experiential source of the theory of Forms?

evidencePack.text:
MODULE 4 EVIDENCE PACK, The Archaeological and Chemical Record
For NotebookLM: generate a 15-18 minute evidence-focused episode.
Format: Two hosts work through the specific evidence in detail, the chemistry, the Catalonia findings, the Eleusis site status, and the scholarly reception.

---

THE CHEMISTRY

Ergot (Claviceps purpurea) is a fungus that parasitizes rye, barley, and other grains. It produces a family of alkaloids called ergot alkaloids. The most dangerous, ergotamine, ergotoxine, cause ergotism, the syndrome that produced the Dancing Plague of 1374 and numerous medieval European epidemics.

But ergot also produces water-soluble alkaloids including ergonovine, ergine (lysergic acid amide, or LSA), and other derivatives. These are structurally related to LSD and are psychoactive at doses achievable without laboratory extraction.

Hofmann's 1978 contribution: he demonstrated that cold-water preparation of ergot-contaminated grain produces water-soluble fractions containing these psychoactive alkaloids. The preparation the ancients would have used for the kykeon, water, barley, pennyroyal, could extract these compounds without any chemical sophistication.

The Antonopoulos-Dadiotis 2026 finding: experimentally demonstrates that lye (wood ash solution, available throughout antiquity) converts the toxic ergopeptides into water-soluble psychoactive forms. This addresses part of the toxicity objection, that ergot in the kykeon would have caused ergotism. The laboratory chemistry is feasible; whether anyone in antiquity actually prepared ergot this way is not shown.

THE CATALONIA EVIDENCE

Mas Castellar de Pontós is an ancient settlement in Catalonia that shows evidence of Eleusinian cult activity from the 3rd-2nd centuries BCE. The site is relevant because it represents the Demeter cult at its western Mediterranean extent, the same ritual tradition as Eleusis, 2,000 kilometers away.

Juan-Tresserras's 2019-2020 analysis found:

In dental calculus from a woman buried at the site (dated to the 3rd-2nd century BCE): apparent ergot alkaloids alongside phytoplankton associated with cereal cultivation.

In a sealed ritual vessel: ergot spores and residues in direct association with beer-making equipment.

This is the first physical evidence of ergot use at a site associated with the Eleusinian Demeter cult. It does not prove that the Eleusis sanctuary used ergot, but it demonstrates that the Demeter cult, at this site, used grain-based preparations that incorporated ergot.

THE ELEUSIS SITE

The sanctuary at Eleusis, the location of the Telesterion, is a protected UNESCO-monitored archaeological zone. The Hellenic Ministry of Culture began a major excavation program in 2015. As of June 2026, chemical residue analysis of vessels from the Telesterion has not been completed. The 2026 Scientific Reports paper explicitly calls for this analysis and notes that the methods required are minimally destructive for chemical sampling.

Eleusis was designated a European Capital of Culture in 2023. This designation brought international attention and EU funding that has created more favorable conditions for innovative research at the site.

THE SCHOLARLY RECEPTION

The Road to Eleusis was received with hostility by classical scholars in 1978. Walter Burkert, the most eminent scholar of ancient Greek religion, argued in Ancient Mystery Cults (1987) that theatrical performance, psychological suggestion, and the powerful ritual context were sufficient to produce the described experiences without pharmacology.

The Burkert objection is the leading alternative: the Mysteries worked through theater and suggestion, not chemistry.

The response: the ancient testimonies consistently use the vocabulary of individual direct visual experience, not collective emotional response to performance. "Vision" language appears consistently across five centuries of independent accounts. Theater produces shared emotional response; it does not reliably produce individual visionary experience of the type consistently described.

Brian Muraresku's "The Immortality Key" (2020) brought the hypothesis to a wide audience and extended it to early Christianity. The scholarly debate has not been settled, but the evidentiary landscape in 2026 is substantially different from 1978.

previewPack.text:
MODULE 5 PREVIEW PACK, The Suppression
For NotebookLM: generate a 12-15 minute preview podcast.
Format: Two hosts tell the story of the collision, the clinical tradition, the counterculture, the CIA, the scheduling. Narrative, not lecture.

---

THE CLINICAL PROGRAM

From 1947, when the manufacturer first distributed LSD under a trade name, to the Controlled Substances Act of 1970, the psychedelic research program produced:

Over 1,000 published scientific papers
Approximately 40,000 patients treated with LSD-assisted therapy
Clinical programs at institutions in the US, UK, Canada, and Europe
Documented success rates in alcoholism treatment (Hoffer-Osmond at Weyburn: ~50% lasting sobriety), end-of-life anxiety, neurotic disorders, and treatment-resistant depression

The program was not fringe science. It operated at respected psychiatric institutions. It published in peer-reviewed journals. It held international conferences. By 1965, it was approaching the stage at which regulatory submissions might have become possible.

THE THREE FORCES THAT DESTROYED IT

Force 1: The CIA. Operation MK-Ultra (1953-1973) used LSD as a potential tool for interrogation and behavioral control. The CIA purchased the world's entire LSD supply from the manufacturer in 1953. It dosed unwitting subjects in safe houses. It produced no useful intelligence. It produced at least one death (Frank Olson, 1953). The program, when revealed by the Church Committee in 1975, permanently tainted LSD's public image.

Force 2: Timothy Leary. The Harvard Psilocybin Project's early work was careful and promising. Leary's pivot to mass public advocacy..."Turn on, tune in, drop out", associated LSD with countercultural rebellion against the social order, providing the political justification for suppression.

Force 3: The Nixon Administration. John Ehrlichman, Nixon's domestic policy adviser, stated in a 1994 interview (published Harper's, 2016): "We knew we couldn't make it illegal to be either against the war or black, but by getting the public to associate the hippies with marijuana and blacks with heroin, and then criminalizing both heavily, we could disrupt those communities." The account rests on Baum's notes alone, and Ehrlichman's family and several former Nixon aides dispute it. The drug war was explicitly a tool of political suppression.

October 6, 1968: The Staggers-Dodd Act made LSD possession a federal misdemeanor. The research stopped.

THE RESUMPTION

The research resumed approximately fifty years later. Johns Hopkins' 2016 psilocybin study for end-of-life anxiety. NYU's 2016 psilocybin study for alcohol use disorder. Industry Phase 3 trials for psilocybin in treatment-resistant depression, reporting in 2025 and 2026.

The research program that was interrupted in 1968 is currently approaching regulatory approval, fifty-five years after it was stopped.

THREE THINGS TO WATCH FOR

1. The distinction between the research being stopped because it failed versus being stopped because it was politically inconvenient. These are different events with different implications.

2. The Leary question. Stevens is careful not to make Leary a simple villain. What is the right framing of his role?

3. The FDA's August 2024 rejection of MDMA-assisted therapy. The Phase 3 efficacy data was significant. The rejection was on methodological grounds. Is this the same pattern as 1968, or a different situation?

MODULE 5 EVIDENCE PACK, The Clinical Record Then and Now
For NotebookLM: generate a 15-18 minute evidence episode.
Format: Two hosts compare the pre-prohibition clinical evidence with the post-resumption clinical evidence. What do we now know that was known in 1968? What is genuinely new?

---

WHAT THE 1947-1968 PROGRAM SHOWED

Alcoholism (Hoffer, Osmond and colleagues, Saskatchewan, 1950s):
uncontrolled reports that roughly half of treated patients improved or stopped drinking. A 2012 meta-analysis by Krebs and Johansen of six randomized controlled trials from the 1960s-70s found a statistically significant positive effect on alcohol misuse, with effects lasting 6-12 months. The result was real.

End-of-life anxiety (Pahnke, Maryland Psychiatric Research Center, 1960s):
LSD-assisted therapy significantly reduced death anxiety in terminal cancer patients. The mechanism identified: mystical experience quality correlated with anxiety reduction.

The clinical principle established: the quality of the experience, whether it reaches the threshold of genuine transformative encounter, predicts the therapeutic outcome more than drug dose alone.

WHAT THE RESUMPTION CONFIRMED

The Griffiths 2016 Johns Hopkins study: psilocybin for end-of-life anxiety in cancer patients. 80% showed clinically significant improvement at 6 months from a single session. The effect size was the largest reported in any psychological treatment study for this indication.

The 2022 Bogenschutz NYU RCT: psilocybin for alcohol use disorder. Significantly better outcomes than placebo, consistent with the Hoffer-Osmond result reproduced 60 years later with better methodology and a different compound.

The first (June 2025) and second (February 2026) Phase 3 trials: psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression. Both met primary endpoints. -3.6 to -3.8 MADRS points at Week 6, p<0.001. 25% of high-dose participants showed clinically meaningful response through 26 weeks.

THE MDMA SITUATION

The sponsor (formerly MAPS Public Benefit Corporation) submitted an NDA for MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD in 2024. The FDA advisory committee voted 10-1 against approval in June 2024. The FDA issued a Complete Response Letter in August 2024 declining to approve.

The Phase 3 data: 67-71% of PTSD patients who received MDMA-assisted therapy no longer met diagnostic criteria at follow-up, versus approximately 32% in the placebo arm.

The FDA's concerns: the trials could not adequately blind participants to whether they received active MDMA or placebo; therapist expectancy bias was not adequately controlled; adverse events (cardiac, hypertensive) were inadequately characterized.

The FDA requested an additional Phase 3 trial with improved design.

This is not the same as 1968. The 1968 scheduling was not a regulatory rejection of a specific trial, it was a political prohibition of the entire research program. The 2024 MDMA rejection is a methodological critique of a specific trial. Whether the methodological critique is legitimate or uses methodological concerns as cover for regulatory caution is debated.

THE WHO CRITICAL REVIEWS

WHO ECDD Critical Review of LSD (2019) [Source not found; under review]: found no evidence supporting LSD's current international scheduling level. No recommendation was implemented.

WHO ECDD Critical Review of Cannabis (2019): recommended rescheduling. The US DOJ proposed rescheduling from Schedule I to Schedule III in May 2024. The process remains incomplete as of June 2026.

The pattern: scientific review bodies find the scheduling scientifically unjustified. The political process of changing it proceeds slowly, partially, and incompletely.

MODULE 6 PREVIEW PACK, The Cultural Reckoning
For NotebookLM: generate a 12-15 minute preview podcast.
Format: Two hosts hold the McKenna problem honestly, neither hagiography nor dismissal. What did he get right? What did he get wrong? Why does the distinction matter?

---

THE McKENNA PROBLEM

Terence McKenna (1946-2000) is the most famous psychedelic thinker of the late 20th century. He was a voluble, brilliant, entertaining lecturer whose audio recordings have circulated in psychedelic communities for decades. He coined or popularized "Archaic Revival," "dominator culture," "stoned ape." He described the machine elves. He built the Timewave Zero theory.

He was also frequently wrong in specific ways that illuminate something important about the difference between visionary thinking and accurate thinking.

THE TIMEWAVE: WRONG, CLEARLY

Timewave Zero predicted that December 21, 2012 would be a singularity of maximum novelty. The prediction was falsified. McKenna had acknowledged the theory was falsifiable. The date passed without incident.

The mathematics were criticized by professional mathematicians: the derivation from the I Ching was arbitrary, and different mappings produce different results. The theory was fitted to historical data post hoc, which violates basic principles of predictive modeling.

THE MACHINE ELVES: RIGHT, SURPRISINGLY

McKenna described "merry elfin, self-transforming, machine creatures" during DMT experiences in 1965. In a 2020 Johns Hopkins survey (Davis et al., J. Psychopharmacol. 34(9):1008-1020) of 2,561 people who had already had a DMT entity encounter, respondents described the encounter in consistent detail. A 2023 Imperial College EEG-fMRI study (Timmermann et al., PNAS 120(13)) mapped DMT's global brain effects but did not isolate entity contact. Many self-selected respondents describe features similar to McKenna's; the survey cannot say how common such encounters are.

THE TELEVISION: RIGHTER THAN HE KNEW

McKenna wrote in 1992 that "television is by nature the dominator drug par excellence", producing passivity, compliance, and the substitution of mediated experience for direct experience. He wrote this about network television.

Sean Parker confirmed in 2017 that Facebook was deliberately designed to exploit psychological vulnerabilities. Jonathan Haidt's 2024 book "The Anxious Generation" documented that smartphone social media correlates with dramatic increases in adolescent depression and anxiety. The mechanism McKenna identified has been implemented with far greater precision and scale than he could have imagined.

THE STONED APE: INTERESTING QUESTION, UNSUPPORTED CLAIM

The specific stoned ape hypothesis, that psilocybin mushrooms catalyzed human cognitive evolution in East Africa, is not supported by archaeological evidence. Psilocybe cubensis is not documented in East Africa during the relevant period. The specific three-stage mechanism McKenna proposed is not verified.

The underlying question, what role did psychoactive plants play in human cognitive evolution?, is real and uninvestigated. McKenna's contribution was to ask the question in modern scientific context when asking it was not academically respectable.

THREE THINGS TO WATCH FOR

1. The difference between McKenna's epistemic performance (confident, entertaining, sometimes overstated) and his epistemic virtue (willing to hold the uncertainty, willing to report what he saw without claiming to know what it meant).

2. True Hallucinations is the honest book. Food of the Gods is the argument book. What's different about McKenna when he's reporting versus when he's persuading?

3. The cultural diagnosis in Food of the Gods, the dominator culture, the Archaic Revival, television as soma, holds up better in 2026 than the specific scientific claims. Why might cultural diagnosis be more durable than specific empirical prediction?

evidencePack.text:
MODULE 6 EVIDENCE PACK, The McKenna Ledger
For NotebookLM: generate a 15-18 minute evidence-focused episode.
Format: Two hosts go claim by claim. Confirmed, partially confirmed, falsified, or remains open? Specific evidence for each. Tone: rigorous, fair, neither hagiographic nor dismissive.

---

CLAIM: THE TIMEWAVE ZERO 2012 PREDICTION, FALSIFIED

The Timewave Zero theory predicted December 21, 2012 as a singularity. The prediction was falsified. McKenna had acknowledged it was falsifiable. No additional defense of the specific prediction is warranted.

The separable philosophical claim, that time has qualitative structure, that novelty is not uniformly distributed, is not scientific in the sense of being falsifiable by current methods, and cannot be evaluated by the same standard.

CLAIM: THE MACHINE ELVES, SIMILAR REPORTS DOCUMENTED IN A SELF-SELECTED SURVEY, EXPLANATION UNRESOLVED

Davis et al. 2020 (Johns Hopkins, J. Psychopharmacol. 34(9):1008-1020, n=2,561 people who had had a DMT entity encounter): Most common description: small, humanoid or non-humanoid, apparently intelligent, apparently communicating. Emotional tone predominantly positive. Most respondents rated encounters as among most meaningful experiences of their lives.

Timmermann et al. 2023 (Imperial College London, PNAS 120(13)) mapped DMT's global brain effects, large increases in global functional connectivity, network disintegration and desegregation, and compression of the principal cortical gradient. It did not isolate entity contact as a distinct neural signature, and no published imaging study yet has: the phenomenology is well documented, the neural specificity is not.

The survey recruited only people who had already had an encounter, so it shows similar reports, not how common they are or whether they hold across cultures. The explanation is unresolved. McKenna's epistemic position, reporting the phenomenon without claiming certainty about its ontological status, is the scientifically appropriate one.

CLAIM: TELEVISION AS DOMINATOR DRUG, SUBSTANTIALLY CORRECT, UNDERSTATED

McKenna's 1992 claims: television induces trance-like passivity; controls content uniformly; makes for spectator culture; is designed for coercion and manipulation.

2017: Sean Parker (founding president of Facebook) acknowledged in an Axios interview that Facebook was "designed to exploit a vulnerability in human psychology." The specific mechanism: variable-ratio reinforcement (slot machine psychology) applied to social validation.

2024: Jonathan Haidt's "The Anxious Generation" documented dramatic increases in adolescent depression and anxiety correlating with the adoption of smartphone-mediated social media from approximately 2012. The correlation is robust across countries and demographic groups.

The algorithmic feed is the dominator drug McKenna described, implemented with incomparably greater precision than network television allowed. His 1992 analysis was correct and understated.

CLAIM: THE STONED APE, MECHANISM REAL, SPECIFIC CLAIM UNSUPPORTED

The neuroplasticity mechanism: Shao et al. (Neuron, 2021) demonstrated that a single psilocybin dose produces rapid and persistent dendritic spine growth in the frontal cortex, detectable at least one month later. This is exactly the type of structural change that could, in principle, produce lasting cognitive changes.

The specific evolutionary claim: no archaeological evidence of psilocybin use by early hominids. Psilocybe cubensis not documented in East Africa during the relevant period. The specific three-stage dose-response mechanism is not verified.

The honest summary: the mechanism is real; the specific hypothesis is unsupported; the underlying question (what role did psychoactive plants play in human evolution?) is genuine and uninvestigated.

CLAIM: THE ARCHAIC REVIVAL, PARTIALLY OCCURRING, NOT AS DESCRIBED

McKenna described a cultural reorientation, not merely increased psychedelic use, but a genuine shift in Western civilization's relationship to plant intelligence, indigenous knowledge, and non-rational epistemologies.

What has occurred: legal psilocybin services in Oregon and Colorado. Hundreds of ayahuasca retreat centers globally. A $40 billion legal cannabis market. FDA Breakthrough Therapy designations for psilocybin and MDMA.

What has not occurred: the cultural reorientation McKenna described. The dominant mode of psychedelic engagement in 2026 is consumer wellness, psilocybin for productivity, branded microdosing protocols, $500-per-night ayahuasca retreats. These are not the Archaic Revival. They are the dominator culture consuming the medicine that was supposed to change it.

previewPack.text:
MODULE 7 PREVIEW PACK, The Politics of Plants
For NotebookLM: generate a 12-15 minute preview podcast.
Format: Two hosts trace the political economy of drug prohibition from 1914 to 2026. Who designed it, who enforced it, who benefited, and who paid.

---

THE HARRISON ACT AND ITS LINEAGE

The Harrison Narcotics Tax Act (1914) was the first US federal drug control legislation. It required registration and taxation of opium and coca product sales. On paper: a tax. In practice: the beginning of federal drug prohibition.

The Marihuana Tax Act (1937) effectively banned cannabis by imposing a tax so prohibitive as to make legal commerce impossible. Congressional testimony lasted two hours. No medical expert testified. The legislation passed without significant debate.

The Controlled Substances Act (1970) created the Schedule I-V classification system still in use. Cannabis, LSD, and heroin were placed in Schedule I. The placement was not based on comparative pharmacological assessment.

John Ehrlichman (Nixon's domestic policy adviser, Harper's Magazine, 2016): "We knew we couldn't make it illegal to be either against the war or black, but by getting the public to associate the hippies with marijuana and blacks with heroin, and then criminalizing both heavily, we could disrupt those communities." The account rests on Baum's notes alone, and Ehrlichman's family and several former Nixon aides dispute it.

This is the primary source confirmation of what Herer argued from corporate history and Hari argued from individual stories.

TWO FRAMEWORKS FOR THE SAME FAILURE

Jack Herer's framework (The Emperor Wears No Clothes, 1985): cannabis prohibition was orchestrated by specific corporate interests, DuPont's synthetic fibers, Hearst's timber paper, to eliminate industrial hemp as competition. The evidence: the timing of the Marihuana Tax Act (October 1937) relative to DuPont's nylon patent (February 1938), the Mellon-Anslinger family connection, the Popular Mechanics "New Billion-Dollar Crop" article (February 1938).

The limits: historians have found the racial panic, immigration anxiety, and moral reform movements to be independently sufficient causes. DuPont benefited from prohibition; whether it orchestrated prohibition is not conclusively proven.

Johann Hari's framework (Chasing the Scream, 2015): addiction is driven by social disconnection, trauma, and lack of meaningful purpose, not by pharmacology alone. The drug war perpetuates the conditions that drive addiction by criminalizing users rather than treating them. Portugal's 2001 decriminalization, combined with social service investment, shows an alternative.

The limits: the fentanyl crisis (107,500 deaths in 2023) shows that even socially connected people die from contaminated supply. The connection model is real but overstated. Decriminalization without social investment does not work, as Oregon's Measure 110 repeal in 2024 demonstrated.

THE CURRENT MOMENT

DOJ proposed cannabis rescheduling from Schedule I to Schedule III (May 2024). As of June 2026, the rescheduling is not complete.

Oregon's psilocybin services program (Measure 109) is operational, with 100+ licensed service centers. Oregon's drug decriminalization (Measure 110) was repealed in 2024 due to implementation failures.

Colorado's Proposition 122 combined regulated healing center access with personal decriminalization of psilocybin, ibogaine, DMT, and mescaline (excluding peyote).

Texas signed $50 million in ibogaine research funding for veterans (2025). Mississippi's ibogaine research bill was signed March 2026.

THREE THINGS TO WATCH FOR

1. The difference between Herer's conspiracy framing (DuPont orchestrated prohibition) and the more defensible claim (prohibition served corporate interests regardless of who orchestrated it). What does the distinction cost the argument?

2. The Rat Park finding and the Vietnam data, what do they actually prove about the relationship between environment and addiction? What do they not prove?

3. The equity gap. The communities most criminalized under the drug war have not received proportionate benefit from legalization. This is the unfinished argument of both books.

evidencePack.text:
MODULE 7 EVIDENCE PACK, The Policy Evidence
For NotebookLM: generate a 15-18 minute evidence-focused episode.
Format: Two hosts work through the specific policy evidence, Portugal, Oregon, fentanyl, rescheduling, harm reduction. What do we actually know?

---

THE PORTUGAL EVIDENCE

2001-2015: Portugal decriminalized personal possession of all drugs. Combined with investment in treatment, housing, and employment services, the results through 2015 were strong:
- HIV transmission among injecting drug users fell approximately 95%
- Drug-related deaths fell significantly
- Drug use among young people did not increase
- The country's drug problem shifted from prosecution to treatment

2015-2023: Austerity measures following the 2008 financial crisis cut the social service programs that had made the decriminalization effective. Drug-related deaths increased. The model deteriorated.

The lesson: decriminalization + social investment works. Decriminalization alone does not produce the Portugal results.

THE OREGON EVIDENCE

November 2020: Oregon passed Measure 110, decriminalizing personal possession of all drugs (replacing criminal penalties with health assessments and referrals).

2024: Oregon's legislature repealed Measure 110. The health assessment provisions had not been implemented, the social service infrastructure required to make referrals meaningful did not exist when the law took effect. Visible public drug use increased. Political pressure mounted.

The lesson confirms the Portugal finding: decriminalization without social investment produces political vulnerability rather than public health improvement.

THE FENTANYL CRISIS

US drug overdose deaths: approximately 52,000 in 2015 (when Hari published). Approximately 107,500 in 2023. Approximately 80% attributable to synthetic opioids, primarily fentanyl.

The mechanism: prohibition pressure on heroin supply created market incentives for synthetic opioids, more potent, more concentrated, easier to smuggle, vastly more dangerous per dose. Fentanyl is approximately 50-100 times more potent than heroin by weight.

The connection model does not adequately address the fentanyl crisis: even socially connected people die from accidentally overdosing on supply contaminated with fentanyl. The supply safety issue requires supply-side intervention (drug testing, safe supply, overdose prevention centers) not addressed by the connection model alone.

HARM REDUCTION EVIDENCE

OnPoint NYC (opened November 2021, East Harlem and Washington Heights): as of 2025, reversed over 1,200 overdoses through naloxone administration without a single on-site overdose death. Serves approximately 500 clients daily.

Naloxone OTC: FDA approved naloxone nasal spray (nasal naloxone) for over-the-counter sale in 2023. Now available without prescription in every US state.

Fentanyl test strips: legalized in most states, distributed through syringe service programs. Allow users to check supply for fentanyl contamination before use.

CANNABIS RESCHEDULING STATUS (AS OF JUNE 2026)

DOJ proposed rescheduling from Schedule I to Schedule III: May 2024.
Schedule III implications: medical use permitted by prescription; FDA pharmaceutical regulation; business tax deductions (currently blocked by IRC 280E); easier research access.
Schedule III does NOT mean: federal recreational legalization; state recreational legalization where currently illegal; automatic expungement of prior convictions.

As of June 2026, the rescheduling process has not been completed. The Trump administration executive order (December 2025) directed expedited completion. The final rule has not been published.

THE RACIAL EQUITY GAP

ACLU 2020 enforcement data: Black Americans are 3.73 times more likely to be arrested for marijuana despite similar use rates across racial groups.

Biden mass pardons (October 2022): covered approximately 6,500 federal cannabis possession convictions and approximately 2,000 DC convictions. Did not address state convictions.

Cannabis industry equity: most states with legal cannabis have passed equity licensing provisions. Implementation has been inconsistent and under-resourced. The communities most criminalized have not received proportionate benefit from legalization.

Herer's argument, that prohibition was an injustice that should be remediated with the same intentionality with which it was created, has not produced a corresponding remediation program.

previewPack.text:
MODULE 8 PREVIEW PACK, The Future Moment
For NotebookLM: generate a 15-20 minute synthesis episode.
Format: Two hosts take stock of where the field stands in 2026, what has changed, what hasn't, and what the most important open questions are for writers covering this space.

---

WHERE WE ARE IN 2026: THE CLINICAL PICTURE

Psilocybin: A psilocybin developer has completed two Phase 3 trials (the first, June 2025; the second, February 2026) for treatment-resistant depression. Both met primary endpoints. NDA submission targeted Q4 2026. Potential FDA approval: late 2026 or early 2027. Usona Institute's Phase 3 trial for major depressive disorder (not treatment-resistant) is ongoing. Australia approved psilocybin for clinical use in February 2023.

MDMA: FDA rejected the sponsor's MDMA application in August 2024 on methodological grounds (unblinding, therapist expectancy). Additional Phase 3 trial requested. Australia approved MDMA for PTSD in February 2023.

LSD: Phase 2 trials ongoing in Switzerland, Canada, UK. Holze et al. (Basel, 2023) showed antidepressant effects in Phase 2. No commercial sponsor for Phase 3 yet.

Ibogaine: Texas $50M research mandate for veterans (2025). Mississippi ibogaine research bill (March 2026). No FDA approval pathway established.

Ketamine/Esketamine: esketamine nasal spray (esketamine) is FDA-approved for treatment-resistant depression under REMS program since 2019. Hundreds of ketamine clinics operating in the US, most without FDA approval for depression indication.

WHERE WE ARE IN 2026: THE POLICY PICTURE

Oregon: Measure 109 psilocybin services program operational with 100+ licensed service centers. Measure 110 decriminalization repealed 2024. Program modified March 2026.
Colorado: Proposition 122 healing centers operational since July 2025. Personal decriminalization of psilocybin, ibogaine, DMT, mescaline in effect.
New Mexico: Medical psilocybin program operational 2025. First state to pass through legislature rather than ballot.
Texas: $50M ibogaine research for veterans. No personal use decriminalization.
Federal: Cannabis rescheduling from Schedule I to Schedule III proposed May 2024, not yet final as of June 2026.

THE OPEN QUESTIONS WORTH WRITING ABOUT

1. THE EQUITY QUESTION: Who will have access to approved psilocybin therapy? synthetic psilocybin, if approved, will cost more than SSRI antidepressants and require certified clinical settings and trained therapists. Insurance coverage is uncertain. The communities most harmed by the drug war are least likely to access the therapeutic benefits of the psychedelic renaissance. Is this outcome inevitable or preventable?

2. THE INDIGENOUS RIGHTS QUESTION: Every approved psychedelic compound is derived from or structurally related to compounds used by indigenous communities for millennia. The psychedelic patent race (one developer's crystal polymorph patents, etc.) is creating intellectual property over compounds that indigenous communities have stewarded without IP protection. The Nagoya Protocol provides partial protection. Is it enough?

3. THE METHODOLOGY QUESTION: The FDA's MDMA rejection raised legitimate methodological concerns about blinding in psychedelic trials. How do you design a rigorous clinical trial of a substance where both participants and therapists know whether active drug was administered? This is not a solved problem.

4. THE INTEGRATION QUESTION: The clinical evidence shows that mystical experience quality predicts outcomes. But the "integration" of mystical experience, incorporating it into how a person actually lives, is a separate project from having the experience. What therapeutic infrastructure exists for this, and is it adequate?

5. THE CULTURAL QUESTION: Is the current psychedelic renaissance producing the cultural reorientation that Huxley, Hofmann, McKenna, and Narby thought these substances could produce? Or is it producing a more sophisticated version of the same consumer capitalism? Who decides?

evidencePack.text:
MODULE 8 DEBATE PACK, The Most Important Question
For NotebookLM: generate a 18-22 minute debate episode.
Format: Two hosts genuinely disagree about which open question in the psychedelic field is most important for writers to engage with now. Each argues for their position with evidence. The debate should not resolve cleanly.

---

POSITION A: THE EQUITY QUESTION IS THE MOST IMPORTANT

Argument: Everything else is downstream of who has access.

The clinical evidence for psilocybin-assisted therapy is strong enough that approval is likely in 2026-2027. synthetic psilocybin, if approved, will be the first psychedelic-assisted therapy with full FDA approval. The question of who has access to this treatment will determine whether the psychedelic renaissance produces justice or the reverse.

The drug war's primary harm fell on Black and Latino communities, 3.73x disproportion in marijuana arrests for similar use rates. Oregon's cannabis industry, the cannabis industry nationally, and emerging psychedelic service industries have all failed to direct proportionate benefit to the communities most harmed by prohibition.

If psilocybin-assisted therapy becomes a treatment for depression available primarily to people with good insurance, high incomes, and access to certified clinical settings in urban areas, while the communities most targeted by the drug war cannot access it, then the psychedelic renaissance will have produced a boutique medical intervention rather than a reckoning with the injustice it was supposed to address.

This is not speculative. Oregon's Measure 109 service centers cost $300-$2,000 per session out of pocket. No insurance coverage as of 2026. The equity gap is already present.

POSITION B: THE METHODOLOGY QUESTION IS THE MOST IMPORTANT

Argument: If the clinical trials can't meet methodological standards, nothing else matters.

The FDA's August 2024 rejection of MDMA-assisted therapy was not a rejection of the science, the Phase 3 efficacy data was significant. It was a rejection of the methodology: the trials could not adequately blind participants, therapist expectancy bias was uncontrolled, adverse event characterization was inadequate.

The same methodological challenge applies to every psychedelic trial: participants who receive active drug almost always know they've received it. This is the unblinding problem, and it is not solved. If the therapeutic benefit comes partly from expectation, which the set and setting literature suggests it does, then placebo-controlled trials may be structurally unable to isolate the pharmacological effect.

This matters for everything downstream of approval: if the methodology can't meet FDA standards, there are no approvals; if there are no approvals, there's no insurance coverage; if there's no insurance coverage, the equity question is moot because only the wealthy can access unregulated services.

The solution to the unblinding problem, active placebos that mimic the phenomenological effects without the therapeutic ones, is the most important technical challenge in the field. The 2025-2026 trials have not solved it.

POSITION C (MODERATOR): NEITHER IS THE MOST IMPORTANT

What if the most important question is the one neither of you is asking?

The cultural question: is the psychedelic renaissance producing the cultural transformation that its proponents claim these substances are capable of producing? Or is it producing a sophisticated pharmaceutical and wellness industry that monetizes altered consciousness without disrupting the systems that create the conditions driving depression, addiction, and anxiety in the first place?

McKenna argued that the dominator culture would consume any medicine that threatened it. The evidence from 2026 suggests he was right. The psychedelic renaissance has produced: branded microdosing products, $500-per-night retreat centers, FDA-approved pharmaceutical analogues, Silicon Valley productivity protocols, and venture-backed biotech companies.

None of these are the Archaic Revival. All of them are the dominator culture adapting to a new market.

The most important question for writers is not who gets access to the treatment or whether the trials are methodologically sound. It's whether the treatment is being developed in a way that addresses what created the need for it, or whether it's being developed in a way that leaves the underlying conditions intact while adding a new product category.
